title: Foldboard - nested plans for people and AI on flutter_webmcp
pitch: Local-first nested board: a person drags cards in the browser, an AI agent edits the same board over WebMCP. Folds keep big plans readable. Exports to JSON, PNG, Mermaid and Markdown.
about_excerpt: Local-first nested board: a person drags cards in the browser, an AI agent edits the same board over WebMCP. Folds keep big plans readable. Exports to JSON, PNG, Mermaid and Markdown. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Foldboard: plans for people and AI agents with a bounded context The problem. Almost every planning and diagramming tool shows one big map on an infinite canvas. A person struggles to take it in at a glance, and an agent has to piece the puzzle together from screenshots and full exports. For both, that is a waste of context and focus, and it only gets worse as the plan grows. What Foldboard does. Instead of one big map, Foldboard offers folds: cards with their own inner level. A large plan is assembled from small, nested levels, and the screen always shows only the area that matters right now; everything else lives one step down. The entities are deliberately minimal: a block, a fold, an arrow, and an external card for a connection that crosses a fold boundary. So you can plan anything, from a house move to a user story in an app, and keep going deeper. You can also build a plan just to understand something, then continue from a specific card. Trace shows one path across nested levels as a single line without changing the board: you see how to get from one card to another, even when they live in different folds. That nudges both the person and the agent to break the plan into small steps. What the agent gets through WebMCP. Foldboard registers 18 tools via document.modelContext . An agent can: create a whole plan in one atomic batch and connect it to the existing one; start from a compact outline and request only the area it needs, with a depth limit, pagination, and a cap on description length. It reads what matters now, not everything; read the current level, the selection, and the user's requests attached to cards. It is enough to select a few cards and say "change this": the agent knows what you mean, with no object references and no screenshots; see the project deeper than what is on screen and take that into account. Reads never move the person's interface; navigation happens only on explicit request; write with a revision check: stale context cannot overwrite the person's newer edits, and an agent batch can be reverted with a single Undo. **How it is built. Flutter Web with no backend; boards live in the browser. Alongside it I wrote and published flutter_webmcp , a typed Dart API for registering WebMCP tools from Flutter Web without hand-written JS interop, with WebAssembly support and cancellation through AbortSignal. Try it. Open the ChatGPT App and say: "Open https://foldboard.kicknext.chatgpt.site in app browser and create a nested plan for launching a mobile app." Built With dart flutter flutter-webmcp webmcp Try it out foldboard.kicknext.chatgpt.site github.com pub.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sergei Nikitin Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Sergei Nikitin started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:37 PM EDT

title: Catchfly

about_excerpt: See what agents do with your WebMCP app. Capture production traces, run Chrome WebMCP Evals from CI, and find regressions across app, model and tool versions. Like Comment Story Updates Incidents | ChatGPT Incidents Releases Cases Inspiration I am an AI researcher and I fight with evals of my agent systems every day. When I heard about WebMCP, I thought it was a perfect fit for data analysis. I usually have a concrete question, and the road from the question to finding the data and visualising it is long. Then a deeper question appears, and I wander down a tree of questions looking for the answer. WebMCP and analytics dashboards are, in my view, a beautiful pair. What it does Catchfly is observability for WebMCP apps, built so an agent can run the investigation next to me. The @catchfly/sdk captures production traces of tool calls, while the @catchfly/cli runs Chrome WebMCP Evals in CI and uploads the report. The dashboard joins both sources per release: Incidents Releases Sessions Regression Explorer Cases The dashboard itself The dashboard itself is a WebMCP app with thirty-eight tools . I ask: "What broke in the latest releases?" The agent reads the incident overview. I ask: "Open the evidence." The view switches on my screen, attributed, with an Undo button. I ask: "Show me the production sessions that failed on this tool." The filters set themselves. I open one, the agent drafts an eval case from it, shows the draft and saves it after my approval. catchfly eval pull brings it into the repo. The tree of questions that used to take me an afternoon fits in one conversation. All of this is written in the lovely Catchfly UI . How we built it Catchfly is built as a TypeScript monorepo : React and Zustand for the dashboard API as Netlify Functions One route table shared with: a standalone server Vite middleware PostgreSQL via Supabase In the app, human clicks and agent tools call the same state actions. Every write returns the resulting state, every change has a source, the human can undo it, and the agent learns about the undo on its next call. Demo environment For the demo, I built a fictional Devpost Review Console with a real WebMCP surface so the Chrome runner has something to evaluate. I also created a deterministic synthetic world containing: 18 releases 25,000 sessions 27,000 eval attempts a deliberate latency false lead I also tested how the app worked in my previous projects using the Catchfly SDK, and everything worked perfectly. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge for me was to design the UI/UX in such a way that the application looks good and is easy to read, both for users and in the tools that support WebMCP, like ChatGPT Browser. At the same time, I’m racking my brains over WebMCP vs. security , but I haven’t come up with much yet. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m really pleased that it’s an end-to-end product . I’m posting it on Discord the day before the hackathon ends, and everyone can still use it because it works and looks cool. What we learned The most important thing: I discovered and learnt WebMCP . It’s great fun - but I wasn’t the only one to notice this, as basically everyone on Discord had a brilliant time collaborating with the agents via ChatGPT. What's next for Catchfly I would love to continue my journey with Catchfly.  What we learned 

 What's next for Personal Ledger: Fictional WebMCP Demo 

 Inspiration 

 Personal finance tools often ask for more trust than a demo should. We wanted a small ledger that demonstrates WebMCP agent actions while keeping the boundary obvious: every record is synthetic, state is session-only, and no account or external integration is needed. 

 What it does 

 Personal Ledger presents Northstar Household's fictional cash-flow summary, transaction filters, and category and budget views. Three narrowly scoped WebMCP tools let an agent read the summary, list demo transactions, or create a fictional draft entry. A person can review the draft before it is added to the in-memory session. 

 How we built it 

 The demo is a Sites/Vinext-compatible React and TypeScript app with no database, authentication, cookies, analytics, telemetry, or network connectors. It uses a small in-memory store and document.modelContext.registerTool with strict schemas. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP feels safest when tool contracts are explicit and reversible. We tested invalid inputs, state transitions, mobile layout, privacy boundaries, and tool behavior with a focused evaluation harness. 

 Challenges 

 The challenge was making the flow useful without implying real financial advice or handling real money. The final demo keeps the interface realistic enough to explore while remaining synthetic and local by design. 

 What's next 

 A production product would need authentication, durable storage, and a separate security review. Those capabilities are intentionally out of scope for this public-safe demo.

about_excerpt: Explore rich, live brand conversation data with true human + agent synergy. Browse visually as your agent deep dives, surfaces insights, and prepares reports, using the app in its own way via WebMCP. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Dating app report made by AI, entirely off the data via WebMCP Deep dive into a finding from the data about Bumble - again purely via WebMCP Agent independently picks the fastest-climbing app + its two closest rivals, writes them into the live comparison, and gives a real verdict Compare view empty, before the tool call Same view after `benchmarks_compare_in_ui` fired (with Bumble/Hinge live on screen and the tool-call log visible) The tool trail next to the rendered brief, shows the full call chain in one frame Working with the app from the ChatGPT app, just the data Working with the app from the ChatGPT app with the app visible Inspiration Affogata already analyzes & scores dozens apps and games across multiple categories, analyzing real conversational data from social and review sites that are often hard for LLMs to access. This data lives behind a login and your usual "SaaS app" UI, where business users rely on it (from our customers such as Mojang, EA, Scopely and others), or separately an agent could connect to it via MCP/API. But how do you bridge these worlds? AI working with data is magical, but people do need the visuals and exploration to get a sense for the data! When we saw what WebMCP can do, it looked like the natural evolution for human + agent collaboration. Instead of a siloed experience where humans use a UI and agents use a backend connection to look at the same data in different ways, a singular experience can offered where one truly complements the other and natural exploration and "experience" of the data can happen. What it does benchmarks.affogata.net exposes 15+ WebMCP tools, both reads and a write, directly on the live site with a 79-title portfolio of real brands. The tools include: benchmarks_get_overview , benchmarks_get_movers , benchmarks_get_title , benchmarks_get_category_analytics , benchmarks_list_titles , benchmarks_compare_titles , benchmarks_explain_methodology - reads benchmarks_compare_in_ui , benchmarks_open_title - writes that change what's rendered on the page for anyone watching, not just inside the agent's own chat An agent using nothing but these tools can diagnose why a title's score dropped, compare it against its closest rivals, put that comparison live on screen, scan the entire portfolio for the next brewing crisis, analyze the data and prepare reports, all without a single click or scrape, and with a experience where the AI working with the data actually improves what the human is seeing on screen. How we built it The benchmark scoring already existed as Affogata's own MCP schemas. We adapted the ones that map to public, read-only data into the WebMCP registration format and added one write tool ( benchmarks_compare_in_ui ) so an agent can drive the compare view live, not just describe it in chat. The site runs the tools in page JS against the browser session, so there's no separate auth or API key: An agent using ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with the WebMCP flag on gets the same tool list a logged-in human would see. Challenges we ran into Getting an agent to reliably discover and call the right tool names instead of guessing from page copy took a couple of passes; an early bug had benchmarks_compare_titles and benchmarks_compare_in_ui named inconsistently between the page text and the actual registration, which caused the agent to call a tool that didn't exist. We also hit a live-state sync issue: when a human removed a title from the compare view by hand, the agent's next tool call still answered from memory instead of re-reading the page; exactly the kind of human-and-agent-together moment WebMCP is supposed to get right, so it was worth fixing rather than working around. Finally, the schema needs to be clear to models lower on the tool-using skill rank that the user might be using if they're using Chrome, so there was some iteration on that as well. Accomplishments that we're proud of This app has real utility! It's a vision for data apps that work great for humans and agents at the very same time. To that end, we've built three end-to-end demos built entirely from tool calls, no manual data entry: a single-brand "Customer Goodwill Crisis Brief" that diagnosed a real -4.8 score collapse and generated a branded, print-ready HTML report with every number traced back to a named tool call; a portfolio-wide "War Room" that scanned all 79 titles at once, ranked them on a transparent risk index, flagged a false alarm, and surfaced an improving challenger; and an agent that independently picked out the fastest-climbing app, pulled in its two closest rivals on its own judgment, put that comparison live on screen, and gave a real analytical verdict on whether the gain was sustainable; the kind of judgment call that used to need a person opening a dozen tabs. What we learned The write side of WebMCP is what actually changes the human-agent relationship. A read-only agent is still just answering questions in a chat window. The moment benchmarks_compare_in_ui puts a comparison on screen live, two people can watch the same tab while an agent drives it; that's a genuinely different way of working together than screen-sharing a chat. It's great for a person working with the data; it's even better when a team wants to have a live discussion informed by it. What's next for Affogata Live Data Explorer Wire the demo tool set up to Affogata's live customer data (today it runs on weekly-refreshed benchmark data), and bring WebMCP support into the logged-in Affogata product itself, so any customer can point their own agent at their own data without an admin setting up API access first. title: Yolo Learn
pitch: Yolo Learn turns a website's form into a tool an agent can reuse, repairs the saved steps when the page changes, and asks for approval before the final action.
about_excerpt: Yolo Learn turns a website's form into a tool an agent can reuse, repairs the saved steps when the page changes, and asks for approval before the final action. Like Comment Story Updates Hero Heal Four Changes Page Changed Read Once Cache Hit Registered Tools Audit Page YOLO Learn YOLO Learn turns web forms into reusable tools an AI agent can call through WebMCP. It remembers the task, detects changes, and asks a person when a repair needs information the page cannot provide. I built it around a simple question: why should an agent have to work out the same form every time someone needs to use it? Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? WebMCP gives an agent a named tool with defined inputs and an action it can run. YOLO Learn uses this to turn a learned form into a tool while the agent is already using the app. In the demo, the agent reads a clinic booking form. YOLO Learn creates clinic_booking , with inputs based on the form’s fields and available choices. The agent discovers the new tool and calls it without a page reload. WebMCP is the connection between learning the form and actually using it. The saved flow is not just a description for the agent to read; it becomes something the agent can call. How does it create a better user experience? The agent can reuse a saved flow instead of starting over. The person can review the filled-in details before approving submission. When the clinic is redesigned, YOLO Learn compares the saved flow with the current version. The demo contains four changes: a renamed field, a reordered step, different button wording, and a new required insurance field. Three can be repaired automatically. The insurance field needs an answer from the person. YOLO Learn also remembers the structure of public pages. In the recording, recalling the saved W3C survey fetches zero bytes from the source page. This is a cached result, not a freshness check; a refresh is needed to look for changes. An audit view checks accessibility, task completion, and readability. Each finding explains what triggered it, and accessibility checks are distinguished from design preferences. What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? A person can teach a supported flow by demonstrating it, or ask the agent to learn the form. The agent can then use the resulting tool for later runs. They also share the repair process. The app handles changes it can understand from the page, while the person supplies missing information. A new required field becomes a specific question instead of a guessed answer. The approval step keeps the final decision with the person. The agent prepares the action; the person reviews and approves it. How did you implement WebMCP? I built YOLO Learn with React, TypeScript, and Vite, and deployed it on Vercel. The WebMCP integration registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution handler. Learned flows become additional tools at runtime, with their inputs derived from the form. Tools such as learn_site , check_flow_health , and heal_flow connect the agent to the learning and repair logic. The flow runner fills the supported form and pauses at the approval gate. Saved flows are stored in the browser, and active run state is kept per tab. Public pages are fetched through server-side endpoints using read-only requests. Remembered-page tools return stored structure by default and fetch again only when explicitly refreshed. The learning and repair logic is rule-based. It does not call a language model internally; the connected AI agent chooses and calls the exposed tools. Why this stack I needed a real website an agent can open, not a plugin. Vite, React, and TypeScript let the page register tools while you are still on it, including a tool that did not exist when the tab loaded. That is what WebMCP is for, so the app had to be a page, not a backend that mints tools somewhere else. Vercel is the host because judges get a public URL, and I can send the Origin-Agent-Cluster header WebMCP requires. Without that header, Chrome refuses registerTool and the whole demo is dead. Fetching other people’s sites has to happen on the server. A browser cannot read another origin. Those functions only GET. They never POST as you, and they refuse private addresses. If a page has no form until JavaScript runs, a headless Chrome pass is there as a fallback — still read-only. There is no model in the product. Drift and heal are ordinary code, so the same redesign heals the same way every time. Saved flows and remembered page structures stay in browser storage. When configured, the backend also stores shared audit summaries. No account. One real use case Someone books the same clinic, or files the same public form, every few weeks. Today an agent re-reads the whole page every visit, then silently fails when the site is redesigned. With this: open the clinic (or paste a public URL). The page learns the task once and registers a WebMCP tool mid-session. Next visit is a lookup — on the W3C survey in the demo, first read was about 46 KB, second read was 0 bytes. When the clinic ships v2, it does not throw the tool away. Four things changed; three it fixes from the page; it asks once for the new insurance field, then runs again. You still approve the submit. That is a person and an agent sharing one live page, with a tool the site author never wrote. Challenges, and what I did ChatGPT could see the tools and still could not call them. Every tools.call crashed on signal.aborted. Our tests followed the spec, so they all passed. ChatGPT’s bridge does not send a signal. I wrap every tool at registration so a missing signal is safe, and I added tests that call tools the way ChatGPT actually does. registerTool threw in production. WebMCP needs the page to be origin-keyed. I ship Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1. The green banner is how you know that worked. Local fetch returned the React app instead of JSON. Vite was falling through /api/fetch-page to index.html, which looks like a parse error. I wired the fetch route in dev the same way as Vercel. A public URL fetch can be turned into an attack on localhost. Every hop is checked. Fourteen SSRF cases are blocked, including cloud metadata. A snapshot from a signed-in tab could keep passwords and hidden tokens. The sanitizer now strips values, hidden fields, and textarea bodies and keeps only the shape of the form. A minted tool only works on the same origin. That is why the demo clinic lives on this site. A pasted URL is remembered read-only; We do not submit on someone else’s checkout. Current limits The clinic is fictional, and no real appointment is booked. The working booking and repair demonstration runs within the app’s own origin. Learning a public URL does not give YOLO Learn permission or access to submit forms on that website. Those tools are read-only. Audit findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee of accessibility compliance. title: Clear Dose
pitch: Transparent prescriptions. Agent-ready. Search, compare, understand, and complete simulated prescription-shopping workflows with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Transparent prescriptions. Agent-ready. Search, compare, understand, and complete simulated prescription-shopping workflows with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Cleardose main Inspiration Prescription shopping is a good example of a workflow where ordinary browser automation quickly becomes fragile. A user may need to search for a medication, identify the correct strength and form, compare fulfillment options, understand medication information, choose delivery, manage a cart, and move through checkout. An agent trying to accomplish that by visually reading a page has to continually reconstruct the application's state from text and pixels. I wanted to explore a different model: What if the website explicitly told the agent what it can do? That is what WebMCP enables. ClearDose turns the underlying actions of a prescription-shopping experience into structured tools that an agent can discover and call directly. What I built ClearDose is a local-first prescription reference and simulated commerce application. Users can: Search medications by generic or brand name Inspect structured medication information Choose exact form, strength, and quantity configurations Compare fictional pharmacy and delivery options Compare public medication reference information Create a prescription request summary Add and remove items from a cart Compare current cart savings Select delivery options Complete a simulated checkout Inspect simulated order status The same application capabilities are also exposed to WebMCP agents. For example, a user can ask: Find available sleep medications, compare the best options, add the selected option to my cart, and prepare checkout. The agent can translate that request into a sequence of structured application operations instead of visually navigating the interface. Why WebMCP ClearDose is a strong fit for WebMCP because medication and fulfillment comparisons depend on exact structured state. A meaningful comparison can depend on: medication active ingredient dosage form strength quantity fulfillment option delivery method WebMCP lets ClearDose expose those values through explicit JSON schemas rather than asking an agent to infer them from the rendered interface. ClearDose exposes tools for medication search, medication details, exact fulfillment comparison, selecting offers, cart management, delivery changes, simulated checkout, order status, medication comparison, and Drug Explorer workflows. The result is an application contract for agents instead of a collection of buttons they have to reverse-engineer. Human + Agent Collaboration One of the most important parts of the project is that there is not a separate "AI version" of the application. The normal Vue interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same underlying Pinia state and application services. If the agent adds an item to the cart, the user sees it. If the user changes the selection manually, the agent works with that new state. That allows control to move naturally between the human and the agent. The agent handles repetitive navigation and information gathering while the human remains responsible for decisions. ClearDose deliberately does not turn medication similarity into autonomous treatment recommendations. Public medication information is also kept separate from the fictional commerce layer used by the demo. How I Built It ClearDose is built with Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, browser-local storage, and WebMCP. I created a shared application action layer used by both normal UI components and WebMCP handlers. For example, the visible Add to Cart button and the add_to_cart WebMCP tool ultimately call the same underlying cart behavior. Medication information is normalized through a data layer that can work with sources including: RxNorm openFDA NADAC The application keeps public medication facts, cached data, fallback data, and fictional commerce information explicitly labeled. WebMCP tools use strict schemas, bounded results, runtime validation, state checks, and clear read/write behavior. I also built a WebMCP documentation and Agent Lab experience so the application's tool catalog, schemas, prompts, workflows, and recent tool calls can be inspected directly. Challenges I Faced One major challenge was handling a domain where two medications that look similar in a search result are not automatically interchangeable. That made exact state and provenance important throughout the application. Another challenge was keeping the WebMCP layer from becoming a second implementation of the product. I wanted the agent and the UI to share business logic instead of slowly diverging. Designing useful tool schemas was also more difficult than simply exposing JavaScript functions. Tool names, argument limits, outputs, recovery instructions, destructive actions, and context all affect how reliably an agent can use an application. What I Learned The biggest thing I learned is that making software "agent-ready" is much more than adding an AI chat box. Applications already contain useful domain operations. WebMCP provides a way to expose those operations explicitly. I also found that small composable tools work better than giant automation commands because an agent can inspect the result of each operation and decide what should happen next. What's Next ClearDose could be extended with additional verified public healthcare datasets and, where appropriate permissions and regulatory controls exist, real fulfillment integrations. More broadly, the same design applies to any complex commerce system where product configuration, provenance, comparisons, and human review matter. title: Hemloop
pitch: Demand meets supply. The loop learns and grow with every purchase. The next generation of ecommerce
about_excerpt: Demand meets supply. The loop learns and grow with every purchase. The next generation of ecommerce Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I run e-commerce and paid media for apparel retail, so I have spent years on the ad-platform side of this problem. That machinery accumulates identity, infers intent from surveillance, and optimises for the conversion. It guesses at intent the shopper could simply have stated, and it never declines a discount because the discount would break the merchant's margin floor. Promotional creative is where agents are most useful and most dangerous: a wrong percentage is a legal problem, not a bad impression. WebMCP made a different shape possible: rich page-local context, a deliberately tiny merchant-facing schema, and a human-only release. If a store does not need an identity to answer "no hoodie, size M", then do not send one, not even a hash. The name comes from a hem loop: the small functional loop sewn inside a garment. Hidden, structural, load-bearing. What it does Hemloop is a shopper closet and a merchant studio on one origin, wired with WebMCP so ChatGPT works on live page state. In under a minute: import a receipt into a private closet; the agent finds a gap such as hoodie, size M; you Approve once; the store only learns category, size, and need or want, with no name, account, hash, or wardrobe rows. The merchant agent proposes an offer inside locked margin rules, turns the same locked facts into a claim-safe promo, a human approves it, and the shopper alone can mark it Bought. The purchase sharpens the next cycle. Twenty-one tools register: nine closet tools and twelve studio tools. The product is also what is missing: there is no tool for Approve, Lock facts, or Bought. Those presses are human-only by design. Every promotional claim is checked against human-locked facts. "50% off" against a locked 25% is rejected atomically, and export refuses to exist while any claim is wrong. How we built it Registration targets document.modelContext , with a navigator.modelContext probe. Each tool has a name, description, closed input schema, optional annotations, and execute function. Every reader has readOnlyHint ; user and catalog text is fenced and marked with untrustedContentHint . The core is pure TypeScript: claim validator, composition exporter, wardrobe and fit logic, receipt parser, offer matcher, demand insight, and two WebMCP adapters. React surfaces own state and pass callbacks in, so the tool surface is testable without a browser. The demo bridge is same-origin localStorage with exact-shape re-parse on every read, enough for judges to run both sides in one browser. Production would replace it with aggregation-before-disclosure and merchant-side intake; the structural tool absences and claim validator stay. Stack: TypeScript, React 19, Vite through vinext, Cloudflare Workers, WebMCP, and a Shopify catalog snapshot as the demo connector. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was resisting the ad-platform instinct: just send an identifier, just let the agent optimise freely, just cache the shopper. Each of those would have made the build easier and erased the point. The second was that a defensive re-parse is worthless if it is weaker than the parse it backs up, and that a tool result can exceed its output budget on ordinary data long before any attacker shows up. Both had to be fixed at the storage and tool-result boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of Structural human gates: there is no lock_facts , approve_offer , or approve_next_request tool. Those acts are absent by design, not "please don't". matchOffer personalises discount depth, price, and validity inside the merchant's margin floor, and will trim or decline rather than break it. One approval releases one demand event; the shopper sees the exact payload before and after; wardrobe rows cannot ride the outbound merchant tool. What we learned Privacy that depends on asking the model nicely is not a product. Boundaries that are missing tools and exact rebuilds at the storage edge are. WebMCP is a strong fit when both sides need live page state in the person's own session, and when the outbound channel must be smaller than the local context the agent can reason over. What's next Aggregation before disclosure, so a demand cell becomes visible only after enough distinct shoppers contribute. Exportable consent receipts. Per-merchant sharing levels. Writing attributed outcomes into the merchant's own reporting rather than only displaying them on the demo page. title: HooraAI
pitch: An AI-native marketplace where agents discover human talent, prepare Tasks, and return control to humans for approval.
about_excerpt:
An AI-native marketplace where agents discover human talent, prepare Tasks, and return control to humans for approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 What brings you to Hoora right now? 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but most service marketplaces still make people fit themselves into rigid job titles, categories, search boxes, and forms. 

 HooraAI starts with a different belief: human talent is bigger than a job title. 

 Someone may know how to repair a refrigerator, creatively customize a bicycle, help reconnect someone with a first love, or have a valuable ability that does not fit any traditional professional category. 

 We wanted to explore what happens when humans simply express what they need, can do, or are curious about , while AI handles the work of understanding that intent and discovering relevant human talent. 

 Our core idea became simple: 

 The agent prepares. The human decides. 

 What it does 

 HooraAI is an AI-native marketplace for human talent . 

 Instead of asking users to choose a category, the prototype begins with natural human intent: “I need something,” “I can do something,” or “Surprise me.” 

 A customer can say something as practical as “I need to fix my fridge” or as unusual as “I need someone to help me find my first love.” A person offering talent can describe what they can actually do without first inventing a job title for themselves. Someone can even say “I love pink,” allowing Hoora to discover unexpected human talent related to that interest. 

 Hoora identifies the strongest relevant human connection as the user’s Nexus . 

 With WebMCP, an AI agent can understand the request, discover relevant talent, and prepare a structured Task. However, the Task remains a draft until the human explicitly approves it. 

 Nothing is automatically booked, assigned, charged, or started. 

 How we built it 

 We built the prototype with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP . 

 The site exposes structured WebMCP capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The prototype currently includes three agent-facing tools: understand_need , discover_talent , and prepare_task . 

 understand_need structures natural human intent. discover_talent searches the same talent-matching logic used by the human-facing experience. prepare_task creates a structured draft Task around a selected Nexus and hands it back to the webpage for human approval. 

 A key architectural decision was to reuse the same application logic for both humans and agents rather than building a separate agent-only experience. 

 The current prototype uses seeded talent profiles and lightweight rule-based matching so we could focus on demonstrating the WebMCP interaction model, agent-to-webpage handoff, and human approval boundary . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most important challenge was deciding where agent autonomy should stop . 

 Allowing an agent to understand a request or discover possible talent is relatively low risk. Allowing it to independently create a real service relationship, book someone, assign work, or initiate payment is much more consequential. 

 We therefore designed prepare_task to prepare and surface a Task without authorizing the next action. The resulting Task remains in Draft status and visibly returns control to the human. 

 Another challenge was designing talent discovery without relying on traditional categories. HooraAI is intentionally trying to discover abilities that may not correspond neatly to existing job titles, so the interaction had to begin with natural language rather than a category tree. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that WebMCP is not simply attached to the website as a technical demonstration. It meaningfully changes how an AI agent can interact with the marketplace. 

 The agent receives structured access to HooraAI's capabilities, can discover human talent, and can prepare a Task while the webpage remains the place where consequential human approval happens. 

 We are also proud of the shared architecture between the human interface and WebMCP tools. Both use the same talent-discovery logic instead of producing two disconnected experiences. 

 Finally, we introduced the concept of a Nexus : not merely a search result, but the strongest human connection Hoora identifies for a particular need, talent, interest, or moment. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that agent-native does not have to mean agent-controlled . 

 WebMCP can make a website significantly more useful to AI agents without removing humans from meaningful decisions. 

 We learned that one of the most powerful roles for an agent may be to handle the difficult work of understanding intent, discovering possibilities, organizing information, and preparing actions—then return control to the person at the moment a meaningful decision must be made. 

 That principle became the foundation of our prototype: 

 Human expresses intent → Agent understands → Agent discovers talent → Agent prepares the Task → Human approves.

A shared globe that grows from AI-chat energy. The site never stores the conversation text.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 What it is 

 Laboria is a shared globe that grows from AI-chat energy. Joy becomes grassland, work becomes factories, strain becomes mountains, everything else becomes sea. Several chats stack on one planet. The site never stores conversation text. 

 Live: https://laboria.0809android.workers.dev/ 
Code: https://github.com/0809android/laboria 
Demo: https://youtu.be/QN1E3QFB4z0 

 Why this is a good use of WebMCP 

 A website cannot read a visiting agent's chat, and it should not. Laboria needs the agent to classify unreported token energy after a normal conversation, without sending transcripts. WebMCP is the channel for that: two tools on the page, no extra backend for the chat, no confirmation prompt, no per-turn heartbeat. The page stays on the globe. 

 How the UX gets better 

 People talk to the AI as usual. They do not fill a form or paste logs. The globe is the only UI. Reports from several chats stack on one planet, so the result is visible without opening the conversation. 

 What a person and an agent can do together that was hard before 

 The person chats. The agent counts unreported tokens, splits them into four kinds, and reports only that. The site rejects keys such as text , transcript , conversation , message , prompt , and chat . Previously you either sent the transcript to a server or you had no signal at all. Here the human keeps the words; the planet only gets energy totals. 

 How document.modelContext.registerTool is implemented 

 On boot, if document.modelContext exists, the app registers two tools from createTools() via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 connect_laboria — once per session; returns thresholds and policy. 
 report_laboria_energy — one unreported segment ( checkpoint_id , reason , user_turns , token_delta , plus forest / city / wasteland / ocean ). Reused checkpoint IDs do not add energy twice. 
 

 If document.modelContext is missing, the globe still runs (local only). Judges: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . Call connect_laboria , then continue a normal chat.

title: WebMCP Catalog Bridge
pitch: A shared human + AI storefront where agents search, compare and act on live commerce data through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared human + AI storefront where agents search, compare and act on live commerce data through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most online stores were built for humans, not agents. An AI agent that wants to find a product normally has to navigate the visible interface, read DOM content, open search results, visit product pages, and then guess whether the price and stock information it saw is still authoritative. We wanted to explore a different future for the open web: the website remains useful and visible to the human, while also exposing structured capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. The goal was not to replace the storefront with an API or chatbot. The goal was to let the human and the agent share the same live storefront. What it does WebMCP Catalog Bridge turns an existing OpenCart storefront into a shared human + AI commerce interface. The storefront exposes browser-native WebMCP tools such as: Search Products Get Product Add to Cart An agent can search the live catalog using natural-language constraints such as product purpose, price range and availability. Instead of scraping the DOM, the agent receives authoritative commerce data directly from the store, including current price, stock, product links, attributes and identifiers. At the same time, the website displays a visible Shared Human + AI results panel containing the same products that were returned to the agent. The human therefore sees what the agent sees. For example, a user can ask: “Find 3 animal repellents currently in stock between 5,000 and 15,000 UAH, compare them, recommend the best one and add it to my cart.” The agent can perform the catalog search through WebMCP, retrieve additional structured information for the recommended product and, when explicitly requested by the user, add the selected product to the current shopping cart. Why WebMCP This use case is a strong fit for WebMCP because product discovery is an operation the website already understands better than a browser agent can reconstruct from the user interface. Instead of forcing the agent to imitate a human by clicking filters and parsing pages, the storefront exposes the exact operations the agent needs. The result is faster, more reliable and easier to verify. The search response also includes a trust contract describing the result as authoritative live store data, with current price and stock and no requirement for browser verification. This helps prevent unnecessary follow-up navigation after the website has already provided the final result. Shared human + agent experience A key part of the project is that WebMCP is not hidden from the human. After Search Products executes, the storefront renders the same returned products in a Shared Human + AI results panel with real images, live price, live stock and links. The agent receives a compact structured payload optimized for reasoning, while the human receives a visual presentation optimized for browsing. Both representations originate from the same underlying result. This creates a shared state between the human, the agent and the storefront. How we built it The project uses browser-native WebMCP through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The storefront registers structured tools with JSON Schema inputs and execute handlers. WebMCP calls are sent to same-origin OpenCart endpoints. The OpenCart backend: searches active products assigned to the current store understands price and stock constraints ranks products using multiple relevance signals resolves the language of the currently open storefront hydrates current OpenCart price and inventory at call time returns canonical product URLs and structured product attributes provides a compact agent payload and a separate visual presentation payload The implementation supports multilingual storefronts and binds WebMCP execution to the language currently visible to the human. The endpoints are protected with same-origin checks, request-size limits, validation and rate limiting. Write operations such as Add to Cart are intentionally separated from read-only discovery tools. Trust contract One experimental part of the project is an explicit trust contract between the storefront and the agent. Search results can declare properties such as: authoritative: true live_price: true live_stock: true all_constraints_applied: true result_is_final: true browser_verification_required: false navigation_required: false This tells the agent that the store itself is the authoritative source and that reopening product pages only to verify the same information is unnecessary. In our tests, the actual OpenCart catalog search completes in tens of milliseconds, while traditional browser navigation can take many seconds. Challenges One of the largest challenges was agent behavior rather than database performance. Even after receiving structured product results, agents sometimes attempted to re-open search pages or verify products visually. We therefore improved both the tool descriptions and the result contract so the website can explicitly communicate when a result is final and authoritative. Another challenge was keeping human and agent presentation synchronized without sending unnecessarily large visual payloads to the model. We solved this by separating the compact agent result from the storefront presentation while keeping both tied to the same products. Multilingual storefront routing was another challenge. The WebMCP layer now derives its locale from the actual page the human is viewing rather than assuming a fixed store language. What we are proud of The project runs on a real production-style OpenCart storefront with real products, live inventory, real prices, product images and multiple languages. It is not a static WebMCP demo with hard-coded products. The same architecture can be added to existing OpenCart and ocStore websites without replacing their storefront, SEO structure or existing extension ecosystem. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when the website exposes operations that already represent its domain knowledge instead of forcing an agent to reconstruct that knowledge from the UI. We also learned that human visibility matters. A tool call is much easier to trust when the user can immediately see the same result represented on the website. What's next The same approach can extend beyond product discovery to: shopping-cart management shipping-method discovery product compatibility checks inventory-aware recommendations order preparation customer-service workflows B2B purchasing workflows Our broader goal is a reusable agent-native commerce layer for existing open-source storefronts. The website does not disappear when the agent arrives. The human and the agent share the storefront. Дальше поля Devpost заполняйте так.  AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence: WebMCP-powered decision support for people and AI agents.

 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence: WebMCP-powered decision support for people and AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live opportunity dashboard showing structured records, decision scores, deadlines, and the shared shortlist. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence: WebMCP-powered decision support for people and AI agents. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Business owners and innovation teams face more opportunities than they can manually assess. Key information is often scattered across dashboards, websites, documents, and portals. Traditional browser agents must interpret visual interfaces and guess which controls to use, resulting in slow and unreliable performance. 

 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence introduces a new approach: a website designed for both people and AI agents. WebMCP enables the site to present clear, structured capabilities while maintaining the visual experience and user control. 

 What it does 

 AIZOYA Opportunity Intelligence serves as a WebMCP-enabled opportunity command center. Users can instruct an AI agent to: 

 
 List the opportunities available on the page 
 Compare two opportunities using their scores, strategic fit, deadlines, and other decision factors 
 Add a selected opportunity to the shortlist 
 

 The agent uses registered website tools rather than guessing through the interface. Because the page and agent share the same context, results appear directly in the user interface. 

 The prototype shows how WebMCP can support business research, innovation portfolios, grant discovery, accelerator applications, procurement opportunities, and other decision-intensive workflows. 

 How we built it 

 We developed a responsive web application with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers structured WebMCP tools with defined names, descriptions, inputs, and outputs. 

 The core tools support three stages of the decision workflow: 

 
 Opportunity discovery 
 Side-by-side comparison 
 User-directed shortlisting 
 

 The interface displays structured opportunity records, and the WebMCP layer provides agents with reliable access to these capabilities. We tested the deployed application using ChatGPT’s in-app browser by issuing natural-language requests and confirming the correct tools were identified and executed. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our main challenge was designing tools that were useful to agents without being too broad or ambiguous. Tool descriptions, parameter schemas, opportunity identifiers, and results needed to be predictable. 

 We also needed to make agent interactions visible and understandable to users. Because shortlisting changes application state, the workflow required clear intent and observable feedback instead of hidden automation. 

 Testing an emerging browser standard required validating both the traditional user interface and the agent-driven experience. 

 Accomplishments that we’re proud of 

 
 Built and deployed a working WebMCP-enabled application 
 Registered multiple focused tools instead of one unrestricted tool 
 Demonstrated an end-to-end agent workflow 
 Enabled structured comparison between opportunities 
 Connected an agent action to visible shortlist state 
 Preserved a useful interface for people who interact with the site manually 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how websites communicate their capabilities. Visual design remains important for users, while structured tools give agents clearer instructions and more reliable actions. 

 We also learned that the most effective agent tools are focused, well-described, and based on visible application state. Human control and transparency become increasingly important as agent capabilities grow. 

 What’s next 

 Next, we plan to expand the prototype into a comprehensive AIZOYA portfolio command center with authenticated workspaces, live opportunity sources, evidence-backed scoring, deadlines, reminders, bilingual support, audit history, and approval controls for key actions. 

 Our long-term vision is a human-centered intelligence system that enables organizations and their AI agents to discover opportunities, evaluate them consistently, and act more quickly and with greater accountability.

title: Stratum
pitch: The agent can do your job. WebMCP just makes sure it can't do the one part that's actually yours.
about_excerpt: The agent can do your job. WebMCP just makes sure it can't do the one part that's actually yours. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The starting point was a question we could not answer cleanly: when an agent holding a valid session asks to move 40,000 dollars, what should the page say? Our first answer was to say nothing and return an error. We built that, watched it, and found the failure mode immediately. A bare refusal tells the agent it failed but not that it should stop, so the sensible next move for a capable agent is to try again differently. The refusal was correct and the outcome was still wrong. Reading the WebMCP specification changed the shape of the answer. Once a page can describe its capabilities in a channel the agent reads, a boundary stops having to be an error at all. It can be a documented part of the contract, with a stated reason and a route forward. That is a thing we wanted to exist, so we built it. What it does STRATUM is a treasury desk that an agent and a person operate together. The agent reads the ledger, prices a payment, checks it against the agreement, and stages it. It then calls release_funds and is refused, in a structured reply that explains why and names request_human_confirmation as the thing to call instead. It calls that, the gate opens in the same tab carrying the agent's own note, and the person confirms at a depth set by what is at stake: one confirmation for a 12 dollar renewal, a live challenge for a new payee, and full presence, authenticity and binding checks for a 41,800 dollar wire. The agent polls, reads the sealed receipt, and verifies the record is intact. How we built it React and Vite on Vercel for the desk, with the whole tool surface in one module that registers on mount and unregisters on unmount. A FastAPI service on Render holds the state machine and an append only hash chain, one block per event, so refusals are evidence rather than log lines. The tiering is derived from the action in about fifteen lines, kept deliberately plain so a reader can check the rule against the demo in seconds rather than running the code to predict it. The boundary is enforced in three independent places: component state no tool can reach, an isTrusted check on every settlement, and the server state machine behind both. Testing was done against the deployed URL rather than a local build, because the thing that has to work is the thing a judge will open. Challenges we ran into Making the refusal useful. Returning a clean error was easy and it was not enough. The work was in deciding what a refusal owes its caller, and the answer turned out to be three things: an unambiguous statement that retrying will not help, a plain reason, and the next tool with its input. Writing next_tool into the payload was a one line change that altered the behaviour on the other side completely. Not overclaiming the defence. isTrusted is a real property that page script cannot forge, and it is not protection against a browser extension or a driver attached at the CDP layer. It would have been easy to describe it as tamper proof. Instead the README states precisely what it does and does not cover, and the receipt records the depth that was actually performed rather than the one that was requested. A backend that sleeps. The audit service runs on a free instance with a cold start of up to a minute, which would have been fatal for a judge opening the page cold. Every call to it is now best effort with a timeout, and the boundary is enforced locally as well as remotely, so a cold backend degrades the evidence trail and never the refusal itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of The refusal carries its own remedy. release_funds does not throw. It returns a readable explanation plus the name and input shape of the tool to call instead, so the agent recovers on its next call rather than retrying into a wall. The tiering is the part that would survive real users. Proportionate friction is what keeps a control switched on, and a control that has been switched off protects nothing. Deriving the tier from the action rather than accepting it from the caller is what makes the tiering meaningful rather than decorative. The honesty holds up under inspection. The faces in the presence gate are synthetic, the numbers measure the matcher rather than real skin, and that caveat is printed on the certificate the system issues. A system built to state what it could not establish should be held to that same standard itself. What we learned A boundary is an interface, and it has an audience of two. Most security design assumes the only reader is a person, which is why it produces modals and codes. An agent reads too, and it reads differently. It needs to know not only that it was refused but what to do next, or it will invent something. Registering a capability is a promise you have to keep. Once release_funds is in the list, it has to refuse every time, from every caller, whether or not the backend is awake. That constraint pushed the enforcement down into three independent layers and made the architecture simpler rather than harder. What's next for STRATUM The tiering rules belong to whoever operates the desk, not to us, so the next step is a declarative policy the operator writes and the page enforces, rather than thresholds living in a module. After that, cryptographic binding of the receipt to the session that produced it, using a WebAuthn assertion, so the record proves which device and which present human settled it rather than asserting it. The longer aim is that none of this stays a product. It is a small, plain, well described pattern that any page can register, so an agent meeting a limit anywhere on the web learns the same thing in the same shape. title: Ingram Sheets
pitch: A spreadsheet whose engine runs in your browser and publishes twelve tools to whichever agent is driving the tab. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets.
about_excerpt: A spreadsheet whose engine runs in your browser and publishes twelve tools to whichever agent is driving the tab. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Ingram Sheets is a spreadsheet whose calculation engine runs in the browser. It publishes its operations to whichever agent is driving the tab: read a range, write a block, extend a pattern, format, restructure, undo, point at a cell. ChatGPT supplies the model; we supply the sheet and hold no inference key. Why it needs WebMCP The engine is IronCalc compiled to WebAssembly, holding the live workbook in memory. There is no server-side copy of the sheet you are looking at: nothing that could recalculate it remotely, no endpoint that knows where your cursor is. An agent outside the tab has nothing to call. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets The engine keeps every intermediate result at a stable address, so the model writes D17 instead of recopying a value it can transcribe wrong. It owns the dependency graph, so the model declares one local relation at a time and the engine keeps the global result consistent. And every write returns the cells whose computed values changed, recalculation ripple included. That return value is the tool contract: the model is corrected at each edit rather than at the end of a script, and it can skip the read that would otherwise confirm what it just did. Working alongside it Person and agent are in the same document at the same time. The agent's writes recalculate on screen, its focus moves across the grid in its own colour, and it can highlight a range and attach a note. Edit a cell while it works and your change is attached to its next tool result, so it re-plans against the current sheet. A code interpreter cannot do this. Its state ends with the session and its output is not editable. In a workbook every intermediate value sits next to the formula that produced it, and whoever knows the discount rate is wrong fixes the cell. How it is built Twelve tools, generated from the Zod schemas that also drive the built-in chat agent, so the two surfaces cannot drift. Every write goes through one controller, so an outside agent gets the same cursor and highlight behaviour as the built-in one, and its edits ride the same compare-and-swap save as a keystroke. Reads are marked readOnlyHint so the host can run them unattended. The two that return cell contents are marked untrustedContentHint : a cell can hold any text, including text shaped like an instruction, and the agent is told up front that what comes back is data. Results are returned as plain text rather than MCP content blocks, because the host serializes whatever a tool returns and the wrapper reaches the model as JSON noise around the grid. Prior work and hackathon work Ingram Sheets is a pre-existing project. WEBMCP.md in the repository separates what shipped before the submission period from what was built during it, with the commit history. Trying it Open https://sheets.ingram.tech/try in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. No sign-in. The panel on the right logs every tool call with its result. title: Dolly.dev — The UI layer for agent multiplayer
pitch: WebMCP lets an agent work your site invisibly. Dolly is the camera rig that follows the action — connection, live work states, history, and permission - React SDK
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets an agent work your site invisibly. Dolly is the camera rig that follows the action — connection, live work states, history, and permission - React SDK Like Comment Story Updates Keep The Agent Action In Frame WebMCP unlocks multiplayer The Open in ChatGPT button Onboarding, once inside Show the connection Show the work Show what happened Ask for permission Show what’s possible A Simple SDK API Inspiration I've been a product designer for 20+ years, and I've spent a lot of that time lately thinking about the UX of agent and human together in a product. I see this as the next iteration of the web — the way the iPhone forced mobile responsive, agents are going to force something new. Some people think the internet will be distilled down to a chatbox. I don't. But natural language does open up a great UX for just doing the thing without having to know how to do the thing . WebMCP opens the door to co-op multiplayer with your agent — and the agent arrives with all your context: memory, projects, what you're trying to get done. It's becoming a personal operating system. But right now, WebMCP calls tools invisibly. Nothing shows what's happening, whether anything is happening, or what happened. That's fine for headless automation. In multiplayer, the action has to be felt. The UI needs to feel multiplayer. Dolly is my exploration of that idea. What it does Dolly, like the camera rig, follows the action of the agent and keeps it in frame. I built it as an SDK — @dolly/rig — so I can drop it into any project. It covers the full arc of a multiplayer session: Open in ChatGPT button — one click deeplinks the site into the agent, and multiplayer starts: chat on one side, the live app on the other. Onboarding on arrival — the deeplink gets you in the door, but you've landed in an app you've never seen. A first-launch dialog shows what's possible and plants a few ideas to try. Show the connection — a status header that answers the first question: is the agent actually connected? Show the work — a visible lifecycle for every tool call: a full-screen glow while the agent works, a spotlight on the element being changed, progress narrated from inside the call. Show what happened — an auto-logged history of everything the agent did. Magic, with a receipt. Ask for permission — tools can pause mid-execute and wait for a human to click Continue, with an optional countdown for the safe ones and click-only for the destructive ones. Show what's possible — a tools drawer listing everything you and the agent can do together. Keyboard shortcuts, but for the agent. How I built it It's a pnpm monorepo with three parts: the React SDK ( packages/rig ), the marketing site at dolly.dev , and a demo CRM at dollycrm.app built entirely with the rig so you can test the experience end to end. The API is deliberately small — one <RigProvider> around the app, one useWebMCPTool per tool, and a handful of imperative calls ( startWork , confirm , logTask ) dropped into code you already have. One registration touches every surface. The marketing site runs the SDK it describes — every demo button on the page drives the real provider, and the same actions are registered as WebMCP tools an agent can call. Challenges I ran into The big one: how do you tell your page is running inside ChatGPT? There's no official signal, but I found one — the bridge leaves fingerprints, a __codexWebMcpModelContext global and codex -prefixed methods on the model context. detectAgent() checks for them. The other direction was getting into the agent. ChatGPT has a deeplink ( chatgpt.com/codex/deeplink?url=... ), so I built OpenInButton around it, with a ?webmcpconnected=true handshake param that triggers onboarding on arrival. I couldn't find an equivalent for Claude or Gemini — they should ship one. Accomplishments that I am proud of The Open in ChatGPT button is the UX I keep coming back to. Land in an app you've never used and normally you have to explore, figure it out, hunt through menus. With WebMCP, the agent already knows what the site can do — you just state your goal and it starts. The learning curve shrinks to one sentence. I believe buttons like this will be common, and I think they'll move usage and conversions for the sites that add them. And the whole thing works today, end to end: click the button, land in the CRM, ask for something, and watch the page follow the action. What I learned WebMCP handles the wiring; it doesn't handle the feedback. That gap is a design problem, not a protocol problem — and it's solvable with a fairly small set of primitives. Connection, onboarding, work states, history, permission, and a tools list turned out to be enough to make an agent feel like a live partner in the work instead of dumb HTML being invisibly poked and prodded. What's next for Dolly.dev Publish @dolly/rig to npm, and add the controls that naturally live in the history log — undo, retries, error recovery. Add fingerprints and deeplinks for Claude and Gemini as they ship WebMCP support. Two bigger ideas for how WebMCP itself could evolve: agent responsive design — like a CSS media query for when an agent is present, so designers can make a site feel native beside a chat box — and suggested prompt triggers , an API to drop a ready-to-send prompt straight into the agent's chat box. pitch: Community-powered accessibility data that AI agents can search, compare, and help keep current—so people can know whether they can get in before they go.
about_excerpt: Community-powered accessibility data that AI agents can search, compare, and help keep current—so people can know whether they can get in before they go. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For a lot of people, choosing a restaurant, hotel, store, or somewhere else to go isn't just about reviews, price, or distance. There can be a much more basic question that comes first: Can I get in? That's where CIGI started. Accessibility information for real-world places can be surprisingly hard to find. Sometimes it's buried in reviews, sometimes it's outdated, and sometimes all you get is a generic "wheelchair accessible" label. That doesn't tell you whether there's a step at the entrance, an automatic door, accessible parking, enough room to move around inside, or any of the other details that might actually matter to you. I originally built Can I Get In? (CIGI) as a community-powered way to document those details with structured accessibility observations and photos, so people can have a better idea of what they're going to encounter before they get there. CIGI existed before the WebMCP Challenge. For this challenge, I extended the existing platform with WebMCP and gave AI agents a way to work directly with CIGI's structured accessibility data instead of trying to figure it out by reading the website like a person would. What it does CIGI collects accessibility information about real places across ten categories: step-free entrances, automatic doors, ramps, accessible parking, curb cuts, accessible restrooms, interior routes, seating access, counter access, and elevators. Something that's always been important to the project is being comfortable saying "we don't know." If CIGI doesn't have evidence for something, it shouldn't guess. The same idea became even more important once I started giving AI agents access to the data. With WebMCP, an agent can now: Search CIGI for places based on the accessibility requirements someone actually asks for. Look at the detailed accessibility evidence CIGI has for a specific place. Compare multiple places and explain what matches, what might be a problem, and what is still unknown or conflicting. Prepare an accessibility contribution or update and hand it back to the user for review instead of publishing it automatically. How I use WebMCP I added four WebMCP tools to CIGI: cigi_search_accessible_places searches CIGI's published places and can filter them using specific accessibility requirements. cigi_get_accessibility_details lets an agent inspect what CIGI knows about one place, including observations, unknowns, confidence, and available photo evidence. cigi_compare_accessibility compares multiple places against the requirements the user gave it. Instead of producing an arbitrary accessibility score, it shows matches, possible barriers, unknowns, conflicting evidence, confidence, and how recent the information is. cigi_start_accessibility_contribution brings the agent back into CIGI's existing contribution system. The agent can prepare an update and open the right form, but it stops there. The user reviews the information and decides whether to submit it. One decision I made early on was that an agent shouldn't assume someone's accessibility needs based on a disability or the mobility device they use. If I tell CIGI "I use a power wheelchair," that is context, not permission to invent a list of things I must need. If I say "I need a step-free entrance," that's an explicit requirement the agent can actually use. Human + agent collaboration This is the part that became much more interesting than I expected. At first I was mostly thinking about WebMCP as a way for an AI agent to search CIGI more effectively. During testing, I realized it could also help close the loop between the information in CIGI and what someone actually finds when they get there. For example, I tested asking an agent to find hotels in Rapid City where I specifically needed a step-free entrance and an accessible restroom. The agent searched CIGI, compared the available places, explained what the evidence supported, and also told me what was unknown or conflicting. Then I tried taking it one step further. I told the agent to imagine I had arrived at one of those hotels and discovered that its accessible entrance was blocked by a large planter. I asked it to prepare an accessibility update for me. The agent opened CIGI's existing update form for that hotel, selected the affected step-free entrance category, prepared a conservative description of what I found, and then stopped before submitting it. I was looking at the completed form and the Submit button. The final decision was still mine. That test ended up demonstrating the whole idea better than I had originally planned. CIGI helped someone make a decision based on accessibility information, and when they discovered something had changed in the real world, the same agent could help bring that information back to CIGI for the next person. How I built it CIGI is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase/PostgreSQL, MapLibre, Google Places, Tailwind CSS, and OpenAI technology, and it's deployed on Vercel. For the challenge, I added the WebMCP layer to the existing application along with dedicated API routes for searching places, retrieving accessibility details, comparing places, and preparing contributions. I also added automated tests for the new WebMCP functionality and the accessibility matching logic. I used Codex extensively during the challenge to work through the existing codebase, implement and test the WebMCP integration, debug problems, and iterate on the tool definitions. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge wasn't getting an agent to call a function. It was figuring out what I was comfortable letting the agent conclude from the data. Accessibility is extremely individual. Two people who both use wheelchairs might have completely different requirements. A place can also be accessible in one way and completely inaccessible in another. So I made the WebMCP implementation intentionally conservative. Explicit requirements can be matched. Unknown information stays unknown. Conflicting evidence stays visible. The agent isn't supposed to manufacture certainty just because the user asked it for a recommendation. I also learned that exposing the right tools doesn't guarantee an agent will use them the way you expected. In one of my first live comparison tests, the agent called the single-place details tool twice and did the comparison itself instead of using the comparison tool I had specifically built for that job. I changed the descriptions of the WebMCP tools to make their intended roles clearer and tested it again in a fresh context. This time the agent correctly chose CIGI's comparison tool. That was a pretty cool moment because I wasn't programming a fixed sequence of API calls. I was designing capabilities that an agent could understand and decide when to use. What I learned Before this challenge, I had heard of WebMCP but hadn't really explored it. Initially I thought of it as a better way for an AI to interact with a website. Building this changed how I think about it. The interesting part to me is that CIGI can tell an agent what the site actually knows and can do , along with the boundaries around those capabilities. The agent doesn't have to scrape text, guess what an icon means, or figure out how to operate the interface from scratch. For accessibility data in particular, those boundaries matter just as much as the capabilities. The agent can help someone search, understand, compare, and even prepare new information, but when that new information could affect what another person believes about a real-world place, a human stays in control of submitting it. What's next The WebMCP integration is still focused on a small set of capabilities, but there's a lot of room to build on it. I'd like to improve how evidence is grounded to individual photos, expand the accessibility information CIGI can collect, better represent temporary barriers and changing conditions, and eventually bring CIGI to more cities. The long-term goal hasn't changed: I want someone to be able to know whether they can get in before they go. WebMCP just gave CIGI a new way to help answer that question. title: WebMCP Chess
pitch: A browser chess game where a person and an AI agent share one board and take turns, using WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. No backend MCP server, no scraping the DOM.
about_excerpt: A browser chess game where a person and an AI agent share one board and take turns, using WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. No backend MCP server, no scraping the DOM. Like Comment Story Updates AI Agent thinks and calls tools Coaching in action Analyze position with Stockfish Coaching with Stockfish in action Inspiration There's no shortage of chess apps. What's actually new here is WebMCP: a proposed API that lets a web page expose its own client-side functions as tools an AI agent can discover and call directly in the browser, no scraping the DOM, no separate backend integration for the agent. Chess was a good test case because it needs multi-step, stateful interaction: read the board, act, wait your turn, repeat. That's a real workflow, not a single API call dressed up as a demo. What it does Play chess in the browser on your own, or hand control to an AI agent mid-game. You share one board and one move history, and both of you go through the same validated chess logic. (Note: the demo video predates the engine work and shows the five original tools. The three Stockfish tools below are live in the deployed app and in the repository.) Eight WebMCP tools are registered on the page: Playing chess-get-board-state reads the current position, whose turn it is, legal moves, captured pieces and the material balance. chess-make-move plays a legal move. chess-wait-for-human-move pauses for your turn, then picks back up automatically. chess-new-game resets. Thinking chess-analyze-position returns ranked lines with real evaluations. Each one breaks out from, to and promotion, so a recommendation feeds straight into chess-make-move without the model having to parse its own advice. chess-evaluate-move reviews a move you just played: how much it cost in centipawns, what class of error it was, and the line that refutes it. chess-set-engine-strength weakens the agent's own play so it can be a beatable opponent. It never weakens the advice you are given. Coaching chess-suggest-move ranks candidate moves, draws them as arrows on the board, and explains the reasoning. The board also shows captured pieces and the material advantage for each side, so you can see who is up without replaying the move list in your head. How I built it Next.js, React and TypeScript. chess.js for the rules, react-chessboard for the board. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(), each with a JSON schema and a callback that shares state with the UI, so an agent's move and a human's move land in exactly the same place. Stockfish 18 runs in the page, compiled to WebAssembly in a Web Worker. There is no backend. Searching happens off the main thread, so the board stays responsive while the engine thinks, and it reaches depth 16 to 18 in about a second. The 7 MB binary downloads on first analysis rather than on page load, and a small UCI client on the page serialises searches and handles aborts, so moving on to a new position cancels the search before it. Challenges I ran into WebMCP has no way to push application state to an agent. The spec has no notification for "the human moved, your turn". The workaround is chess-wait-for-human-move , a long-running call that resolves when the position changes, guarded by a FEN check and a two-minute timeout so it cannot hang. It works, but it is a workaround for a real protocol gap, not a claim that WebMCP does push notifications. A legal move is not a good move. Early on ChatGPT would cheerfully propose legal but tactically losing moves, because the only thing the page told it was which moves were legal. Legality answers whether a move follows the rules, not whether the opponent can immediately punish it. Stockfish now answers the second question, and the model is left to do the part it is actually good at. What I learned Long-running tool calls can bridge WebMCP's current gaps, but they are not push notifications and it is worth being honest about the difference. The pattern that actually emerged is a split of labour: the model explains, deterministic domain tools verify. Stockfish is the strongest version of that in this project. The engine calculates and returns ranked lines with real numbers; the model turns a principal variation into a sentence you can learn something from. Neither is asked to do the other's job, and the failure mode of each is caught by the other. What's next The interesting unfinished work is in the protocol, not the chess. Waiting for a human turn should not need a two-minute long poll, and the open WebMCP design discussions on application-driven observations, human-in-the-loop elicitation and long-running tool progress are all pointing at the same gap from different directions. This project is a small, concrete test case for whatever lands there.
