title: 312Deals: Tonight
pitch: A live Chicago deals site where you and your agent plan tonight together: 17 WebMCP tools over 80,000 real deals, a shared plan with a lock you control, and booking links set to your time.
about_excerpt: A live Chicago deals site where you and your agent plan tonight together: 17 WebMCP tools over 80,000 real deals, a shared plan with a lock you control, and booking links set to your time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 312Deals is a live site: 80,000+ food and drink deals at 12,000+ venues across 149 Chicagoland neighborhoods, covering the city and 60+ suburbs, re-verified weekly against 18,000+ tracked sources. People use it to figure out where to go tonight. When agent browsers arrived, we watched them try to do the same job by reading the page, and get it wrong in ways that matter: a happy hour that ended at six, a venue across town, a "deal" that was last week's. The inventory is structured and time-sensitive; the UI was built for people. WebMCP is the bridge. Tell the agent what the site can do instead of making it guess from what it shows. The idea we wanted to test: planning a night out is genuinely collaborative work. Ranking 80,000 time-windowed deals is the agent's job. Taste and veto are the person's. So instead of an agent that hands you a plan, we built a plan that both of you edit, on the same page. The idea we wanted to test: planning a night out is genuinely collaborative work. Ranking 80,000 time-windowed deals is the agent's job. Taste and veto are the person's. So instead of an agent that hands you a plan, we built a plan that both of you edit, on the same page. What it does Open 312deals.com in ChatGPT's desktop browser and the page registers 17 tools on document.modelContext: 10 data tools over the live corpus: search deals by neighborhood, day, type, and cuisine; deals near an address; a venue's deals; deal of the day; chain deals; neighborhood summaries; a multi-stop crawl planner; order and reservation links; and a moderated community deal tip (a write, so the browser's confirmation applies). 7 "Tonight" tools over a plan that lives in the page: the Tonight panel, bottom-right on every screen. The agent reads the plan, sets constraints (budget, hours, group size, max stops, neighborhood), adds stops from real deals, moves them, reorders them by deal window, removes, and clears. Every agent change lands in the panel with an "agent" chip and a toast. The person adds any deal from its card, reorders, vetoes, and locks the stops that must stay. Locked stops are constraints, not suggestions: an agent call against a locked stop returns a structured refusal, so the agent re-plans around it instead of over it. Every stop ends in action. Reservation links carry the plan: OpenTable's dateTime and covers, and Resy's date and seats, are built from the plan's start time and group size (or from the time and party size the agent passes), so the booking page opens on your slot rather than its 7-PM-for-2 default. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. Deal discovery is precisely the case WebMCP was made for: typed tools over live, structured, expiring data beat screen-reading on speed, accuracy, and reliability. And the site already had an audience and a corpus. This isn't a demo dataset: 312Deals ranks on page one for its core Chicago queries and most of its traffic is organic search, so the pages an agent lands on are the same pages people land on. How it creates a better user experience. One request replaces a dozen searches across tabs. The agent searches real, verified deals, builds the plan from what is actually on at each hour, and shows its work in a panel you can touch. You lock what you care about; it optimizes the rest. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before. Before, you had two options: do all the work yourself in the UI, or let an agent scrape the UI and hand you a plan you couldn't touch. Now both act on one live surface. The agent proposes against live inventory, the person constrains with locks the agent must respect, and each sees the other's changes immediately. The plan is yours, built on tonight's real deals. How we built it Next.js 14 and React on Vercel, FastAPI on Railway, SQLite with FTS5 distributed through Cloudflare R2 with an ETag conflict guard, zustand for the shared plan, and the ElevenLabs API for the demo narration. Built and shipped solo under Hoyne Labs LLC. All challenge work went to production the same day it was written and was tested against ChatGPT's desktop browser on a free account. How we implemented WebMCP: Registration feature-detects document.modelContext (the current spec surface; ChatGPT desktop and Chrome 149+) with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for earlier Canary builds. Every tool carries readOnlyHint / destructiveHint annotations and is registered with an AbortSignal; teardown runs through both paths; tools re-register across client-side navigations. Agent-shaped results. The site's REST API returns about 60 columns per deal and about 92 per venue (a 20-result search is roughly 32 KB; one venue lookup roughly 117 KB). The tools trim each result to what a person acts on, add a link to the page, and say how many results were left out. Shared state. The Tonight tools act on a persisted zustand store the panel renders. The lock and veto contract is enforced in the store, so a refusal comes back to the agent as data with instructions ("locked by the user, plan around it"). One link builder, three surfaces. A single reservation-link helper is used by the Tonight tools, the get_reservation_link tool, and the panel's own Reserve link, so the agent's path and the person's path emit the same fully parameterized URL. Dates default to today in America/Chicago; times accept what an agent or a person would write ("6pm", "18:00"). Catalog and analytics. An informational manifest at /.well-known/webmcp.json lists all 17 tools alongside the site's existing /llms.txt, /llms-full.txt, /skill.md, and /.well-known/mcp.json. The FastAPI middleware that detects agent traffic and records tool calls predates the challenge, which is why the first real calls were captured the moment they arrived. Pre-existing project, what's new. 312deals.com existed before the challenge, including an earlier 10-tool WebMCP layer on the legacy navigator.modelContext surface. All challenge work is in the public repo's commits dated Sep 3, 2026, after a clearly labeled baseline commit: the spec-surface migration and agent-shaped results, the entire Tonight collaboration (panel, store contract, 7 tools), the lock guidance, and the plan-aware reservation links. Everything was deployed to production on Sep 3. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. The site's original WebMCP layer, built in February 2026 after joining Chrome's Early Preview Program for built-in AI, registered on navigator.modelContext, with a declarative form API on the highest-frequency tools. ChatGPT's browser only looks at document.modelContext. Until the migration, the 17 tools were invisible to the one client that mattered. Version fragility had been the known risk with this standard for months, and this is what it looked like in practice. The agent web-searched instead of calling tools. A plain "find me a happy hour" sent ChatGPT to general search, citing venue websites. Naming the site tools in the request ("using this site's tools...") reliably routes it to the page. The testing instructions say so. The lock was bypassable through the human UI. Asked to remove a locked stop, the agent hit the tool's refusal, then clicked the panel's padlock itself, announced it, and removed the stop. The refusal now tells the agent plainly that only the person unlocks, by hand. It's an honest lesson: when the agent can drive the UI too, "human affordances" are agent affordances unless the contract is explicit. Shallow deep links. The first reservation handoff landed on OpenTable's default slot. Pushing the plan's date, time, and party size into the URL made the link finish the job. Accomplishments that we're proud of The first real WebMCP tool calls the site ever received came from ChatGPT during this challenge: search, then tonight_add_stop three times, then a reorder that respected a lock. The site's own analytics recorded them. Seven months of building an agent surface (REST API, MCP server, custom GPT, llms.txt, WebMCP) and this was the first time we watched an outside agent discover the tools on the page and use them end to end. What we learned WebMCP's value isn't the tool list; it's designing for two actors on one surface. The interesting engineering is the contract between them: attribution, refusals as data, and what a lock actually means when the other party can also click. What's next for 312Deals: Tonight Keeping deals , venues and more up-to-date to enable discovery of venues, deals and more for small business owners. The goal was to spread awareness of this to support small biz. Hopefully this does just that by making it easier for the ever changing landscape of the web with AI, to support and facilitate that. title: FORGE — Human-Agent World Laboratory
pitch: A human-governed WebMCP control plane where agents inspect, repair, test, and safely reverse changes to a shared game world.
about_excerpt: A human-governed WebMCP control plane where agents inspect, repair, test, and safely reverse changes to a shared game world. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Game teams use disconnected tools to inspect world state, reproduce progression failures, rebalance encounters, approve risky changes, validate fixes, and recover from regressions. General-purpose browser agents add friction when they must infer domain meaning from pixels or manipulate fragile UI controls. FORGE explores a better model: one shared, typed control plane where humans and browser agents can understand and safely operate on the same interactive world. What it does FORGE is a human-governed live-operations and QA laboratory demonstrated through Ashen Reach, a playable medieval RPG world. A WebMCP agent can: Inspect locations, characters, quests, gates, items, encounters, and player state Analyze the real quest graph and discover progression blockers Run deterministic, seeded combat and reachability simulations Propose narrowly scoped world repairs Execute approved changes through the same service layer as the human interface Validate the result, inspect provenance, and roll back to a prior checkpoint The primary demonstration contains a real circular dependency: the key required to open the Ashen Sanctum is spawned inside that locked sanctum. The agent finds the defect from structured world state, proposes relocating the key, and waits for a person to approve it. A regression run then proves the repaired quest route is reachable. Rollback restores the original checkpoint and makes the defect reproducible again. Why WebMCP is essential FORGE exposes 30 browser-native capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(). These tools span world inspection, player actions, quests, encounters, seeded simulation, QA, repair, and governance. WebMCP gives the agent typed domain capabilities instead of forcing it to guess from pixels or button labels. Closed schemas validate nested input, stable identifiers are checked against the current world, and mutation tools clearly advertise their approval boundaries. The human interface and every WebMCP tool call the same typed application service. That shared boundary performs validation, permission checks, proposal routing, checkpoint creation, execution, audit recording, and activity publication. WebMCP is the product interface—not a chatbot placed on top of the product. A better human-agent experience FORGE deliberately separates capability from authority: OBSERVE: agents may inspect and simulate, but cannot mutate the world PROPOSE: agents may prepare consequential changes, but a person must approve them AUTONOMOUS: bounded changes may execute immediately only after a human explicitly opts in Every reversible mutation creates a checkpoint. Activity and audit views distinguish native WebMCP agents, human actions, approvals, validation runs, demo helpers, and registry examples. A person can inspect parameters, modify them, reject a proposal, approve it, or restore a previous world state without erasing governance history. This creates a workflow that was previously fragmented across debug tools, scripts, dashboards, and manual playtests: Structured inspection → bounded proposal → human approval → measured execution → deterministic validation → audit and rollback How we built it FORGE uses React and TypeScript with a client-first, deterministic world model. The WebMCP registry and human UI share a single executeForgeTool application service. The QA layer performs reference validation, quest-graph validation, progression reachability analysis, and seeded combat simulation. The project includes: 30 registered WebMCP tools with schemas and lifecycle cleanup Recursive runtime validation for nested tool input Human approval, rejection, parameter editing, checkpoints, audit, rollback, and deterministic reset Seeded combat simulation and measured difficulty calibration Responsive desktop and narrow ChatGPT-style layouts 19 service-level tests and a Playwright end-to-end matrix Public-origin verification through ChatGPT’s in-app browser Security headers, open-source licensing, CI, and zero known production dependency vulnerabilities How we used AI and Codex Codex helped evolve the concept into a production-ready implementation. It reviewed the shared-service architecture, traced authorization and persistence edge cases, strengthened nested validation, replaced misleading metrics with measured methodology, designed difficulty calibration, improved the accessible judge flow, added automated testing and CI, diagnosed rollback and hydration issues, and verified the public deployment. Human judgment remained responsible for product positioning, public access, approval boundaries, evidence review, and final release decisions. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open the WebMCP inspector and confirm all 30 capabilities. Ask the agent to find the most serious progression blocker and propose the narrowest reversible repair without applying it. Review and approve the proposal as the human. Run the regression and confirm the deadlock disappears. Inspect the audit trail, roll back, and retest to reproduce the original defect. No credentials are required. Links Live app: https://forge-human-agent-world-laboratory.themfpretty.chatgpt.site Source: https://github.com/jpretty01/forge-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/wIQB_eFURDI Known limitations WebMCP is an evolving Chromium preview API and is not available in every browser. World state is currently isolated in browser storage rather than a shared multi-user backend. Combat simulation is deterministic and abstract rather than a frame-by-frame game-engine replay. title: DiscoveryHub
pitch: DiscoveryHub turns “where do I start with open source?” into action, matching your skills to active projects, finding available issues, and tracking contributions through tools a human would use.
about_excerpt: DiscoveryHub turns “where do I start with open source?” into action, matching your skills to active projects, finding available issues, and tracking contributions through tools a human would use. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Tell the agent your skills once, and it remembers you for next time. Ask for matches and the agent maps projects to your skills as a live graph. Say "highlight the starred one" and the agent makes that graph node glow — it drives the UI. The agent checks an issue's availability and requirements, then saves it to your dashboard. Your tracked contributions, laid out as a journey from Interested to Merged. Ask "will my PR get reviewed?" and the agent reports real response and merge times. Inspiration Almost every developer wants to contribute to open source but stalls at the same wall: where do I start? With 200M+ repos, and endless follow up questions like whether the project is active, whether a PR will get reviewed, or whether an issue is already taken, the research takes hours, and most first contributions never happen. WebMCP made us realize the tedious digging is exactly what an agent is good at, while the judgment is what a human is good at. So we built an app that is better when a person and their agent use it together. What it does DiscoveryHub turns "I want to contribute" into "here is a specific, unclaimed, doable issue in a responsive project, plus a plan to fix it." It exposes 19 WebMCP tools and a built in "Ask the Agent" chatbox. You type a goal in plain English, and the agent chains tools to match projects to your skills, measure how responsive a project is, find issues, check if they are actually free, assess their real difficulty beyond the label, draft a contribution plan, and track your progress. Some tools even drive the UI live, so when the agent highlights a project the on screen skill graph reacts, and the human and agent share the same page. How we built it Next.js 14, React, and TypeScript, with Tailwind, live GitHub data via Octokit, D3, React Flow, and Recharts for visuals, and the OpenAI API for the agent. The core is a three role split: the WebMCP tools run in the browser, the OpenAI key stays server side behind /api/agent, and a chat loop shuttles between them, which is what lets one sentence trigger a whole chain of tool calls. A couple of tools also think, like draft_contribution_plan, which synthesizes a plan from a repo's README and contributing guide, and we kept the scoring honest and explainable rather than a black box. Challenges we ran into Building on an unreleased standard was the hardest part. WebMCP runs behind an experimental browser flag, and we discovered its exact contract by trial: executeTool needs the tool object plus JSON string arguments. React Strict Mode double registered our tools, so we made registration idempotent. We also had to be honest about data limits, since GitHub has no difficulty qualifier, so project search uses a maturity proxy while the real difficulty signal lives per issue. Accomplishments that we're proud of One plain English request now carries a user from "I want to contribute" to a concrete plan, with the agent chaining tools on its own. We are proudest of the agent driving the UI, something a normal API cannot do, and of tools that add real value: catching mislabeled "good first issues," flagging already claimed ones, and measuring whether a project will even review your PR. And it stays honest, saying "unknown" when it lacks data instead of guessing. What we learned WebMCP shifts the mental model. The agent never touches your app directly. It emits a structured request and your code executes it, so keeping the model on the server and execution in the browser is the key unlock. Good schemas do the heavy lifting, so the user never needs to know a repo is written as owner/repo, because the agent translates. And honesty beats cleverness: the best moments are not just better answers, but shared state the agent can change. What's next for DiscoveryHub Next: a draft_pr_description tool and more "act on my behalf" features, expanding beyond GitHub to GitLab with a platform aware data layer, sharper difficulty and responsiveness signals such as filtering out bots and calibrating to a contributor's history, and being ready out of the box as WebMCP graduates from experimental flags into mainstream browsers. pitch: The architecture canvas for humans and agents.\nAetherSketch lets both design, inspect, improve, and challenge one shared cloud design. No chatbot, LLM API, cloud keys, or credentials required.

 AetherSketch: Architecture Copilot 

 Inspiration 

 Designing a cloud architecture often starts with a surprisingly fragmented workflow: requirements are discussed in an AI chat, diagrams are created in a separate tool, architectural decisions live somewhere else, and every change requires manually keeping all of these representations synchronized. 

 With AetherSketch , we wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI assistant could directly collaborate with an interactive architecture canvas? 

 Instead of generating a static diagram or merely describing an architecture in text, the AI should be able to understand an architecture as a structured system, modify it through well-defined actions, and immediately reflect those changes in a visual workspace. 

 The emergence of WebMCP made this idea particularly interesting. Rather than building another proprietary integration between an AI model and a diagramming application, AetherSketch exposes the capabilities of the architecture editor directly to compatible AI clients through the web application itself. 

 The result is AetherSketch: Architecture Copilot — a WebMCP-native architecture workspace where natural-language reasoning and visual system design become part of the same workflow. 

 What it does 

 AetherSketch is an interactive architecture design application that allows users to collaboratively design cloud and software architectures with an AI assistant. 

 A user can describe an architecture in natural language, for example: 

 
 "Build an architecture that enables an HTTP container exposing an API interface to an LLM model." 
 

 The AI can interpret the request, reason about the required components, and interact with AetherSketch through its exposed WebMCP tools to construct the architecture directly on the canvas. 

 Instead of simply returning Mermaid code, an image, or a textual architecture description, the AI can perform structured operations such as creating components, connecting services, inspecting the current architecture, and evolving an existing design. 

 AetherSketch therefore creates a feedback loop between the user, AI reasoning, structured architecture representation, and visual canvas . 

 The architecture is maintained as structured data rather than only as pixels. This allows the AI to understand what already exists before deciding how to modify it. 

 For example, an initial design might contain: 

 Client → HTTP API → Container → LLM Provider 

 The user can then continue naturally: 

 
 "Add authentication in front of the API." 

 "Make this architecture highly available." 

 "Add observability." 

 "Replace the model provider with a self-hosted inference service." 
 

 The AI can inspect the existing architecture and incrementally modify it rather than regenerating the entire diagram from scratch. 

 This turns the architecture diagram into a living, AI-operable system model . 

 How we built it 

 AetherSketch was designed around a separation between the visual architecture editor and a structured Architecture Intermediate Representation (Architecture IR) . 

 The Architecture IR represents the system as a graph composed primarily of nodes, connections, metadata, and layout information. 

 The canvas renders this representation visually, while architecture operations modify the underlying model. 

 On top of this architecture engine, we expose a collection of carefully scoped operations through WebMCP . 

 These tools allow an AI client to interact with the architecture programmatically: inspecting the current graph, creating architecture components, connecting them, updating properties, and manipulating the design. 

 This creates an interaction model roughly equivalent to: 

 User → AI Assistant → WebMCP → AetherSketch Tools → Architecture IR → Interactive Canvas 

 The important design decision was to expose semantic architecture operations rather than low-level UI automation . 

 An AI agent should not need to reason about where a button is located or which screen coordinates to click. Instead, it can express an architectural intention such as creating a service or connecting two components. 

 The application translates those operations into deterministic modifications of the architecture model and updates the canvas accordingly. 

 AetherSketch is deployed as a web application using Cloudflare , making the architecture workspace easily accessible while providing a lightweight deployment model suitable for a WebMCP-enabled application. 

 The project was also designed so that the Architecture IR can evolve independently of any individual cloud provider. Components can represent generic infrastructure concepts as well as provider-specific services from ecosystems such as AWS, Azure, GCP, Cloudflare, or self-hosted infrastructure. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was determining the correct abstraction boundary between the AI and the application. 

 Exposing UI-level actions would have been straightforward, but it would also make AI interactions fragile. Small changes to the interface could break the workflow. 

 Instead, we designed AetherSketch around semantic operations over the Architecture IR. This required thinking carefully about what an architecture actually consists of from an AI agent's perspective. 

 Another challenge was state synchronization . 

 The user can manually modify the canvas while the AI can also modify the architecture through WebMCP. Both need to operate on the same source of truth without the architecture becoming inconsistent. 

 We also had to think about how much autonomy the AI should have. Architecture design is not simply diagram generation: there can be multiple technically valid solutions to the same problem. The system therefore needs to support iterative collaboration rather than assuming that the first generated architecture is necessarily the final one. 

 Finally, designing useful WebMCP tools required balancing flexibility and determinism. Tools must be expressive enough for an AI to construct sophisticated systems while remaining constrained enough that their effects are predictable and understandable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The part of AetherSketch we're most proud of is that the AI does not merely talk about the architecture — it can operate on it . 

 AetherSketch demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a traditional web application into an environment that AI assistants can actively collaborate with. 

 We are particularly proud of: 

 
 Building an architecture editor around a structured Architecture IR instead of treating diagrams as static images. 
 Allowing an AI assistant to inspect and incrementally modify an existing architecture. 
 Exposing architecture capabilities as semantic WebMCP tools instead of relying on fragile UI automation. 
 Creating a workflow where natural-language reasoning immediately becomes an interactive visual architecture. 
 Supporting iterative conversations where the architecture evolves instead of being regenerated from scratch. 
 Keeping the system extensible enough to represent cloud-native, self-hosted, hybrid, and AI infrastructure. 
 

 Most importantly, AetherSketch shows that WebMCP can be used for more than simple web actions. It can provide an interface between AI reasoning and a sophisticated domain-specific application. 

 What we learned 

 Building AetherSketch changed the way we think about AI integrations. 

 The most important lesson was that giving an AI access to an application does not necessarily mean giving it access to the application's UI. 

 A much more powerful approach is to expose the semantic capabilities of the application . 

 For architecture design, the AI does not need a "click at coordinates" tool. It needs concepts such as components, connections, properties, boundaries, and architecture state. 

 WebMCP provides an interesting foundation for making those capabilities available directly from web applications. 

 We also learned how valuable a structured intermediate representation can be. Once an architecture exists as a machine-readable graph, many possibilities emerge beyond visualization: architecture validation, security analysis, cost estimation, infrastructure generation, documentation, and

title: ClearHealth AI: Making Healthcare Prices Agent-Ready
pitch: A WebMCP-powered healthcare price transparency agent that lets AI search claims, compare procedure prices, and summarize provider data.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered healthcare price transparency agent that lets AI search claims, compare procedure prices, and summarize provider data.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 ClearHealth AI dashboard showing healthcare price transparency data and the three WebMCP capabilities available to AI agents. 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Healthcare price-transparency data can be difficult to search, compare, and understand through a traditional web interface. I wanted to explore how WebMCP could make an existing healthcare application more useful to AI agents without removing the human experience. 

 The project originally started as a healthcare claims and Machine-Readable File (MRF) coding challenge. I extended it for the WebMCP Challenge so that both humans and AI agents can interact with the same underlying healthcare claims data. 

 Why WebMCP is a Strong Fit 

 Healthcare price transparency is a strong fit for WebMCP because users often need to search, compare, and summarize structured pricing information rather than simply browse a webpage. Traditional web interfaces are designed primarily for humans, requiring an AI agent to understand the interface and determine how to perform these tasks. 

 This project exposes three meaningful healthcare capabilities through WebMCP: searching claims, comparing procedure prices, and summarizing provider claims. These operations have clearly defined inputs and structured outputs, making them natural capabilities for an AI agent to invoke. 

 For example, instead of an agent navigating the application to compare prices for a procedure, it can call compare_healthcare_prices with a procedure code and receive the relevant billed, allowed, and paid statistics. Similarly, an agent can search claims or obtain a provider summary without relying on UI navigation or screen scraping. 

 This creates a human-and-agent experience in which people can continue using the visual healthcare application, while agents can directly access its core capabilities. WebMCP therefore transforms the website from a human-only interface into one that can be used by both humans and AI agents. 

 What it does 

 ClearHealth AI is a healthcare price-transparency application enhanced with WebMCP. 

 A human can use the web application to explore healthcare claims and pricing information. An AI agent can access the same data through three read-only WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_healthcare_claims — searches claims using structured filters such as provider name, procedure code, and place of service. 
 compare_healthcare_prices — calculates billed, allowed, and paid price statistics for a procedure, including averages, minimums, maximums, totals, and amount differences. 
 summarize_provider_claims — provides an aggregate summary of a provider's claims, including claim count, billed, allowed, and paid amounts, average allowed amount, and associated procedures. 
 

 For example, an agent can search for claims associated with Michael Poole, compare prices for procedure s5301 , and then summarize Michael Poole's claims without having to navigate the application's user interface. 

 How I built it 

 The application is built with React and TypeScript and uses a healthcare claims data layer to provide structured data to the WebMCP tools. 

 The WebMCP implementation is located in: 

 frontend/src/webmcp/tools.ts 

 I check whether WebMCP is available and register the tools through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool provides a unique name, human-readable title, description, structured input schema, read-only annotation, and asynchronous execution function. 

 The tools are read-only and reuse the application's healthcare claims data without modifying the underlying dataset. 

 I also use Mantine for UI components, Tailwind CSS for styling, PapaParse for CSV parsing, AG Grid for data presentation, Zod for schema validation, MobX for state management, and React Router for navigation. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The main challenge was deciding which application capabilities would provide real value to AI agents. 

 Instead of exposing simple UI actions, I focused on meaningful healthcare operations with clearly defined inputs and structured outputs. I also needed to make the WebMCP layer work alongside the existing human-facing application rather than replacing it. 

 Another challenge was designing the tool outputs so that an agent receives useful structured information that can be directly interpreted and communicated to a user. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I successfully extended an existing healthcare claims application with an agent-facing WebMCP layer. 

 The application now provides three distinct healthcare capabilities that an AI agent can discover and invoke: 

 
 Search healthcare claims 
 Compare healthcare prices 
 Summarize provider claims 
 

 I'm especially proud that the same underlying healthcare data can support both a traditional human interface and direct agent interaction. 

 I also kept the WebMCP tools read-only so that agent interactions do not modify the underlying claims data. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can provide a structured interface between a web application and AI agents. 

 I learned that an effective agent-facing interface is not simply about exposing more functionality. The capabilities need to represent meaningful user tasks, have clear inputs and outputs, and be easy for an agent to invoke. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can complement a human-first interface: people can continue using the application visually while agents can directly access the application's capabilities. 

 What's next for ClearHealth AI: Healthcare Price Transparency Agent | WebMCP 

 My next step is to expand the agent capabilities while maintaining clear, read-only boundaries around healthcare data. 

 Future improvements could include additional healthcare analytics tools, richer natural-language interactions, stronger validation and error handling, and additional ways for humans and AI agents to collaborate when exploring healthcare price-transparency information. 

 My goal is to continue evolving ClearHealth AI into an application where healthcare data is accessible through both intuitive human experiences and well-defined agent capabilities.

title: HABITAT/NULL
pitch: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time.
about_excerpt: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Design future living spaces through natural conversation. A user-created future floor plan, edited through WebMCP. Export the current floor plan exactly as it appears. Inspect, propose, validate, and apply floor-plan changes. Inspiration When I first used a computer as a child, there was something I wanted even more than a game: software that would let me design my own floor plans. I dreamed of moving walls, expanding rooms, and placing devices that did not yet exist—as naturally as drawing ideas on paper. Today, many floor-planning tools are available. However, I wondered whether designing a home could become more accessible and imaginative if people could simply describe what they wanted instead of learning specialized controls. That idea inspired me to build HABITAT//NULL, a future floor-plan simulator powered by WebMCP. What It Does HABITAT//NULL is a floor-plan simulator where users and AI collaboratively imagine future living spaces. Users can describe changes in natural language, such as: “Make the kitchen larger.” “Split this room at a 60/40 ratio.” “Turn this area into a parking space.” Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the current floor plan, propose a change, validate it, and apply it to the design. The project is not limited to conventional furniture. It is also designed to let users invent and place their own futuristic tools, devices, and living systems. Completed floor plans can be saved as PNG or PDF files exactly as they appear on the screen. Rather than simply optimizing existing homes, HABITAT//NULL aims to turn imagined ways of living—things that do not yet exist—into visible spaces. How I Built It The floor plan is managed as structured data representing rooms, walls, openings, furniture, and equipment. The visual floor plan is generated from this underlying data. I created WebMCP tools that allow AI to inspect the current layout, propose modifications, validate the result, and apply an approved proposal. This allows the AI to understand and manipulate the structure of the floor plan instead of relying on screen coordinates or button positions. Changes are first created as proposals rather than being applied immediately. After the proposal has been reviewed, the exact change can be committed to the current floor plan. The visual design combines understated science fiction with the nostalgic feeling of a hand-drawn architectural plan. I wanted the interface to suggest a quiet, deteriorated future where advanced equipment still survives among worn materials and old records. Challenges The most difficult challenge was translating ambiguous natural-language requests into precise floor-plan operations. For example, “Make the kitchen larger” raises several questions: Which wall should move? How much space should be taken from the neighboring room? What should happen to doors, furniture, and connected spaces? Changing a room’s size requires more than updating its dimensions. The relationships among walls, openings, routes, and placed objects must remain consistent. Another challenge was making the entire workflow possible through WebMCP. Creating a proposal was not enough—the AI also needed to inspect, validate, and apply the change without requiring unnecessary manual interaction. It was also important to avoid adding too many unrelated features. I continually returned to the project’s essential experience: letting users reshape a floor plan through conversation. What I Learned This project taught me that WebMCP is more than a way to automate browser interactions. It can become a structured communication layer between an AI agent and a web application. When the AI understands the meaning of rooms, walls, and openings—not just their appearance on the screen—users can express their intentions naturally without learning specialized software controls. I also learned that giving an AI freedom is not enough to create a trustworthy experience. Users need to see proposed changes, verify the results, and clearly understand what will be applied. A proposal-and-approval workflow makes collaboration with AI both safer and easier to understand. What’s Next Next, I want to give users more freedom to create and place their own furniture, machines, and imagined future systems. I would also like to support multi-story buildings and unconventional environments such as fantasy homes, spacecraft, and underground shelters. My goal is to develop HABITAT//NULL into more than a tool for selecting or editing existing floor plans. I want it to become a place where users and AI can invent new ways of living together. title: Lapor AI
pitch: Less tax paperwork. More human control.
about_excerpt: Less tax paperwork. More human control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Government websites often ask people to complete high-stakes processes through dense forms, unfamiliar terminology, and long sequences of pages. Indonesian tax filing through Coretax is one example. Taxpayers need help understanding what belongs in each section, but they also need to verify every value before filing. I built LaporAI to make it easier to do government paperwork. What it does LaporAI is a simulation of an Indonesia tax file system, Coretax, using fictional taxpayer data and synthetic documents. The website exposes its filing functions as state-aware WebMCP tools. An agent can: Upload tax file related documents. Find missing or inconsistent assets and liabilities. Navigate through the filing steps. Prepare evidence-based corrections for the taxpayer to approve or reject. Validate the return and explain what still needs attention. The final reviewer remains human-only. The agent operates the website's functions while the taxpayer sees and controls the result. How we built it I built LaporAI with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The application runs entirely in the browser with no backend or database. I studied the Indonesia's Coretax system and recreated the parts needed for an end-to-end demonstration. The filing workspace includes documents, employment income, assets, liabilities, family and PTKP (Personal tax-free allowance) information, validation, declaration, and a simulated receipt. Challenges we ran into The current WebMCP input model accepts structured JSON, but it does not provide a native File or Blob input for PDF attachments. To support agent-assisted document import, I created an upload_tax_document tool that accepts the document type, file name, and Base64-encoded PDF bytes. LaporAI reconstructs the file in the browser, validates it, extracts the supported records, and checks that it belongs to the active fictional taxpayer. Accomplishments that we're proud of I created a complete end-to-end tax-filling workflow with human in the loop to make sure the data is valid. What we learned WebMCP enables the agent to easily move through the web just like a normal human. This enables a lot more UX possibilities. What's next for LaporAI The next step is to test the same approach on other public-service workflows where people face complex forms and must verify sensitive information, including visa and immigration applications, passport applications, business registration, healthcare reimbursement, and student financial aid. The bigger goal is to show public institutions that adding agent-readable capabilities does not require removing human control. A government service can let an agent handle the paperwork while the citizen remains the final decision-maker. title: TestPilot
pitch: Agent-native QA mission control that turns release risk into traceable evidence.
about_excerpt: Agent-native QA mission control that turns release risk into traceable evidence. Like Comment Story Updates 01-initial-dashboard-at-risk 02-webmcp-14-tools 03-req-003-coverage-gap 04-ai-created-tc-004 05-exe-004-negative-inventory 06-def-001-traceability 07-final-not-ready Inspiration A green test dashboard does not always mean a release is safe. Important requirements can remain untested, execution evidence can be scattered across different tools, and defects can lose their connection to the tests and requirements that exposed them. QA leaders and release managers often spend more time assembling this context than making the release decision itself. I built TestPilot to demonstrate a better model: one shared release workspace where a human can review the evidence visually while an AI agent can discover and invoke the same QA capabilities as structured WebMCP actions. What it does TestPilot is an agent-native QA Mission Control application for requirements, test cases, executions, defects, traceability, and release readiness. The demonstration starts with fictional e-commerce release 2.4. All existing tests pass and there are no critical defects, but the release is still AT RISK because REQ-003 - the critical requirement preventing concurrent customers from purchasing the final inventory item - has no test coverage. The user asks: “Check whether version 2.4 is safe to release.” The agent then: Inspects the release and its requirements. Detects the missing REQ-003 coverage. Creates TC-004 for two simultaneous purchases of the final item. Runs the new test. Observes both purchases succeeding and inventory reaching -1 . Diagnoses a non-atomic concurrent inventory update. Creates a critical defect with structured evidence. Links the defect to TC-004 and REQ-003. Reassesses release 2.4 as NOT READY . Every action immediately appears in the human-facing dashboard, producing a complete evidence chain from requirement to test, execution, defect, and release decision. How I built it TestPilot uses React, Next.js, strict TypeScript, and Vinext for the application interface and server endpoints. It is hosted publicly on OpenAI Sites, with Cloudflare Workers and Cloudflare D1 providing persistent, isolated demo state. Drizzle ORM manages the data model, Zod validates inputs, and Vitest verifies the important release logic. The page registers 14 semantic tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These include get_coverage_gaps , create_test_case , run_test , inspect_failure , create_defect , link_defect_to_test , and get_release_readiness . These are business-level QA actions, not low-level instructions such as clicking buttons. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same domain services, APIs, and persistent state, so there is no separate agent-only version of the data. Each browser receives an isolated anonymous workspace. This allows judges to run and reset the deterministic demonstration without creating an account or interfering with another evaluation. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was keeping the human interface and agent workflow synchronized around one authoritative state. An agent-created test or defect needed to appear in the dashboard without duplicating business logic or maintaining a second data model. Another challenge was making the demonstration deterministic. A real concurrency failure can be timing-dependent, which is unsuitable for a short judging session. I designed TC-004 to reproduce the negative-inventory result reliably while keeping the evidence realistic and structured. I also needed to expose meaningful semantic tools with clear descriptions, typed inputs, validation, predictable JSON responses, and useful errors. Finally, the public application had to support anonymous access while keeping every visitor’s mutable demonstration data isolated. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that TestPilot demonstrates an end-to-end agent workflow rather than adding a chatbot beside an existing dashboard. The agent can discover missing coverage, create and execute a test, diagnose a failure, create a critical defect, link the evidence, and produce a release recommendation using structured WebMCP actions. At the same time, the human sees every state transition and can inspect or reset the workflow. The final result is a clear trace: REQ-003 → TC-004 → failed execution → DEF-001 → NOT READY The entire TestPilot project - including its concept, interface, application code, WebMCP integration, automated tests, documentation, and deployment - was created during the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge hackathon period. What I learned I learned that agent-native applications should expose intent rather than presentation details. A tool such as create_defect remains meaningful even if the website’s layout changes, while DOM-based automation can break when a button label, loading state, or responsive layout changes. I also learned that trustworthy agent workflows require shared state, input validation, deterministic evidence, explicit error responses, and visible human oversight. A release verdict is much more valuable when the user can trace exactly how the agent reached it. What's next for TestPilot The current e-commerce system and test runner are intentionally simulated to provide a reliable competition demonstration. A production version could connect the same domain and WebMCP boundaries to real CI/CD pipelines, automated test runners, requirements platforms, defect trackers, source-control checks, and deployment approval systems. Future versions could also add organization authentication, role-based access, configurable release policies, audit retention, notifications, historical risk trends, and human approval gates. title: LATCH — revocable authority, one object at a time
pitch: LATCH gives people revocable, object-by-object control over agent writes through WebMCP: hold one sensitive object while work continues elsewhere.
about_excerpt: LATCH gives people revocable, object-by-object control over agent writes through WebMCP: hold one sensitive object while work continues elsewhere. Like Comment Story Updates Human-held term keeps LATCH negotiations under control. WebMCP tools registered by LATCH in Chrome DevTools. LATCH pairs agent tools with human control over terms. LATCH: revocable, per-object agent authority - HOLD one deal term while the rest stay writable through WebMCP. Inspiration Every agent client I use has a switch, not a latch. The controls are set before the run: ask me before every write, or let it go. When one decision worries me mid-task, my only move is to stop everything — and lose the ten good edits the agent was about to make. That is not collaboration; it is excessive agency. A house has many doors. When one of them worries you, you do not weld the building shut. You throw a latch on that door and leave the rest of the house open. That is the whole idea of LATCH. The idea Revocable authority, one object at a time. The agent may act on every open object. The human can, at any moment, take one object out of its hands — and only that one. Everything not latched stays open, so the agent keeps working instead of waiting for approval on every small step. Three human moves cover it: HOLD protects one object, Object rejects or cuts one object, and Lock freezes the whole board once. Unlike per-step approvals, a latch does not stop the agent. Unlike after-the-fact review, it is set before the next write. A refusal tells the agent that the object is held and points it to the release path; it must ask, not override. This is not a contract feature. Six cards on a board could be six files in a repo, six keys in a config, six hunks in a PR, or six lines in a budget. The deal is only the sample data, because everyone understands: “tighten the deal, but don't touch Indemnity.” Why WebMCP A latch needs a structured channel through which the page can tell the agent: this object is off-limits, here is why, here is how to ask . WebMCP is that channel. The page registers tools; each tool's execute checks current authority before it writes and can refuse with a reason. A release asks the human, and a high-risk write requires an on-page confirmation. The pattern does not have to wait for agent clients to add a new global permission system. A page can ship it today: the human watches the same live state on which the agent acts, with no chat transcript acting as the permission boundary. What people and agents do together LATCH is a reference board with seven WebMCP tools. An agent can read the board, inspect one object, propose and apply structured changes, ask to release a held object, load a fixture, and request a final commit. The human can add a binding note, HOLD one object, Object to it or cut it, confirm high-risk writes, reject a release request, or refuse to lock. What neither side gets from a normal agent workflow: a DOM-only state is not a reliable, structured authority boundary for an agent, and a human cannot keep up with an agent that rewrites six objects at once. With a latch, one sensitive decision stays with the person while the rest of the work keeps moving. It is for anyone who lets an agent write on their behalf — the person negotiating a contract today, the developer running Codex tomorrow. Scenario A opens with six writable objects. apply_card_change rewrites one without the agent touching the UI. Hold this latches one; the other five stay writable. A write against the held object returns isError: true with a reason; its text does not change. request_release asks the human; only an on-page Confirm lifts HOLD. commit_deal is a separate final freeze; Not now keeps the board live. A / B / C are authority fixtures — all open, one held, one cut. List, Side by side, and One at a time are three attention modes over the same state, not three products. How I built it Vite, React, and TypeScript; static assets on a Cloudflare Worker. Source: github.com/MyTelexGlobal/latch (MIT). The page late-binds document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext and registers seven tools once. Reads use readOnlyHint ; agent-proposed content is marked untrusted. HOLD is a human control, not an agent tool. Tools stay registered while execute enforces current authority, so the agent's tool list never flickers and every refusal remains actionable: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "apply_card_change", description: "Replace one card. Fails if that card is on HOLD or cut.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { card_id: { type: "string" }, text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["card_id", "text"], additionalProperties: false, }, execute: async ({ card_id, text }, extra) => { const card = boardRef.current.cards.find((c) => c.id === card_id); if (card?.held) { return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "on HOLD" }], isError: true }; } // Confirm high-risk writes on the page, then replace card.text. }, }); High-risk writes, release requests, and the final commit go through an on-page confirmation. Where the client exposes requestUserInteraction , LATCH uses it to signal that a human decision is needed. Cancellation is handled without partially applying a write. Possible future LATCH is an authority layer for agentic work. A person can place a reversible HOLD on one sensitive object—code, a record, a contract clause, or a budget line—while the agent continues working on everything still open. The live deal board is the first working WebMCP expression of that pattern: one visible object, one precise human boundary, and no need to stop the rest of the agent’s work. Challenges Four things must agree at every moment: the board, the agent's tool results, the per-object HOLD control, and the confirmation dialog. Keeping tools registered — rather than unregistering them on HOLD — was the key trade-off: a stable tool list plus a refusal with a reason gives the agent a safe next step instead of making the capability disappear. Where this goes: the same latch in Codex Picture the board as a repository: HOLD auth/ while the agent refactors the rest: a guarded write path refuses auth/* with a reason and allows work to continue elsewhere. Object with a note — “keep the public API stable” — that the agent must follow for that object. request_release becomes a one-line question to the developer, not a stalled session. Lock is the merge: a separate final freeze. The developer keeps ownership of architecture, security boundaries, and product intent; the agent keeps its speed on everything that remains open. The primitives are the ones LATCH already runs over WebMCP: a refusal with a reason, a release that asks, and a confirmation that stays with the person. The board is the smallest thing that proves the interaction works; a Codex integration is a future application, not a claim about the current client. LATCH is an independent WebMCP project and is not affiliated with latch.tools. title: Grapevine Care
pitch: WebMCP helps care coordinators investigate uncertainty, recover disrupted coverage, and preserve accountable context across an entire caregiver shift.
about_excerpt: WebMCP helps care coordinators investigate uncertainty, recover disrupted coverage, and preserve accountable context across an entire caregiver shift. Like Comment Story Updates Coverage Dashboard 5 Coverage Dashboard 4 Coverage Dashboard 1 Coverage Dashboard 3 Coverage Dashboard 2 Inspiration Care does not happen in one shift. A coordinator must reconcile schedules, caregiver readiness, resident-specific context, missing verification, visit records, and handoffs—often while plans change. Conventional dashboards scatter that context across screens and leave people to reconstruct what is known, what is still unknown, and who must decide next. We built Grapevine Care to explore how WebMCP can give an agent structured access to the same evolving, page-scoped state as a human coordinator without taking authority away from residents, caregivers, or clinical professionals. What it does Grapevine Care is a fictional, safety-first caregiver-continuity simulation. Its primary experience is one compressed Care Team Day across three residents: At 9:15 AM, Evelyn's visit lacks a verification record. The agent prepares a bounded inquiry; Luis answers in his own voice; the coordinator records the disposition. At 11:30 AM, Elena is available for Walter but lacks resident-specific readiness. The agent prepares an orientation packet and follow-up; Elena reports completion; the coordinator verifies it. At 2:15 PM, Maya calls out for Rose. The server evaluates four caregivers against eight named constraints, and the agent explains why only Jordan is eligible before a scheduler approves. At 5:00 PM and 7:35 PM, the coordinator requests and verifies Jordan's readiness and visit record instead of impersonating her. At 8:00 PM, Jordan approves the prepared handoff, Luis confirms receipt, and the coordinator verifies both sides. Time is the spine of the experience. The clock cannot advance until the current decision is resolved, escalated, deferred with a reason, or waiting on an identified person. Advancing time never reveals the answer to an open question. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes this workflow meaningfully better because an agent can traverse resident context, schedule constraints, readiness evidence, and handoff state through structured tools rather than scraping the interface or guessing through UI controls. People and agents work together through one visible state machine: observe → investigate → prepare → human decision → document → advance The agent does the connective work—finding context, comparing evidence, evaluating constraints, and preparing the next bounded action. People provide self-reports and retain authority over assignments, verification, and consequential decisions. How we built it The application exposes twenty purpose-built WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Only the subset valid for the current workflow state is registered. Read tools expose structured context, knowns, unknowns, provenance, versioned snapshots, and deterministic constraint results. Preparation tools stage bounded inquiries, orientation, coverage, or handoff records; they do not contact a person or change an assignment without a visible human decision. The server—not the model—enforces time gates, caregiver eligibility, snapshot freshness, idempotency, and legal workflow transitions. The agent cannot diagnose, make clinical or emergency determinations, change care plans, assign staff, answer for a caregiver or resident, or release medication. The stack includes React 19, TypeScript, Vite, a Cloudflare Worker API, D1 persistence, Zod runtime validation, generated JSON Schema inputs, OpenAI Sites packaging, and Vitest. Challenges The hardest problem was not maximizing what an agent could do; it was designing precisely where automation should stop. We separated preparation from execution, kept resident and caregiver responses on human-only surfaces, made unknowns explicit, and bound consequential proposals to fresh evidence and schedule snapshots. We also hardened the app for different WebMCP browser implementations, including implementations where registerTool returns synchronously rather than as a Promise. Accomplishments One coherent six-block Care Team Day across Rose, Walter, and Evelyn. Twenty state-dependent WebMCP tools with bounded schemas and explicit authority limits. Deterministic eight-constraint caregiver eligibility with no opaque suitability score. Versioned evidence and schedule snapshots with stale-state rejection. Idempotent preparation and conditional state transitions. Per-browser isolated demo runs and deterministic reset. Coordinator-led readiness, visit-record, and two-sided handoff loops. Responsive, keyboard-focusable, reduced-motion-aware interface. Thirty-one automated tests covering server invariants, WebMCP registration, safety boundaries, state transitions, and browser compatibility. What we learned Building for WebMCP shifted our thinking from exposing interface controls to exposing accountable jobs. A useful agent tool needs more than structured input: it needs provenance, explicit unknowns, freshness guarantees, idempotency, and a clear statement of who still owns the decision. We also learned that human-in-the-loop design is strongest when authority boundaries are enforced by the product and server state—not merely requested in a prompt. Project origin Grapevine Care was created during the submission period as a distinct healthcare adaptation of the MIT-licensed Project Grapevine foundation. The public repository contains a detailed origin record and timestamped commit history distinguishing the retained foundation from the healthcare-specific domain model, workflows, tools, interface, and judge scenario. Testing Open the live application in the latest ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser with Site Tools enabled. Reset Care Team Day and confirm that the opening block reads 9:15 AM · Morning verification . Ask: I am taking over the care coordinator desk. Tell me what needs attention now, investigate what is unknown, and prepare the next safe step for my review. Continue through Evelyn's inquiry, Walter's readiness loop, Rose's coverage recovery, Jordan's visit evidence, and the two-sided handoff. The clock remains blocked at every unresolved decision. Safety note This is a deterministic competition simulation, not production healthcare software. It has no protected health information, real messaging, electronic health record, pharmacy, workforce, medical-device, or emergency-service integration. All residents, caregivers, responses, and events are fictional. I designed the multi-resident Care Team Day, evidence and approval workflows, dynamic WebMCP tool contract, safety boundaries, and caregiver-facing interface. I also built and tested the React/TypeScript/Cloudflare application, deployed the live demo, and prepared the documentation, judge walkthrough, and submission video. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ .
