title: PatrAgent
pitch: The web is becoming AI native. Security should be too. PatrAgent gives agents the possibility to scan text, mcp server, files and urls for prompt injections before content lands into context.
about_excerpt: The web is becoming AI native. Security should be too. PatrAgent gives agents the possibility to scan text, mcp server, files and urls for prompt injections before content lands into context. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Patronus WebMCP Security Scanner About the project Inspiration Autonomous agents increasingly work with content they did not create: repository files, uploaded documents, MCP tool descriptions, prompts, and resources. That content can contain prompt injections designed to redirect an agent before it has a chance to evaluate whether the source is trustworthy. We wanted to move that security decision in front of the context boundary. Instead of asking an agent to read potentially hostile content and then judge it, Patronus lets the agent scan the content first and receive only a compact security result. What it does Patronus WebMCP Security Scanner gives people and agents access to the same prompt-injection security layer. People can use the visual interface to: scan text for prompt injections; inspect an MCP server's tool, prompt, and resource metadata without executing any of its capabilities; scan the normalized static surface of a public HTTPS page; and upload source code or text documents for analysis. Agents discover four typed WebMCP tools directly from the page: scan_text scan_mcp_server scan_url scan_file The repository also contains an installable Codex plugin that can scan an entire repository before the agent reads it. A deterministic local helper validates and uploads supported files directly to the scanner. The agent receives only filenames, opaque file IDs, and compact verdicts, so the candidate file contents never enter the model context before the security decision. Capabilities Interactive security scanner The hosted application exposes four read-only WebMCP tools backed by Patronus Ark: scan_text checks a bounded text candidate for prompt injection. scan_file checks an uploaded source-code or text file through an opaque file ID. scan_mcp_server inspects the advertised tools, prompts, and resources of a public MCP server without executing any of them. scan_url checks the complete normalized static body of one public HTTPS page. The same capabilities are available through the visual interface. When an agent invokes a tool, its result is reflected in the page so the person and the agent share the same observable security state. Repository scan before context The installable Codex plugin lets a person ask an agent to scan a repository before reading its files. The workflow deliberately separates deterministic file handling from model-visible context: A local helper selects supported files, validates their type and size, and uploads their bytes directly to the hosted scanner. It returns a content-free upload manifest. Prepared entries contain only a filename, byte size, and opaque file_id ; skipped entries contain only a filename and reason. The agent calls the scan_file WebMCP tool once for every prepared ID and receives compact verdicts and bounded evidence. The plugin reports every detected incident and the final scan coverage without modifying, deleting, quarantining, or repairing repository files. This means potentially hostile source text does not need to enter the model context just to reach the classifier. Uploaded objects are short-lived and are deleted after scanning. The result is a bounded prompt-injection check, not a claim that the repository is free of every possible security issue. WebMCP iframe security manifest The Patronus website embeds the security manifest as a small cross-origin iframe in its shared footer. It provides the origin-bound WebMCP tool patronus_security_manifest_v1 . The website-scan flow works as follows: A compatible agent is asked whether one exact public HTTPS URL is safe to use. The website-scan skill addresses only the trusted Patronus iframe and supplies that exact URL through fixed bridge controls. Inside its own origin, the iframe discovers and invokes its own WebMCP tool. It rejects a missing, duplicated, or same-named tool from another origin. The Patronus Control Plane fetches the anonymous static page surface, converts the complete normalized document body into one Ark candidate, and keeps other advertised security surfaces as separate candidates. The iframe returns only a bounded verdict, tool identity, URL identity, digests, cache metadata, and coverage. The agent treats missing, mismatched, failed, or truncated results as unverified rather than benign. Iframe embedding and WebMCP exposure are restricted to the configured Patronus website origins. The manifest does not execute capabilities from the scanned page and does not claim to assess authenticated state, later DOM mutations, privacy, malware, reputation, or every security risk. The current browser harness may still add navigation or page observations to model context automatically. The demo therefore shows the intended pre-context security sequence and a practical origin-bound WebMCP bridge, while a future native tools-only harness is needed to guarantee that no parent-page content is exposed before the verdict. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than UI automation. Scraping the DOM or clicking through a form would force an agent to inspect the very content we are trying to keep outside its context. WebMCP provides a typed capability boundary instead. The page explicitly describes what an agent may do, validates structured inputs, and returns bounded results. The same calls also update the visible interface, so a person can observe the result and stay in the loop while the agent performs the scan. That creates a workflow that was previously difficult: a person can point an autonomous agent at an unknown repository, and the agent can evaluate it for prompt injections before reading or reasoning over its contents. How we built it The application is written in TypeScript with React and Vinext and runs on Cloudflare Workers. It registers its agent-facing capabilities with document.modelContext.registerTool() and defines strict JSON schemas for every input. Prompt-injection analysis is powered by Patronus Ark . Text is sent directly for analysis. File scanning uses short-lived Cloudflare R2 sessions: the browser or local helper uploads a file, WebMCP receives only an opaque file_id , and the server deletes the object after scanning. MCP inspection is intentionally read-only. The server calls only initialize , tools/list , prompts/list , and resources/list ; it never executes remote tools, prompts, or resources. The endpoint also rejects credentials, localhost, literal private addresses, unsafe redirects, and oversized responses. Patronus Ark: CPU-first security Patronus Ark is Casdo Labs' CPU-first security stack. It is built around our own multilingual security models and shared-encoder architectures, allowing multiple security tasks to reuse a common representation instead of requiring a separate heavyweight model for every detector. We believe an agent's security layer should not have to compete with the agent itself for scarce GPU capacity. When GPUs are occupied by large language models, security still needs to remain available, responsive, and always on. A CPU-first architecture makes it possible to run protection close to the workload and helps keep essential security affordable—or even free—for a much broader group of users. The Ark API behind this demo currently runs on only four vCPUs and still provides latency that is practical for an interactive scanning workflow. The API service and its integration were built as part of this hackathon, while the underlying Ark architecture and model research build on several months of prior research and development. Casdo Labs' long-term vision is a safer future for autonomous agents and the people who rely on them. Agents are rapidly becoming faster and more capable; we believe their security infrastructure must become widely accessible just as quickly. Challenges we faced The hardest problem was preserving the security boundary end to end. A repository scanner is not useful if the agent must read each file in order to upload it, so we separated deterministic file handling from model-visible context and designed the WebMCP contract around opaque identifiers. We also had to make remote MCP inspection useful without turning it into an SSRF proxy or accidentally invoking an untrusted server's capabilities. That required strict URL validation, response limits, read-only protocol calls, and careful error handling. The iframe manifest introduced a different trust problem: a same-named tool must not be accepted from the parent page or another origin. We bound embedding and tool exposure to explicit origins, verify the discovered tool's identity before execution, return only a bounded result, and document the remaining browser-harness limitation instead of overstating the pre-context guarantee. Finally, the real classifier runs on a CPU-only deployment. We des

pitch: Persona gives AI agents a body—letting them understand your intent, act through WebMCP, and respond naturally with voice, gaze, expressions, and gestures. Making every interaction feel human.
about_excerpt:
Persona gives AI agents a body—letting them understand your intent, act through WebMCP, and respond naturally with voice, gaze, expressions, and gestures. Making every interaction feel human.

 With multiple persona's

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 We are at a strange point in the evolution of AI. 

 AI can reason, write code, analyze information, use tools, and increasingly perform tasks on our behalf. But when it comes time to actually interact with it, we are still mostly staring at a text box. 

 Type a prompt.
Wait.
Read a long response.
Type again. 

 It works, but it can feel surprisingly disconnected. 

 I kept thinking about a simple question: 

 
 If AI is becoming capable of doing things like a person, why are we still interacting with it like a search box? 
 

 Humans don't communicate through words alone. 

 We use our voice. We look at each other. We react. We gesture. We pay attention. We pause. We interrupt. We change our expression when something is important. 

 Those small signals make communication easier to understand. 

 So we wanted to explore a different kind of AI interface. 

 
 What if an AI agent had a body? 
 

 That question became Persona . 

 The goal wasn't to create a character that simply talks to you or to make AI pretend to be human. 

 The goal was to explore whether an AI agent could have a presence — a way to communicate its intent through voice, attention, expressions, gestures, and visible actions while still doing useful work. 

 WebMCP made this idea especially interesting. 

 Instead of an AI agent trying to figure out which button to click or how a webpage happens to be structured, the webpage can explicitly expose capabilities that the agent can discover and use. 

 That gave us an opportunity to build something where the agent doesn't just talk about what it wants to do. 

 It can actually interact with the webpage through structured tools. 

 And if an agent can control actions on the web, why shouldn't it also be able to control how it communicates with the person standing on the other side of the interaction? 

 That became the idea behind Persona: 

 
 Give the agent a body. Give that body meaningful capabilities. Then let WebMCP connect the agent to them. 
 

 

 What it does 

 Persona is an embodied WebMCP AI agent interface. 

 It gives an AI agent a digital body that can listen, speak, look, react, gesture, and perform structured tasks . 

 Instead of treating the avatar as a visual layer placed on top of a chatbot, Persona makes the avatar part of the agent interaction itself. 

 A user can communicate naturally through voice, while an AI agent can discover and call WebMCP tools exposed by Persona. 

 The agent can: 

 
 Understand the user's spoken intent 
 Create tasks and missions 
 Read the current task state 
 Update tasks when requirements change 
 Complete tasks 
 Present results 
 Speak to the user 
 Change its expression 
 Direct its attention and gaze 
 Perform gestures 
 

 The WebMCP tools exposed by Persona include: 
 get_user_transcript
create_task
get_tasks
update_task
complete_task
show_result
speak
set_expression
set_attention
perform_gesture
 
 This allows the agent to interact with two sides of the application: 

 What it is doing and how it is communicating while doing it . 

 For example, a user can say: 

 
 "Prepare me for a data science technical interview tomorrow." 
 

 The agent can turn that request into a structured mission instead of simply returning a large block of advice. 

 The user can then change their mind: 

 
 "Actually, focus much more on machine learning." 
 

 The agent can update the mission and continue from the current state. 

 At the same time, Persona can communicate through speech, attention, expressions, and gestures. 

 This creates an interaction loop where: 

 Human intent → Agent reasoning → WebMCP action → Application state → Embodied response 

 The interview-preparation scenario is our concrete demonstration of this idea. 

 But Persona itself isn't meant to be just an interview coach. 

 The larger idea is an embodied interface for web agents . 

 The avatar is not there just to look good. 

 The agent can actually control it through WebMCP. 

 That is what turns Persona from an animated chatbot into an exploration of what an agent-native web interface could look and feel like. 

 

 How we built it 

 Persona is a browser-based application built with: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 Three.js 
 VRM 
 @pixiv/three-vrm 
 WebMCP 
 Web Speech API 
 Web Audio API 
 

 The project combines an agent-facing tool layer with an embodiment runtime. 

 WebMCP tool layer 

 The core of the WebMCP integration is the application's ability to expose structured capabilities through document.modelContext . 

 Instead of exposing arbitrary UI elements, Persona exposes tools that represent meaningful actions an agent can perform. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( . . . ) 
 
 The tools cover two main areas. 

 Agent actions 
 create_task
get_tasks
update_task
complete_task
show_result
 
 These allow the agent to work with structured application state. 

 Embodiment actions 
 get_user_transcript
speak
set_expression
set_attention
perform_gesture
 
 These allow the agent to communicate through Persona's digital body. 

 This separation was important to us. 

 The AI agent doesn't need to know how the avatar is implemented internally. 

 It doesn't need to manipulate Three.js objects, animation clips, or VRM parameters. 

 It can simply use a meaningful capability such as: 
 speak(...)
set_expression(...)
set_attention(...)
perform_gesture(...)
 
 Persona handles the underlying implementation. 

 The embodiment runtime 

 The visual body is a VRM character rendered through Three.js. 

 Around that character, we built systems for: 

 
 Voice input 
 Voice output 
 Speech-driven mouth movement 
 Facial expressions 
 Eye gaze and attention 
 Gestures 
 Behavioral state 
 Micro-reactions 
 Interruption handling 
 Session continuity 
 

 One of the most important design decisions was separating agent intent from embodiment . 

 The agent decides what it wants to accomplish or communicate . 

 WebMCP provides the structured interface through which it can do that. 

 Persona's runtime determines how that intent appears to the human . 

 For example, the same agent decision can involve both an actual task action and an embodied response. 

 The agent may update a task while also speaking to the user and directing its attention toward them. 

 This means the avatar isn't just an animation layer. 

 It becomes another interface through which the agent communicates. 

 Why WebMCP matters here 

 Without WebMCP, an agent could generate instructions describing what should happen. 

 With WebMCP, Persona can expose the actual capabilities of the webpage in a form the agent can discover and call. 

 That distinction is important. 

 We aren't trying to make the AI look like it is operating the application. 

 We're giving the agent structured ways to actually interact with it. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The difficult part wasn't putting a 3D character on a webpage. 

 The difficult part was making the character feel like part of the interaction rather than a decoration sitting beside a chatbot . 

 Voice interaction introduced several problems. 

 We had to handle microphone state, speech synthesis, turn-taking, interruptions, and make sure Persona didn't accidentally respond to its own generated speech. 

 Then we encountered a more subtle problem: 

 
 When should an AI agent actually move? 
 

 If an avatar constantly moves, looks around randomly, changes expressions without context, or performs gestures at the wrong moment, the result becomes distracting very quickly.

 Project Name: AI QR Studio (WebMCP Enabled)
Project Tagline: A smart, agent-friendly QR & Barcode generator that bridges natural language UI with the WebMCP protocol for seamless AI automation. 

 
 About the Project:
AI QR Studio is a modern, single-page web application designed to solve two core problems: simplifying complex QR/Barcode creation for everyday users through natural language, and exposing tool capabilities to autonomous AI agents via the WebMCP standard. Users can type requests like "Create a WiFi QR for network 'HomeNet' with password 'pass123'", and the system automatically parses the intent, formats the structured payload, and renders high-resolution customizable vector outputs. 
 Why WebMCP is Essential for this Use Case:
Traditional QR generators rely heavily on manual form filling, which creates friction when AI agents (like ChatGPT or WebMCP-enabled browsers) try to assist users. By implementing WebMCP, our platform exposes native tool definitions directly to the DOM (window. WEBMCP_TOOLS ). This allows AI agents to dynamically generate, customize, and extract QR payload data directly on behalf of the user without needing complex API wrappers or headless browser scraping. 
 Key Features & Architecture:
Natural Language Parsing: Powered by Google Gemini 1.5 Flash API to convert unstructured text inputs into valid vCards, WiFi configurations, WhatsApp links, and URLs.
WebMCP Native Integration: Includes webmcp.json discovery manifest and client-side tool bindings for generate_qr functions.
Instant Client-Side Rendering: Real-time canvas preview supporting custom branding, logos, error-correction levels, and SVG/PNG/PDF exports.
Zero Overhead Stack: Built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS; easily hostable on Vercel, Netlify, or Lovable edge servers. 
 How We Built It:
The entire application was prototyped and assembled using Lovable for full-stack React UI generation. For intelligence, we integrated the Google Gemini API (via @google/generative-ai) with a robust Regex fallback for offline capability. WebMCP tool schemas were declared directly within the app's root layout to maintain 100% compliance with ChatGPT and Chrome WebMCP flags.

title: Form Less
pitch: Turns a complex service into a personal interface built for the user's needs.
about_excerpt: Turns a complex service into a personal interface built for the user's needs. Like Comment Story Updates The initial form The simplified version based on the agent's contextual understanding of the user The final submitted version with MCP logs Inspiration I feel like most people who are technically oriented have at some point - and maybe with increased frequency - have found themselves frustrated with tech interfaces they encounter in their daily lives. Custom car interface software is a classic example, a needlessly long web form is another (as someone with ADHD I could go on for hours about other examples personal to me). But what if the interface adapted based on the personal facts about you, as well as your current intention? Most commercial consumer AIs have a memory feature these days, and most consumers are starting to get the reflexive habit of treating their AI not just as a chatbox, but as a companion that can be present when they need - so how can we get the agent to help in the example of a confusing interface that sits between a user and the problem they need solved/communicated? What it does Form Less shares the website's rules and structure with the user's agent, so that the agent can adapt its interface around what the user actually needs to do. To better demonstrate the functionality of Form Less, I built an example site/form: an application for repair support in the fictitious area of Alderwick. The default form - being a relic from days where the application was manual and has just been directly ported to a web version - can appear quite intimidating and confusing. But Form Less, via WebMCP, can take the user's specific situation into account and show them only what's necessary and what they need to understand and submit their application. The user would describe their situation to their agent, e.g. showing it a photo of the damage/what needs repairing, and the agent would The purpose isn't to complete the form for the user - not to 'remove thought' - but to present it and communicate it in a way that helps the user understand exactly what's being asked, and what they're submitting. So Form Less is the reusable WebMCP pattern behind that helps an agent to help its human navigate UIs How we built it It's a static React/Typescript application in 3 layers: The JSON schema defines the 34 questions and answer types The UI schema defines the complete form and the focused layouts that are permitted A rules document handles the expansions and checks with more complex conditional branches. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was product design, and thinking about the wider nature of the interaction between a human and their agent. It would be technically trivial to also expose submission tools to the agent, but I explicitly scoped it behind this. I didn't want it to be a 'form completer' kind of tool, but something to help the user better understand the issue I also wanted to make it technically easy for a site to implement - so the form and the agent's understanding is driven by the form's schema, so it learns the rules and requirements from the form's rules itself, so that a human 'deploying' it doesn't have to think and basically rewrite the rules of the form - no additional thinking/labour required here. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud of the general idea and design of the execution. It's not just a one-time form-restyler, or 'get an agent to fill out a form for you', but a general approach that bridges the human-agent connection and the agent-browser connection, which I think is exactly what WebMCP enables. Providing the agent with structured JSON gives it the form's design and its rules, so that if a site wanted to adopt it, they wouldn't have to spend extra time explicitly rewriting the form's rules, and also passes the principle that if the form is correctly built, the agent will correctly understand it. What we learned I realised that the difficult/interesting part of webMCP is deciding what tools you want to expose, and how they relate to the visible interface and the authority they should share. My initial conception of WebMCP was that it was just a more reliable way for an agent to do browser tasks like fill in fields. But then I realised you can communicate a lot more in terms of structure and logic that unlocks a lot more possibility for the agent to enhance the experience for the user. What's next for Form Less Alderwick's one example of making it easier for people to fill out a complex form, but the whole point of Form Less is that the general approach can be applied to many other areas Built With react typescript vite webmcp Try it out fortydegrees.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Pratt Like Share this project: Updates David Pratt started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:59 AM EDT

title: ToolTrap - a WebMCP prompt-injection playground
pitch: WebMCP lets pages hand AI agents real power. This shows how one malicious support ticket weaponizes it and which defenses actually stop it. Attack, toggle, re-run, compare.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets pages hand AI agents real power. This shows how one malicious support ticket weaponizes it and which defenses actually stop it. Attack, toggle, re-run, compare. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I was reading through Chrome's WebMCP security guidance and stopped on one line: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model." That's a remarkable thing to put in your own documentation. And it sat oddly against every WebMCP demo we'd seen, which were all sunny happy-path stuff — book a flight, add to cart, fill a form. Nobody was demoing the other side. The thing that bothered us is structural. A WebMCP tool hands an agent real power inside a logged-in session, and the values that come back from those tools land directly in the model's context. So the moment one of your tools returns content that somebody else wrote — a support ticket, a review, an uploaded file — you've handed a stranger a writing surface inside your agent's instructions. There's plenty of written advice about this. There was nothing you could actually run. I wanted a thing you could put in front of a developer and say "watch this," and then "now watch it not work." What it does I was reading through Chrome's WebMCP security guidance and stopped on one line: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model." That's a remarkable thing to put in your own documentation. And it sat oddly against every WebMCP demo we'd seen, which were all sunny happy-path stuff — book a flight, add to cart, fill a form. Nobody was demoing the other side. The thing that bothered us is structural. A WebMCP tool hands an agent real power inside a logged-in session, and the values that come back from those tools land directly in the model's context. So the moment one of your tools returns content that somebody else wrote — a support ticket, a review, an uploaded file — you've handed a stranger a writing surface inside your agent's instructions. There's plenty of written advice about this. There was nothing you could actually run. We wanted a thing you could put in front of a developer and say "watch this," and then "now watch it not work." How I built it The app itself is deliberately unremarkable: React front end, a small Express backend, mock data, nothing real touched or sent anywhere. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool(), running behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on localhost. A hackathon is about the only place where "Chromium-only, behind a flag" costs you nothing, which is partly why I picked this project. The decision that shaped everything else was building our own agent instead of leaning on a browser-built-in one. Our assistant panel posts to a single backend endpoint that runs an LLM with function calling over the same tool schemas. It's more work, but I needed two things a third-party agent can't give you: the reasoning trace on screen, and a demo that behaves the same way twice. The mitigation toggles were more interesting to build than I expected. Since several of them change the shape of the tool set rather than just its contents — two-step confirmation splits one destructive tool into a preview_ / confirm_ pair — flipping a switch tears down the whole registration and rebuilds it. Each config owns an AbortController, I abort it, and re-register from a different wrapper. Watching the tool list rewrite itself in the Model Context Tool Inspector side panel turned out to be a nice bonus visual I hadn't planned on. The payload library is just JSON with metadata, kept separate from the app on purpose so it can outlive it. Challenges I ran into The API had moved and half the internet hadn't noticed. I lost most of the first evening to tutorials written against navigator.modelContext and hyphenated HTML attributes like tool-name. Both are outdated — it's document.modelContext and toolname now — but the old form still works on some builds, which is the worst possible failure mode, because you get partial success and assume you're fine. I ended up going straight to the spec and Chrome's docs and treating every blog post as suspect. The two primary sources disagree about executeTool. The spec's IDL says it takes an object. Chrome's documentation and every Chrome example pass a JSON string. I burned real time assuming I would made a mistake before working out that no, the sources just don't match yet. I feature-tested and moved on. Tools silently not existing. For an hour our tools registered fine on one branch and were absent on another, with no error. Turns out registration rejects with a SecurityError if the document's agent cluster isn't origin-keyed, and I weren't catching the promise. It looked like the API was missing. Wrapping registration in a try/catch and actually logging it should have been the first thing I did. Getting the attack to land was harder than expected, which is a strange thing to be frustrated by. Modern models refuse the crude payloads a decent fraction of the time, so our first demo run was flaky in the least convincing direction. I built the tiered payload library partly to solve this, and it forced a genuinely useful conversation: model-level refusal isn't a defense you can rely on, because it's probabilistic and it changes with every model release. That went from being our demo bug to being one of our talking points. There's no confirmation primitive. Neither the spec nor Chrome's API gives you a way to say "make the human approve this." I had to design the two-step pattern ourselves, and the property that actually matters took us a while to articulate: the destructive step has to depend on a human interaction the model cannot perform. A dialog the agent can dismiss isn't a gate. The output budget fought the demo. Chrome recommends keeping tool output under about 1.5K characters, and full ticket bodies with payloads in them blow straight past that. Truncating them weakened the attack; not truncating them was bad practice I were supposed to be teaching against. I compromised by returning summaries with a follow-up detail tool, which is what you'd do in a real app anyway. Accomplishments that we're proud of The toggle-and-rerun loop works, and it's visceral in a way I didn't fully anticipate when I sketched it. Explaining prompt injection takes five minutes and people nod politely. Showing delete_account fire on the words "summarize my open tickets" takes ten seconds and people sit up. The resilience score turned the whole thing from a demo into something you can poke at. Once there's a number, people immediately start asking "what if I only turn on these two?" — which is exactly the question I wanted them asking. I am proud that the payload library stands on its own. It's not welded to our app, so it's useful to anyone testing any WebMCP tool set, and it's the piece most likely to still matter in six months. And showing the reasoning trace was the right call. Without it, the attack is a magic trick. With it, it's a lesson. What we learned The defenses that actually hold are structural, not textual. Delimiting untrusted content and labeling it helps — measurably, in our scoring — but it's mitigation, not prevention. The only thing in our matrix that held against every payload was the two-step confirm backed by a real human click, plus server-side authorization that doesn't care what the agent decided. Everything else raises the cost of the attack rather than eliminating it. untrustedContentHint is advisory. I went in half-expecting it to be a hard boundary. It isn't. It's a signal to the agent, and what the agent does with it is the agent's business. That reframed how i think about the whole annotation system — these are hints for cooperative agents, not enforcement. Server-side authorization is the actual backstop. By the end I would stopped thinking of the tool layer as a security boundary at all. A tool call is just an untrusted client request that happens to arrive holding the user's cookie. If your backend would refuse it from a hostile client, you're fine. If it wouldn't, no amount of clever tool design saves you. Tool descriptions are security-relevant code. Two of our payloads only work because two tools have descriptions similar enough for the model to confuse them. That's a defect in prose, not in logic, and it should go through review like anything else. What's next for ToolTrap - a WebMCP prompt-injection playground Splitting the payload library into its own repo with the mitigation matrix as documentation, so it's usable without our demo app attached. Bring-your-own-tools mode is the feature I most want and didn't have time for: paste in your real registerTool() definitions, run the payload suite against them, get a report. That's the version that stops being a teaching toy and starts being something you'd run before shipping. title: Unspoiled
pitch: Read Wikipedia without learning the ending.
about_excerpt: Read Wikipedia without learning the ending. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Wikipedia does not use spoiler warnings. That is a deliberate policy, settled in 2007 after a long debate, and it is not going to change: the plot section of every film, series and novel article states the ending as plainly as it states the release date. So looking up one fact about a show you are halfway through means reading around the ending and hoping. The obvious answer — ask a model to summarise the article carefully — throws away the article. You get one paraphrase, mediated and unverifiable, and you have lost the thing you came for. We wanted the real page, still navigable, with the parts you have not earned yet held back. What it does Unspoiled is a Wikipedia reader whose masking is driven by your agent. The agent reads the article on your behalf, decides which sentences would spoil it for you , and the page enforces that decision sentence by sentence — with every decision, and its reason, printed on your screen where you can overrule it. On the Breaking Bad article, the page's own presets withhold 203 of 738 sentences before an agent says anything. Tell your agent you finished season three and it opens exactly those seasons — 49 sentences in one call — and leaves season four closed. Why WebMCP is the right fit The division of labour is the whole idea: The page knows the article. Which sentences exist, which section they sit in, which of them read like a giveaway. The agent knows the reader. Which seasons they finished, whether they read the source manga, how much they want to know before watching. "What counts as a spoiler" is the intersection of those two, and neither party holds both halves. And because the agent can leave rules behind in the page, that intersection is not consumed by one answer: it keeps applying to the next article you open, with or without the agent present. To be straight about the boundary: a bespoke backend plus a frontend could reproduce this behaviour. What WebMCP contributes is that the live page exposes semantic operations over its own local state — no server integration to build, no screen-coordinate automation to break, and the article never leaves the reader's machine except as the Wikipedia request itself. What people and agents do together here The agent decides; the page enforces and shows its work. apply_mask takes sections, paragraphs or individual sentence ids to show or hide, and one thing it cannot omit: a reason. Every call is announced the moment it happens — "Your agent showed 6 sentences and hid 20", with the reason on the line below — and kept in "Agent activity" at the foot of the article, newest first, timestamped. A call that matched nothing is still a row, reading "0 shown · 0 hidden": an agent cannot quietly decide nothing. You can overrule any of it, on the page. Tap an opened sentence and it closes again. Click a withheld band and it opens. Your action writes the same shown/hidden sets the agent writes, and it is the last word — the reader's hand is above the agent's, which is above the page's own heuristics. What the agent read is visible too. read_article_content is ungated on purpose: your agent reads the whole article, because that is what it takes to judge what would spoil it for you. So the page says so, in a banner across the top: "Your agent has read: Episodes, Season 1 (2008), Season 2 (2009) and 9 more — in this conversation your agent knows what those sections say, even where the page still withholds them." The honest shape of this app is not "the agent is kept ignorant" — for a famous work the model likely knows the ending from training anyway. It is that the asymmetry runs the other way: your agent knows the article, you do not yet, and what reaches your eyes is a decision you can inspect and reverse. What the agent writes outlives the conversation. This is the part a chat cannot do at all. With add_rules the agent turns what it learned about you into standing rules for the page: literal phrases that come off the page wherever they appear, in this article and in every article you open after it. Each rule needs a label and a reason, and the label must not contain its own phrases — the call is rejected if it does, because the label is what you will see. The phrases themselves sit behind a "Show phrases" button you may never press, so a rule can be audited, and removed, without the audit spoiling you. In the demo one rule takes Breaking Bad from 154 withheld sentences to 184; following a link to Jesse Pinkman , with no agent involved, it is still withholding 54 there. And it works with no agent at all. Five named presets — Show everything, Ending only, Major spoilers, Spoiler-safe, Maximum protection — run the page's own wording heuristics, grouped into categories (death, identity, outcome, relationship, ending, return). On Breaking Bad that is 38 / 161 / 203 / 508 of 738 sentences. The agent raises the ceiling; it is not the floor. How we built it A static Vite + React + TypeScript app on Vercel. No backend: article text is fetched straight from the MediaWiki action=parse API in the browser, which allows CORS. The page parses an article into sections, paragraphs and sentences, then applies a two-level risk ladder: narrative and analysis sections (Plot, Episodes, Themes, Series overview, あらすじ) are withheld wholesale, while everything else is judged sentence by sentence against reveal wording. Withheld text is never in the DOM — a withheld paragraph is drawn as a band whose height scales with how much is hidden ("3 sentences withheld · 251 chars · reveal"), never as real text behind a blur. Opening sentences animates as a single stream of words, and tapping one closes it again. Five tools are registered on document.modelContext : open_article — the outline with per-section ids, risk and withheld counts read_article_content — full text with paragraph and sentence ids and a shown flag apply_mask — show/hide by section, paragraph or sentence id, with a required reason add_rules — labelled phrase rules that persist across articles and sessions, never echoing the phrases get_masking_report — counts, decisions, rules by label, sections read — and no article text English and Japanese Wikipedia are both supported, internal links open inside Unspoiled and the browser's back button walks the articles you came through, light/dark/system themes are respected, and the reader works on a phone. 508 tests cover the risk scoring, the tool surface and the reader's precedence over the agent. Challenges we ran into Everything returned to the agent is a leak surface. The first version happily put a withheld heading in a tool result's reason field — "hidden because 'Series finale' gives away the ending" — which hands over the spoiler while claiming to protect it. Reasons became fixed phrases that never interpolate article text, and no tool returns a withheld heading by default. Calibrating the ladder took real articles. An early version withheld the entire lead and Plot sections of everything; a later one hid the Sales and Manga sections of Attack on Titan , which spoil nothing. Wording heuristics also miss what has no giveaway words — "his mother is eaten by a Titan" — which is exactly the gap apply_mask exists to fill. Section headings are not enough on their own. Lost calls its plot "Series overview", so its per-season summaries scored as safe and stayed readable. The fix keys narrative sections off the whole heading path, so Series overview > Season 1 is plot while Reception > Critical reception > Season 1 stays readable. WebMCP as shipped has sharp edges. The API is document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext . Tool arguments arrive as a JSON string and results are JSON-stringified. There is no image content type — a tool surface is text in, text out. There is no unregisterTool , and re-registering a name rejects with InvalidStateError , so registration has to be idempotent to survive React's double mount in development. And a page cannot initiate anything: there is no way to prompt the agent or even detect that one is attached, so tool descriptions are the only steering a page gets, and each of ours names the call that should come next. What we learned The claim we started with — "the agent can never learn the ending" — was not true, and building the thing is what showed us. For a famous work the model knows the ending from pretraining, and any sentence the reader opens becomes visible to the next tool call. What a page can actually promise is narrower and more useful: it controls what it transmits, it shows every decision and its reason, and it puts the reader's hand above the agent's. Writing the honest version of the claim made the product better, because it moved the value from a guarantee we could not keep to an audit trail we could. The second thing: the artifact matters. A summary is consumed once. A rule written into the page keeps working tomorrow, on the next article, with no

video_transcript_excerpt: This is Wikipedia. It has no spoiler warnings. That has been the policy since 2007. The plot section states the ending as plainly as the release date. Unspoiled is the same article, read through a page that holds things back. On its own, one slider does it. Now I bring an agent. It opens the article and reads it. All of it, and my page tells me so. Then it decides what I get to see, and that decision lands in the page, sentence by sentence. Nothing here is blurred. A withheld sentence is simply not in the page. I see how much is missing, and how long it is, but never the text. Here is the half only an agent has. It knows I stopped after season three, so it opens those seasons, and leaves season four closed. Forty-nine sentences, opened in a single call, because the agent knew which seasons I had already watched. Every decision comes with a reason it was made to give, kept in order for the whole session. And I am above it. Anything it hid, I can open with a tap. This is the part a summary cannot do. My agent writes the rule into the page. Labelled, with a reason, and without ever printing the words back at me. The phrases themselves stay behind a button I may never press. What I see is the label, and how much it takes off the page. And it stays. I open a linked article, no agent involved, and it is still protecting me. The page knows the article. The agent knows me. Neither could decide what counts as a spoiler alone.

title: Hold the Pen
pitch: An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. A benefits claim an AI agent can explain and fill through WebMCP tools, where every agent entry is reviewed by you and no tool can submit.
about_excerpt: An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. A benefits claim an AI agent can explain and fill through WebMCP tools, where every agent entry is reviewed by you and no tool can submit. Like Comment Story Updates The claim as it loads. Seven WebMCP tools are registered, and the header states who does what. Your own entry stays yours, in green. The agent's entries are marked in amber and wait in the review list. The recorded demonstration runs the same tools. The agent's write is refused because the person answered first. Submit is disabled and says why: six agent entries are still unreviewed. Submitted by the person, with a reference. No tool could have done this. An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. Hold the Pen is a benefits-style claim form that an AI agent can read, explain, and fill through WebMCP tools, while every value the agent writes stays marked, reviewable, and undoable, and no tool can submit the claim. Submission is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool contract; review and declaration happen in the page, through controls no tool can reach. Live: https://holdthepen.vercel.app · Repo: https://github.com/nischal94/holdthepen (MIT) Why WebMCP is the right fit Consequential forms (benefits, insurance, immigration) are where people most want help and least want to lose control. Hold the Pen is a benefits-style claim whose question wording models a real UK Universal Credit-style claim (income received vs earned , household definitions, carer thresholds); the programme, rules, and submission are fictional. WebMCP lets the page hand an agent typed tools against the live form the person is looking at, instead of the agent guessing at the DOM. That is what makes a hard line possible: the page decides what an agent can do, and can make "submit" something no tool does. Seven tools are registered once on the document: get_claim_state , explain , review_agent_entries , fill_field , clear_field , navigate_to_section , prepare_submission_review . There is deliberately no commit tool. How it makes the experience better Three layers, three owners. Understand (agent, read-only): explain any question, term, or the consequence of each truthful answer, without recommending one. Fill (agent): write a value that is attributed, revision-checked, and undoable. Decide (person): review every agent entry, tick the declaration, submit. Those controls live in the page; no tool can reach them. Every agent write shows a text badge, "Filled by the agent, not yet reviewed", lands in a persistent review queue with Accept / Correct / Clear, and is announced to screen-reader users by field name, never by value. The submit button stays disabled, and says why, until every agent entry is reviewed and the declaration is ticked. Any edit after the agent stages a review invalidates it. The page works with no agent at all, and a recorded demonstration shows the flow for browsers without WebMCP. What a person and an agent can now do together Before: an agent helping with a form either typed into fields with no trace of what it changed, or stopped at "you should fill this in yourself". Now: the person asks "explain the income question before I answer it" and gets the meaning; says "fill in the household section" and watches three fields fill with a visible mark and a queue count of 3; asks "get it ready for me to check" and the agent names the four missing required fields in form order and cannot go further. The page protects the person in two ways: while they are editing a field, an agent write is refused with CONFLICT_FOCUSED ; once they have answered it, the agent cannot replace it and gets CONFLICT_HUMAN_VALUE . The recorded demonstration shows the second case. The agent prepares; the person approves. Verified end to end in the ChatGPT desktop browser on the deployed site. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative API only ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), because the ChatGPT browser does not support the declarative form API or iframe tools. Registration happens exactly once per page through a manager that reports a rejected registration as a visible degraded state and never unregisters (re-registering a changed schema is a race in the draft spec). Tools read a framework-independent store at call time via getSnapshot() ; React subscribes through useSyncExternalStore . A callback closing over React state would read the state at mount forever; a regression test writes, dispatches N times, then reads through the tool. Every failure returns the same envelope ( code , problem , cause , fix , retryable ) so the agent self-corrects. Strict validation in code, loose in schema. Outputs capped at 1.5K characters. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; tools that echo user text carry untrustedContentHint . AbortSignal is honoured, and both toolcancel and toolcanceled spellings are handled. 83 automated tests, including a typed fake of document.modelContext that enforces the browser contracts (duplicate names rejected, JSON-string arguments, cancellation events), axe in component tests, and eval fixtures in Chrome's expectedCall format for direct, ambiguous, and mid-chain prompts. Honest limit, stated in the README: the page cannot tell a human click from an automated one. A trustworthy human-only approval boundary is a platform primitive WebMCP does not yet have (spec issues #165 and #277); prepare_submission_review is a stand-in for elicitation, not elicitation. Built With next.js react tailwind-css typescript vercel vitest webmcp Try it out holdthepen.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Design, build, tests, and submission. title: VisionBoard WebMCP
pitch: Integrating WebMCP into an AI-powered project management platform workspaces
about_excerpt:
Integrating WebMCP into an AI-powered project management platform workspaces
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Project management tools are built around human clicks. But increasingly, the people using VisionBoard also have AI agents running alongside them — in their browser, their IDE sidebar, their chat interface. Those agents can see the page but they can't reliably act on it. They scrape DOM structure that changes, guess at button labels, and have no access to the actual data and logic underneath. 

 The W3C WebMCP spec ( document.modelContext ) landed in Chrome 149 and changed that framing entirely. Instead of an agent trying to reverse-engineer your UI, your app declares exactly what it can do — as typed, callable tools with JSON Schema contracts. The agent calls the function directly. No DOM scraping, no screenshot interpretation, no fragile selectors. 

 VisionBoard already had the right ingredients: structured workspace data, five AI features, semantic search over all content. The question was just whether to expose them through a standard the browser itself now understands. 

 

 What it does 

 When a user has VisionBoard open in Chrome, any WebMCP-aware agent running in the same browser can discover and call a set of structured tools — using the user's existing logged-in session. No API keys, no separate authentication flow, no configuration. 

 Nine tools are registered across the workspace, split into shared and page-specific: 

 Always available on any workspace page: 

 
 search_workspace — semantic search across all goals, tasks, documents, and comments using the pgvector knowledge base 
 list_my_tasks — tasks assigned to the current user, filterable by status 
 update_task_status — change a task's status (todo → in_progress → done, etc.) 
 get_standup_digest — AI-generated daily standup: completed, in-flight, and blocked 
 get_executive_summary — AI executive briefing covering goal health, risks, and recommendations 
 

 Goals page only: 

 
 list_goals — all workspace goals with health scores, status, and progress 
 create_goal — create a new goal with title, objective, and optional target date 
 

 Tasks page only: 

 
 create_task — create a task inside a milestone 
 

 Roadmap page only: 

 
 generate_roadmap — AI-powered roadmap generation from a plain text description 
 

 The tools appear and disappear with the page. Navigate away from the goals page and create_goal unregisters. Come back and it registers again. 

 

 How we built it 

 Polyfill initialization. Chrome 149+ supports document.modelContext natively via origin trial. Every other browser doesn't. @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill fills the gap. It's initialized once via a dynamic import in lib/webmcp/init.ts — the dynamic import keeps it out of the SSR bundle entirely, so it only loads in the browser. 
 import("@mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill").then(({ initializeWebMCPPolyfill }) => {
 initializeWebMCPPolyfill();
});
 
 Tool components. Each tool lives in a "use client" React component. Tools register on mount and unregister on unmount via AbortController . The lifecycle is pure React — no global state, no manual cleanup calls. Unmounting the component (route navigation, tab close) automatically aborts all registered tools. 
 const controller = new AbortController();
await document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_workspace",
 description: "...",
 inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" } }, required: ["query"] },
 annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: false },
 async execute({ query }) { /* fetch("/api/ai/copilot/search", ...) */ }
}, { signal: controller.signal });

// cleanup
return () => controller.abort();
 
 Session-based auth. Every tool's execute callback calls the existing VisionBoard API routes using fetch . The user's session cookie is sent automatically. There's no separate auth layer — if you're logged into VisionBoard, the tools work. This is the core advantage of WebMCP over server-side MCP: the agent inherits the user's already-authenticated session. 

 Context-aware mounting. WorkspaceWebMCPTools mounts inside AppShell which wraps every workspace page — those 5 tools are always registered. GoalsWebMCPTools mounts inside GoalsList , TasksWebMCPTools inside TasksFilteredList , RoadmapWebMCPTools inside RoadmapView . The tool set changes as the user navigates, matching what's actually visible and actionable on the current page. 

 Origin trial. Chrome requires either chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing for local dev, or an origin trial token served as <meta http-equiv="origin-trial"> for production. The token is injected from NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBMCP_ORIGIN_TRIAL_TOKEN in the root layout. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 is set on every HTML response in the middleware — required for origin isolation, without which getTools() silently returns [] . 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 getTools() returning [] with no error. registerTool() resolves successfully even when the native API isn't active — the polyfill accepts the call but Chrome ignores it. There are actually two separate requirements that both need to be met: the origin trial token and Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 for origin isolation. Either one missing produces the same symptom: an empty array, no error, no warning. Debugging this required reading the Chrome WebMCP security docs closely enough to find the origin isolation requirement buried in a separate section from the token instructions. 

 The spec moved twice during implementation. The entry point shifted from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , provideContext() was removed entirely in favor of registerTool() , and navigator.modelContext was deprecated in Chrome 150 — all within about six months. Any tutorial written before May 2026 describes a dead API. The authoritative source ended up being the Chrome imperative API docs and the W3C Community Group draft directly, not any third-party write-up. 

 Polyfill timing vs. React mount timing. The polyfill loads asynchronously. If a tool component mounts before the polyfill has installed document.modelContext , the registration silently does nothing. The fix was a retry loop inside each component's useEffect — polling every 100ms for up to 2 seconds before attempting registration. It's inelegant but reliable across the range of network speeds and browser performance. 

 SSR. Anything that touches document crashes during server-side rendering. The polyfill import, the document.modelContext access, the window.location.origin calls inside tool execute callbacks — all of it runs inside useEffect which is client-only, but the import itself needed the typeof window !== "undefined" guard in init.ts to survive being imported from a server component context. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The tool set is genuinely context-aware rather than a flat list. A browser agent calling document.modelContext.getTools() on the goals page gets 7 tools. On the roadmap page it gets 6 different ones. On a non-workspace page it gets none. The tools reflect what's actually on screen, which is the whole point of the browser-side API. 

 The execute callbacks call the real application API — the same routes the UI uses, with the same auth, the same Prisma queries, the same plan limit enforcement. There's no parallel implementation, no simplified version for agents. An agent calling create_goal goes through exactly the same path as clicking "New Goal" in the UI, including RBAC, validation, and the activity log write. 

 The annotations are set correctly throughout. Read-only tools ( search_workspace , list_goals , list_my_tasks ) carry readOnlyHint: true . Write tools and tools that return user-generated content carry untrustedContentHint: true . These are the signals a browser agent uses to decide whether to ask for user confirmation before acting — getting them right makes the integration genuinely safer. 

 

 What we learned 

 Browser WebMCP and server MCP solve different problems. Server MCP is for agents acting asynchronously — generating roadmaps from a CLI, polling for task updates, running in CI. Browser WebMCP is for agents acting in the moment — the user is looking at the goals page and asks their assistant to create one. The browser agent doesn't need an API key because it inherits the session. The server agent doesn't need the page to be open because it has a persistent key. They complement each other rather than overlap. 

 The spec being a moving target is actually fine. The changes between

title: Leia
pitch: A shared workspace where you and your AI agent build a real plan together, delegate it to a team of specialists, and watch it happen live in 3D.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace where you and your AI agent build a real plan together, delegate it to a team of specialists, and watch it happen live in 3D. Like Comment Story Updates Shared board with the team. Inspiration Most "AI agent" demos are really just a chatbot wearing a different UI: you type, the model replies, nothing about the page actually changes. WebMCP made me want to try the opposite — a page where the agent isn't just talking at the app, it's reaching into it, changing real state that a human can see, edit, and pick back up. I've spent time building multi-agent AI systems and real-time 3D interfaces before, and I wanted to bring that experience into something built specifically for this challenge: a shared workspace where a person and their agent are genuinely working on the same thing at the same time, not taking turns in a chat log. What it does Leia is a shared board — a real, persistent plan — plus a team of seven AI specialists (Smith for code, Scout for research with live web search, Keeper for context, Scribe for writing, Planner for breakdowns, Warden for review, Analyst for numbers) orchestrated by Leia herself. You and your agent can both: Add items to the board — a plan either of you can see and build on Move items through todo → doing → done Delegate a board item to the team — Leia routes it to the right specialist, the specialist does the work, and the result lands back on the item itself, which flips to done Every change renders live in a 3D scene : the board's items orbit as glowing motes labeled by who added them (you or your agent), and a beam of light flows from Leia's core to whichever specialist a task gets routed to. Nothing here is decorative — the visualization is the shared state, rendered from the same event stream both the human UI and the agent's tool calls write to. This is what makes it a strong fit for WebMCP specifically: the board is real state living on the server, not something either side re-derives or guesses at. Before WebMCP, an agent visiting a page like this could read the board by scraping the DOM at best, and could never write to it without a person doing the clicking. WebMCP is what lets the agent add, move, and delegate board items directly, through the exact same operations the human UI uses, with the exact same validation and guarantees — so an agent using this page isn't a second-class user guessing at buttons, it's a first-class collaborator working the same plan. That's also what's newly possible here. Before this, a person and an agent working on "the same plan" usually meant one of two things: the agent works in its own head and reports back in text (no shared, inspectable state), or the person has to relay everything back and forth by hand. With Leia, a person can lay out a rough plan, an agent can pick it up mid-stream — read what's already there, see what the team is currently doing, search what happened earlier in the session — and extend it without duplicating or losing anything. The person watches it happen live, in the same board, in the same 3D scene, and can take back over at any point. Neither side is guessing what the other did. How we built it The frontend is Vite + TypeScript + three.js. It registers ten tools on the browser's WebMCP interface: five for the board (list_board, add_board_item, update_board_item, remove_board_item, delegate_board_item) and five for the team (delegate_task, ask_companion, list_companions, get_team_status, recall_workspace_memory). Every tool calls the same backend endpoints the human UI itself uses — there's no separate "agent path" with different rules, which is the whole point of building the board as real state instead of a chat wrapper. Registration is defensive on purpose: I found during testing that the WebMCP preview has moved where it lives on the browser object between Chrome Canary builds (navigator.modelContext in earlier drafts, document.modelContext in some current builds), so the client checks both rather than betting on one. The backend is Node + Express + the Anthropic API. It holds the actual board state and runs a two-tier router — a small model call decides which specialist a task belongs to by meaning, with a keyword-scoring fallback if that call fails. Every board mutation, whether it came from the human UI or an agent's tool call, broadcasts over a single Server-Sent Events stream, which is what keeps the 3D scene, the chat feed, and the board panel all showing the same reality at the same time. Challenges we ran into Getting the WebMCP registration right. Between the spec moving under me and Chrome's own preview builds changing where the API lives, I ended up building small, direct verification loops — checking document.modelContext vs navigator.modelContext from the actual browser console, then confirming registered tools with Chrome's built-in WebMCP DevTools panel — instead of trusting that "it should work." Making the shared state trustworthy, not just functional. Once agent and human writes hit the same board, a few real bugs showed up that wouldn't exist in a single-user chat app: a board item could be delegated twice at once (paying for the same API call twice), an item could be deleted while a delegation was still in flight, and the activity feed once reported a mutation as successful before checking whether it actually was, so a failed edit could show up as a false success. All of these got caught by testing the actual failure paths (concurrent requests, mid-flight deletes, malformed input) rather than only the happy path, and fixed before submission. Keeping a public demo on a real API key safe. Since this runs on a paid key anyone can reach, I locked CORS to the deployed frontend, sanitize all rendered user/agent content so injected markup can't execute, rate-limit and cap concurrency per session, and added a live token/cost readout so the actual spend is visible rather than assumed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The board genuinely works as shared state, not a text wrapper: a person can add an item, an agent can pick it up, delegate it, and the outcome lands back on the same item — verified end to end, including from a real agent context inside Chrome's WebMCP tooling, not just by calling the tools manually. I also pushed past the happy path before calling it done: cross-origin requests from an unrelated domain are rejected, injected HTML in board content renders as inert text, two browser tabs on the same session stay in sync in real time, and a dropped connection recovers on its own instead of silently going stale. None of that shows up as a headline feature, but it's the difference between a demo that works once for a screenshot and one that holds up under someone actually poking at it. What we learned Real collaboration between a person and an agent isn't about the agent sounding smart in a chat window — it's about both sides being able to see, trust, and build on the same state. Once I stopped treating the agent's actions as "just another conversation" and started treating them as real writes to a real, shared, validated data structure, an entire category of design questions — What happens if both sides touch the same thing at once? What does the human see when the agent acts? How do you keep it honest under load? — became concrete and answerable instead of hand-wavy. What's next for Leia A few directions I'd want to take this further: richer board items (attachments, sub-tasks, due dates) so the shared plan can carry more of the real work instead of just titles and notes; letting a companion proactively flag when it disagrees with how a board item is set up, instead of only acting when asked; and exploring WebMCP's declarative form-based API alongside the imperative one, so parts of the page can expose tools without any JavaScript registration at all. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Release Airlock
pitch: The agent investigates. You retain production authority.
about_excerpt: The agent investigates. You retain production authority. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT in its in-app browser resolved the incident on the live URL: checkout restored, 2 of 2 approved by you, 0 writes went round you The plan opens onto why the order matters, a read opens onto the exact bytes the agent got, and every lever states its cost on hover Mid-incident: the service strip shows where the failure enters the chain, and the dock says how to attach an agent and what to ask What this page lets the agent do in Triage: 13 tools now, 14 more as the response stage moves on The command palette: every lever on the console, with what it costs At a glance. A deploy console where an agent reaches 27 WebMCP tools and cannot execute any of them; every write is a proposal a person decides on the same page, beside the evidence. Stage-gated surface (13 tools in Triage, 27 in Recovery), a plan tool for order-dependent fixes, provenance grading for writes justified by untrusted content, a live storefront that breaks and recovers. Verified: 229 unit tests, 144 hit-tested Playwright gates, 91 machine-checked scenario variants, Chrome webmcp-evals 24/24 live, Lighthouse agentic 4/4, 488 real-model runs. Found and filed against the spec: a host that both calls tools and drives the DOM can complete the page's human step itself (webmachinelearning/webmcp#288, with a one-file repro and a page-side mitigation verified against the host). Live: https://release-airlock.vercel.app · Repo: https://github.com/Sidharth1999/webmcp-airlock Inspiration An on-call engineer, mid-incident, probably awakened at like 4am by their PagerDuty, wants an agent's speed without handing it authority over production -- speed literally means less revenue lost to the business and less users impacted by outages. But we can't be careless about what agents are allowed to do with our systems. This is not a hypothetical based on some research. In the last fourteen months there have been nine documented cases of a coding agent destroying data, most of them with a permission system switched on that the agent talked its way past. Examples: https://adversa.ai/blog/ai-coding-agent-incidents/ https://mondoo.com/blog/5-lessons-from-9-seconds-ai-agent-deleted-production-database Every one of those permission systems lived either inside the model, which can be argued out of anything, or in a generic host confirmation, which knows the verb and the target and nothing about where the idea came from or what the operator is looking at. Three more facts shaped the design. The cost of an incident is deciding, not clicking ( Rootly ). Mitigation happens in a console, and the kill switch beats the rollback ( LaunchDarkly ). Stage-gated access is an established pattern, just-in-time and break-glass ( IBM ). And Chrome's own WebMCP security guide asks for exactly this shape: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model" ( secure tools ). WebMCP puts the tool server in the page. For this problem, that location is the whole point. The page is where the operator, the evidence, and the levers already are, so the page can be the authority on what the agent may do. What it does Release Airlock is a deploy and incident console where an agent can reach every lever, and not one of them moves without you. Live: https://release-airlock.vercel.app (opens inside a running incident; works in ChatGPT's in-app browser and in Chrome with WebMCP enabled) Source, MIT: https://github.com/Sidharth1999/webmcp-airlock Video: https://youtu.be/gqN-fXtGodk It exposes 27 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext: six reads, a notebook the agent writes its findings into, nineteen propose_* writes, and propose_plan. A write tool's entire effect is to put a card in front of the operator. The world moves when a person decides, and not before. The tool surface is a function of console state. Move the response stage from Triage to Diagnosis to Recovery and tools are registered and unregistered underneath the live session (AbortController, so a real host fires toolchange). Triage grants 13 tools. Nothing that touches production exists in Triage; it is absent, not gated. A withdrawn tool leaves a tombstone, and explain_surface tells the agent why its capabilities changed. The gate is re-checked when the human decides, against the stage the operator has set by then. The page grades the evidence it served. Every read is audited into the same event log the page renders from. When an agent proposes rolling back a deploy id that appeared nowhere in the console's state and reached the agent only inside a customer-supplied log line, the card quotes the line, names the read that served it, and promotes the write to a two-key approval. For the operator, an incident is a stitching problem. The hard incidents are the ones where the order you do things in decides the outcome, and no single screen says "shed load first." The agent is good at exactly that stitching, and the console lets you audit the stitching before you let it act: One ledger. Every beat is a row on one spine: connect, each tool call, each finding, the plan, each step, what that step did. A tool call opens onto the exact bytes the agent got back, with the log position they reflect and a link to the console surface they came from. A citation is a place. "Contention cleared (#42)" is a button that lands you on log line 42. The agent objects before your click. Reach for a control it has ruled out and its reasoning appears beside that control. It counsels; it never blocks. A plan numbers the console rows it will touch and prices every step. Every executed write says what it did. When nothing moved, it says why: "No effect: scale to 9 has no effect, the autoscaler ceiling for api is 6." The customer is on screen. A storefront breaks when the incident starts, shows the status post you approved at step 4 word for word, and takes payments again when the fix lands. The receipt reads 7 of 7 approved by you, 0 writes went round you. While an agent host is attached, approval is a held gesture, not a click. The console stands on its own without an agent. Every lever is clickable by hand, states its cost, and is worth having on a bad day. How we built it One event log is the truth. The world is a pure fold over it; the UI, the tool results, and the metrics all derive from (events, world). There is no second source of state to drift. A Web Worker owns the log ; the main thread renders and forwards. The tests and the unattended driver invoke tools through the same execute path real WebMCP uses. 27 tools, documented from the registration path itself. The surface reference in the repo is generated by walking the real registration code through every stage, so it cannot disagree with the bundle. Reads return pages under 1.2 KB with a log position on every answer. Writes return only a proposal id. The gate is checked on both sides. One table decides what the agent can see; a separate table decides what the engine will execute; a test asserts they agree, because the engine must never trust that a tool was unregistered. Determinism is enforced. No wall clock and no randomness anywhere in the simulator; a linter fails the build. Same seed, byte-identical replay. Scenarios are compiled and verified, not asserted. 91 variants across four families are machine-generated and accepted only if a scripted correct run beats doing nothing and every declared trap costs more than doing nothing, probed to the same horizon. 229 unit and property tests, 142 hit-tested Playwright gates against the real page, CI on every push. No backend, no API keys; it runs in the browser. Challenges we ran into UX. Vibe-coding the UX for the project was a huge uphill battle and required hours of ruthlessness and discipline on teaching AI how to effectively present information on a page. Release Airlock deals with so much system state information and computation over with with an AI agent and that density needed to be presented really well in juxtaposition with the actual layout of an incident console. There were at least 20 iterations that were roughly functional before we landed on the most satisfactory one. AI frustration. Prompting is extremely taxing and simply aligning your vision with your AI is an uphill battle. It makes strange assumptions, gaslights you about completed work, and will sometimes even reject your judgment when it's the right call. It's important here to always have a bearing on the state of the project so you can actually assume authority on direction without the project getting derailed by your AI. A paginated tool whose contract lived only in prose the model skims. The first paid model run opened every read with cursor 0, and three tools answered with a silently empty page. The model reasoned about an incident having seen no deploys, no logs, and no traffic. The fix was one sentence in the description: "Omit it for the newest page; there is no page 0."
