title: Glassmap
pitch: A web map is a WebGL canvas — a black box to AI agents. WebMCP makes it glass.
about_excerpt: A web map is a WebGL canvas — a black box to AI agents. WebMCP makes it glass. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Inspiration I come from a GIS background, and I have worked on many web map applications for different clients. One problem I keep running into is that AI agents are still not very good at dealing with maps. When I use AI to help with application development, debugging, or QA, everything usually works fine until the agent reaches the map. A web map is often rendered as a WebGL canvas, so the agent cannot easily understand what is actually on the map, which features are being displayed, or what happened after an interaction. Sometimes it simply cannot continue. Other times, it tries to rely on screenshots and visual interactions, but the result is often inaccurate or unreliable. This has always felt like a major limitation to me, especially because maps are not just visual content. Behind the screen, they contain structured geographic data, layers, coordinates, features, spatial relationships, and actions. When I learned about WebMCP, I immediately saw a way to solve this problem. Instead of forcing an agent to understand a map through pixels, the map can directly expose its data and capabilities as tools. That idea became the starting point for GlassMap . My goal was to make a web map that is no longer a black box to AI agents. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from this project was WebMCP itself. I spent a lot of time thinking beyond the basic question of “how do I expose a function as a WebMCP tool?” The more interesting question for me was: What kinds of experiences become possible when an AI agent can directly interact with a website through structured tools? While building GlassMap, I kept looking for use cases where WebMCP could do more than simply make an existing feature easier to automate. For example, instead of an agent looking at a screenshot and guessing which places are inside an area, it can directly ask the map for features within an exact spatial boundary. Instead of trying to reproduce a sequence of mouse clicks, it can work directly with map objects, coordinates, routes, and geographic queries. That changed how I thought about the project. WebMCP is not only a better way for an agent to operate an existing interface. In some cases, it can enable an entirely different user experience where the human, the application, and the AI agent all work with the same underlying state. That gave me many new ideas for projects I would like to explore in the future. How I built it GlassMap is a web map built with Next.js, MapLibre, OpenStreetMap data, Turf.js, and Zustand . MapLibre handles the map visualization, while Turf.js performs spatial operations directly in the browser. The application exposes map capabilities through 15 WebMCP tools , including operations for searching places, querying nearby features, working with map objects, changing the map view, adding notes, and planning routes. I designed the WebMCP layer separately from the map UI through a common store interface. This makes the tools easier to test and allows both the human interface and the AI agent to operate on the same map state. I also added a development shim so that the WebMCP tools can be tested in browsers that do not yet support the API natively. One thing this project also reminded me of is that, with today's AI coding tools, actually implementing an application is becoming much easier. The harder questions are increasingly: How should the system be designed? and What should the user experience actually be? Those were much more difficult for me than writing the code itself. Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was actually deciding how to use WebMCP well . This is a WebMCP hackathon, so it would have been easy to build a normal web application first and then add a few WebMCP tools on top of it just to satisfy the requirement. I did not want to do that. I wanted GlassMap to be a project where WebMCP is fundamental to the experience — where removing WebMCP would remove one of the main reasons the product exists. Because of that, I spent a lot of time thinking about the user experience instead of simply adding more tools. I asked questions like: What should an agent be able to understand about the map? What operations are actually useful as tools? What should happen when both a human and an agent are working on the same map? When should the agent return structured information instead of trying to manipulate the interface? And most importantly, what can WebMCP enable that would be difficult or unreliable with a traditional screenshot-based agent? That design process was probably the hardest part of the project. Building the features was relatively straightforward. Deciding which features should exist, how they should work together, and how WebMCP could genuinely improve the experience took much more thought. For me, that is also the most interesting part of building AI-native applications today. The bottleneck is becoming less about whether we can build something, and more about whether we can design the right system and the right experience around it. title: EasyTax - Your convenient tax WebMCP
pitch: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission.
about_excerpt: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates The Problem Filing an annual individual tax return (1770 S) under Indonesia's centralized Coretax system creates a learning curve for salaried workers. Translating personal life events into rigid government tax classifications creates a high burden and confusion across generations. Knowing your salary or family situation is different from knowing which tax field or classification it belongs in. While the system offers spreadsheet bulk uploads to bypass manual entry, they frequently fail due to minor error, forcing users back to rework manual entry or exposing them to server timeouts during peak traffic. Independent sentiment analysis of over 53,000 digital conversations during the early rollout Coretax system revealed that 39% of user sentiment was negative, driven by procedural confusion and system navigation (Source: Journal UII / 2025 ). Despite these points, the submission is massive. By late April 2026, over 13 million annual tax returns were filed following the activation of nearly 12.9 million individual accounts (Source: Tempo.co ). The Solution: Human-Agent Collaboration via WebMCP This project demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a complex tax administration portal into a collaborative interface. Rather than hiding the form's complexity or forcing users to navigate hidden form logic, the browser exposes section-level tools directly to the assistant, keeping the detailed form visible to ensure user review control capability. The Workflow Conversational Extraction: The assistant conducts a plain-language interview to extract necessary tax facts such as salary, deductions, and family status without requiring users to memorize form codes or tax classifications. They can use their own ways to describe their condition and an AI assistant will translate it. For example, when a user says, “My employer was PT Nusantara Digital, gross salary 180 million for the year, 6 million in pay deductions,” WebMCP translates it into: “Records the employment slip, derives net income, recomputes the tax.” Deterministic State Updates: As facts are confirmed, the assistant invokes section-level WebMCP tools (such as updating taxpayer profiles, recording employment, or adding cash and assets). The website itself handles all validation, calculation, and conditional branching, deriving fields like PTKP (e.g., K/1) and recomputing the tax balance automatically. Manual Submission: Final review, resolution of data conflicts, declaration, and submission remain strictly manual. No tool can execute a final filing, and the assistant explicitly states this if asked. title: RippleTrace
pitch: RippleTrace lets agents investigate enterprise evidence and propose remediation via WebMCP, while humans retain review and approval-making change discoverable, verifiable, and safe to execute.
about_excerpt:
RippleTrace lets agents investigate enterprise evidence and propose remediation via WebMCP, while humans retain review and approval-making change discoverable, verifiable, and safe to execute.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The idea for RippleTrace came from my experience working at a software company. Whenever a feature, configuration change, or update was pushed to production, I watched DevOps engineers manually check multiple platforms to trace its potential consequences. 

 They had to move between deployment dashboards, monitoring tools, logs, incident systems, and other services to understand whether the change had caused something downstream to fail. The information was available, but it was fragmented across different interfaces. During a production incident, every minute spent switching platforms and reconstructing context mattered. 

 That experience inspired RippleTrace: a faster way to trace the ripple effects of a production change, understand which systems may be affected, and identify where an investigation should begin. 

 What it does 

 RippleTrace helps engineering and DevOps teams investigate the potential impact of production changes from one place. 

 A user can begin with a deployment, commit, service, or incident. RippleTrace then gathers the relevant signals, connects related events, and presents them as a single investigation trail. Instead of manually checking every platform, the user can follow the path of a change and see how it may have affected the wider system. 

 RippleTrace is designed to help answer questions such as: 

 
 What changed immediately before an issue appeared? 
 Which services or dependencies could be affected? 
 Are errors, alerts, or other events connected to the deployment? 
 What should the team investigate first? 
 What evidence can be shared with the rest of the team? 
 

 The goal is not to replace engineers’ judgment. It is to reduce the repetitive work required to collect context so engineers can spend more time understanding and resolving the actual problem. 

 How we built it 

 We built RippleTrace as a unified investigation experience for production changes. It organizes information from different engineering platforms into a consistent model of changes, services, events, and possible consequences. 

 We used WebMCP to make the product’s capabilities directly understandable to AI agents. RippleTrace exposes structured tools that describe the actions an agent can perform and the information it can retrieve. 

 This allows an AI assistant to work with explicit application capabilities instead of attempting to interpret the interface through screenshots, page text, or fragile click sequences. An agent can request relevant deployment context, examine related signals, and help the user navigate an investigation through well-defined inputs and outputs. 

 The human-facing dashboard and the WebMCP tool layer operate on the same underlying context. This means users can visually inspect the evidence while an AI assistant helps them explore it. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was connecting information from platforms that represent the same incident in very different ways. A deployment, an alert, an error, and a service may all have different identifiers and timestamps. Establishing useful relationships between them requires careful normalization and correlation. 

 Another challenge was determining how much confidence RippleTrace should place in a possible connection. Events that occur close together are not necessarily related. We therefore designed the experience to present evidence and potential relationships without claiming certainty where it does not exist. 

 Designing the WebMCP tools was also an important challenge. Each tool needed to be focused enough for an agent to use reliably while still returning enough context to support a meaningful investigation. Clear descriptions, predictable parameters, and structured responses were essential. 

 Finally, we had to keep the AI workflow transparent. Production investigations are high-stakes, so users should be able to see why something was surfaced and verify the underlying evidence themselves. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that much of incident response is not a lack of data—it is a lack of connected context. Teams already have valuable information, but it is distributed across tools that were designed for separate stages of the software lifecycle. 

 We also learned that building an agent-ready web application requires more than placing a conversational interface on top of it. An effective AI experience needs clearly defined capabilities, structured data, useful metadata, and strong boundaries. 

 WebMCP provides a practical way to expose those capabilities directly from the web application. It gives an AI agent a shared language for interacting with the product while keeping the user in control. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that RippleTrace turns a fragmented, multi-platform investigation into a more coherent workflow. 

 We created an experience that supports both people and AI agents: engineers can inspect the information visually, while agents can access the same capabilities through structured WebMCP tools. We are also proud that the product focuses on assisting human decision-making rather than hiding the investigation behind an unexplained AI answer. 

 Most importantly, RippleTrace was built around a real problem we observed in production environments—the time and effort engineers spend tracing the consequences of every change. 

 What's next for RippleTrace 

 Next, we want to expand the number of platforms and data sources that RippleTrace can connect with. We also plan to improve event correlation, service-dependency mapping, investigation timelines, and team collaboration. 

 Future versions could proactively identify unusual signals after a deployment, compare current behavior with previous releases, generate incident summaries, and recommend the most relevant next steps. We also want to add configurable policies so organizations can control which actions AI agents may perform and what information they can access. 

 Our long-term goal is for RippleTrace to become the starting point for every production investigation: one place where teams can trace a change, understand its ripple effects, and respond with confidence.

title: Space Auto - MCP for Dealerships
pitch: Space Auto made car dealership websites agent-native: WebMCP tools serving live inventory and submitting real leads to dealership's CRM. Example sites: evauto.com, svgmotors.com, mandalautogroup.com
about_excerpt: Space Auto made car dealership websites agent-native: WebMCP tools serving live inventory and submitting real leads to dealership's CRM. Example sites: evauto.com, svgmotors.com, mandalautogroup.com Like Comment Story Updates MCP via ChatGPT's built-in browser User submits a lead inquiry to the dealership's CRM. MCP via browser extension Judges: Open one of these example sites in the ChatGPT in-app browser, and ask about inventory or store hours: evauto.com mandalautogroup.com svgmotors.com Then run SpaceWebMCP.debug() in the console, if you'd like to explore the tools as well as a live counter of actual agent tool invocations on the page ("calls"): { "api": "document", "tools": ["search_inventory", "get_vehicle_details", "get_dealership_info", "submit_lead"], "calls": { "search_inventory": 1 } } In Chrome 149+, enable the WebMCP flag. Our origin-trial token is already active on evauto.com. You can also point Model Context Tool Inspector at the tab. Inspiration Buying a car might be one of the most agent-worthy purchases a person can make. Shoppers can spend hours filtering inventory, comparing vehicles, checking prices, and jumping around multiple websites. Those sites also tend to be JavaScript-heavy, which makes them especially easy for screen-scraping agents to get wrong. And when an agent gets something wrong on a car site, it might be misquoting the price of a $40,000 purchase. We run Space Auto, a platform behind real dealership websites, so we made every website on our platform agent-native. Then we took it a step further. If an agent can search a dealer's inventory and help someone choose a vehicle, it should also be able to finish the job and hand the dealership a real customer. What it does Every dealership site on Space Auto's website platform registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . search_inventory Searches the dealership's current, live inventory by condition, make/model, body style, fuel type, price, year, and mileage. It returns real vehicles with current prices, photos, and links to each vehicle detail page. get_vehicle_details Returns the full vehicle specs and the itemized price breakdown for a VIN using the same pricing engine that renders on the website. An agent cannot quote a price the dealer doesn't advertise. get_dealership_info Returns dealership locations, phone numbers, hours, and holiday-aware open/closed status. submit_lead With the shopper's explicit consent, submit_lead sends their name, contact information, and the vehicle they're interested in to the dealership as a real sales lead, or a test drive appointment. Every answer from the read tools ends with a natural next step, like asking whether the shopper wants to schedule a test drive or check availability. If the user says yes, the agent collects their contact information, confirms consent, and submits the lead. If the user says no, it drops the subject. show_search_results Drives the dealership's own search results page so the shopper can actually watch the filters being applied. The full funnel The demo video shows the entire process: Inventory Search Live results from the dealership's current inventory. Inventory Question Vehicle details and pricing using the same tools. Inventory Selection The assistant offers the next step of the process, such as making a test drive appointment or checking availability. Submit Lead With explicit consent, submit_lead sends the shopper's information to the dealer's Auto Agent Protocol endpoint. No API keys are required. See it in the CRM The lead arrives in the dealership's Space Auto CRM within seconds, attributed to the AI assistant. How we built it The read side is JavaScript file with no build step necessary. It wraps the Space Auto platform's native services, including the public inventory API client, a shared vehicle cache, and dealership config globals. There's nothing an agent can access that a shopper couldn't access themselves. The lead path took more thought. The browser tool posts to a small REST proxy on the dealership site. That proxy validates everything before a lead can go anywhere. It requires a real name, a valid email address or phone number, and explicit confirmation of consent. It also rate-limits submissions by IP. Once validated, the proxy builds an Auto Agent Protocol lead.submit request and sends it to the dealership's own AAP endpoint. Every dealership on the platform already publishes a public agent card. The proxy reads that card to discover the dealership's AAP endpoint automatically. That means there are no API keys required anywhere in the end to end flow, and nothing to provision for each dealership. Repeated submissions for the same shopper and vehicle on the same day are deduplicated, and every lead includes a formal consent record: { "consent": { "granted_at": "2026-09-03T18:11:14+00:00", "allowed_channels": ["email", "phone"], "consent_text": "I agree that the dealership may contact me by email or phone about this vehicle.", "scope": ["lead_submission"] } } Challenges we ran into Our first lead design used per-dealership API keys for our external API. However, provisioning and managing keys across a network of dealership sites would be a huge chore, so the agent-card approach solved that problem. We went from managing credentials for every dealership to requiring zero credentials in the browser flow. ChatGPT's in-app browser exposes document.modelContext . Our tools registered successfully. Then ChatGPT answered inventory questions by reading the page anyway. Registered does not mean invoked; we found a registration race first. We had been registering the tools inside an idle callback, which could delay registration by up to four seconds. Agents can snapshot the available toolset as navigation settles, so sometimes our tools simply weren't present when that happened. We fixed the timing and added call counters to SpaceWebMCP.debug() . Accomplishments we're proud of This isn't running against sample inventory or a hackathon-only environment. It's live, in production, on every dealership website on our platform. What we learned Progressive enhancement is what made WebMCP practical to ship. A dealership page with WebMCP tools still behaves exactly the same for every browser and shopper that doesn't use them. What's next We are already looking at the next pieces: Fleet-wide Chrome coverage once the API reaches GA, or through a third-party trial token in the meantime. Support trade-in inquiries through the same lead flow. Better offer language, based on real conversation and invocation data from our tool call counters. The goal is simple: a dealership website shouldn't just be readable by an AI agent. It should give the agent a safe, structured way to actually help shoppers explore dealership websites as they're searching for their next vehicle. title: Kitty
pitch: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed.
about_excerpt: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group orders always end the same way: one person becomes the unpaid dispatcher, allergies get missed, and the bill math takes longer than the meal did. We wanted agents to take over the boring parts — without losing what makes ordering together social. What it does Kitty is a shared order page where everyone's own AI agent adds their items and dietary restrictions straight into one live cart via WebMCP tools — no forms, no relaying your order through one exhausted human. The host locks the order in, and Kitty splits the bill automatically. How we built it Seven document.modelContext.registerTool() calls — browse_menu , add_item , remove_item , set_dietary_restriction , get_order_summary , split_bill , finalize_order — on a Next.js app on Vercel. Every mutating call is scoped server-side to the calling participant's identity, so an agent can only ever touch its own order. State lives in a lightweight session store, synced to every viewer with plain polling — no infrastructure we didn't need. Challenges we ran into Letting several independent agents write to one shared cart safely was the real problem. WebMCP's tool boundaries had to double as both a UX contract and a security boundary — otherwise a confused or malicious agent could overwrite someone else's order or invent a priced item that doesn't exist on the menu. Accomplishments that we're proud of Real multi-agent collaboration on one mutable session — not just one agent talking to one app — with guardrails (menu allow-lists, per-participant scoping, host-only finalize) tight enough we'd trust it with an actual office lunch order. What we learned WebMCP tools aren't just an API surface — they're a trust boundary. The moment more than one agent can touch the same state, "what should this tool refuse to do" matters as much as "what should it do." What's next for Kitty Itemized (not just equal) bill splitting, real restaurant menu imports, and letting a host's agent negotiate directly with a restaurant's own WebMCP tools once more storefronts expose them.  Inspiration 

 I love solving Sudoku puzzles like many of us. Sudoku is one of the world’s purest logic games. 

 But online Sudoku has a physical barrier for some people. Solving a hard puzzle requires numerous micro-clicks. For many people living with essential tremors, RSI (repetitive strain injury), or motor disabilities, the physical tax ruins the mental joy. 

 Purpose of Agentic Sudoku is to enable users to play online Sudoku hands free , assisted by Agent. 

 What it does 

 Human Speaks in Codex App -> Agent uses WebMCP -> Action happens on Sudoku Board. 

 Agentic Sudoku is an online Sudoku puzzle application powered by WebMCP. 

 It enables the human and agent to collaborate while solving Sudoku. 

 Human can play Sudoku hands free with help of Agent. 

 18 WebMCP tools are configured which let user do everything by talking to agent. 

 A Codex Skill is delivered to open the web application in the in-app browser and just solve Sudoku puzzle hands free (by talking to agent). 

 How it was built 

 Agentic Sudoku is a 100% client-side, zero-backend application designed for seamless WebMCP integration. 

 Frontend - Next.js (App Router), React, and Tailwind CSS. 

 WebMCP Architecture - WebMCP tools which can read, annotate, act and control Sudoku. So that human only has to speak to agent without placing hands on keyboard. 

 Puzzle Engine - sudoku-gen for client-side board generation. 

 Codex Skill Integration - A dedicated standard Codex Skill included in the repository, giving OpenAI agents an out-of-the-box playbook for navigating the site, executing coaching sequences, and providing hands-free accessibility. 

 Hosting - Deployed on Vercel. 

 Spec-Driven Development - The project was built using SpecKit. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was designing the WebMCP schema. Had to carefully engineer the tools to ensure they never expose the puzzle’s final hidden solution. The agent must reason dynamically using only the visible board constraints to guide the player. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Successfully decoupled joy of Sudoku from the physical friction of playing it. 
 Shipped robust WebMCP tools. 
 

 Learnings 

 Hands on experience with WebMCP. It turns the browser DOM into a shared, collaborative workspace. 

 What's next for Agentic Sudoku 

 
 Allowing users to scan a Sudoku puzzle from a physical newspaper using their camera, parse it into the web app.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Faultline
pitch: Design a cloud architecture with your AI agent on a shared canvas, then fail an availability zone or region and watch the blast radius spread. Price it, lint it, generate the Terraform, together
about_excerpt: Design a cloud architecture with your AI agent on a shared canvas, then fail an availability zone or region and watch the blast radius spread. Price it, lint it, generate the Terraform, together Like 1 Comment Story Updates Failing a zone: the agent runs the blast-radius analysis, nodes go red, resilience score drops to 61/100 with a DDIA-cited finding The agent swaps the database to Aurora and prices it: a before/after table showing +$49/month, beside the tool-call log "Explain the database node." The app panel and the agent both trace what depends on it and what fails if it dies The /learn route: all 13 WebMCP tools and their live schemas, as the agent sees them Per-resource monthly cost of a resilient three-tier stack, about $377 "Cheapest thing that runs." The agent reads the intent and lays down a single-AZ stack at $202/month Inspiration I work as a solutions architect. The job runs on a loop: sketch a topology, ask what breaks if an availability zone dies, argue the trade-off, write the Terraform, run a lint, repeat. A language model is good at that kind of reasoning, but only when it can work against the same diagram I'm looking at. An agent that takes screenshots and clicks can't read a canvas, and it can't run a blast-radius analysis over one. WebMCP fixes that. The page hands the agent the architecture graph and the analysis engine as typed tools, so it edits the same model I'm dragging around. What it does Faultline is an infinite canvas where you and your browser agent design cloud infrastructure together. You describe a system in a sentence and propose-architecture lays down a connected, configured, placed topology. The agent wires up dependencies, picks provider variants, explains any node or edge (its role, its blast radius, the principle behind it), and estimate-cost attaches a monthly-dollar figure to the design and to every change you make. Either of you can then run simulate-failure on one availability zone or a whole region, and the diagram turns red and amber as the outage spreads along the edges. Single points of failure get ringed. resilience-lint names the anti-patterns it finds and points each one at the chapter of Designing Data-Intensive Applications that explains why it matters. generate-iac writes the Terraform. Every tool also has a button in the UI, so the app works on its own; the agent is what makes the loop fast. How we built it A Rust compute core compiled to WASM. The graph model, the sentence-to-topology proposer, the blast-radius analysis for zone and region failures, the single-point-of-failure scan, the cost estimator, the resilience-lint rules, and the Terraform emitter all live in one pure library with #![forbid(unsafe_code)] , no async runtime, and about 90 tests. Both the UI and the WebMCP tools call into it, so they can't drift apart. A Svelte 5 and Vite shell. The canvas (pan, zoom, drag, orthogonal edges, status overlays) is hand-written SVG with no diagram library. 13 intent-level WebMCP tools in thin TypeScript against document.modelContext , one file each. They stay coarse rather than CRUD: propose-architecture turns a sentence into a topology, configure-resource sets variant, region, zone, and validation in a single call. Pure reads are marked readOnlyHint ; anything that echoes a label a human typed is marked untrustedContentHint . The /learn route lists every tool and its schema, live. Test-first, and the git history shows it. CI runs formatting, clippy, unit tests, headless-Chrome WASM tests, cargo-deny, Biome, the build, and a Playwright run of the full demo on every push. The site deploys statically to Cloudflare Pages under a strict CSP. Challenges we ran into In real Chrome, executeTool receives its input as a JSON string rather than an object, and the polyfill I developed against is more forgiving, so every tool's execute had to accept both. Keeping the tools intent-level took restraint: the quick version is set-node-property , the version worth having is configure-resource checking variant, region, and zone against a bundled provider profile before it commits. Everything crossing the WASM boundary is a string, so the Rust side has to keep its JSON readable by older documents as the schema grows. And because the agent never sees the rendered canvas, every visible cue (red nodes, failure rings, the outage banner) had to be computed from data the agent can read back just as easily. Accomplishments that we're proud of The resilience lint cites a specific book chapter for every finding rather than hand-waving, and the findings come from deterministic graph checks, so the agent can explain them instead of guessing. The failure simulator covers two failure domains, which lets it show you that a Multi-AZ database survives a zone outage but still goes down with its region. Because every tool runs through the same core the UI uses, the agent behaves like a design partner rather than a brittle UI script. Tool calls return in a few milliseconds. What we learned WebMCP works best when the page is a real domain model with an MCP interface on top, not a pile of buttons to press. Once the tools delegated to a tested core instead of carrying their own logic, the agent got noticeably more reliable. The Rust and WASM core turned out to be worth the setup cost: few other entries take that route, and the determinism it buys is what you want when an agent is going to read your results back to a user. What's next for Faultline GCP and Azure profiles over the same neutral core. The profile is already plain JSON, so another provider is a config file rather than a release. A staged accept-or-reject overlay so the agent's bigger edits preview before they land. Importing an existing Terraform state and linting that. Packaging Faultline as a standalone MCP server, so faultline check can run in CI and publish the resilience score as an artifact. Built With amazon-web-services biome cloudflare-pages document.modelcontext github-actions hcl model-context-protocol playwright rust svelte svg terraform typescript vite vitest wasm-bindgen wasm-pack webassembly webmcp Try it out faultline-studio.pages.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo project. I designed the concept and built all of it: the Rust/WASM compute core (graph model, blast-radius analysis, cost estimator, resilience lint, Terraform emitter), the Svelte canvas, all 13 WebMCP tools, the CI pipeline, and the Cloudflare deploy. title: CapStash WebGPU Verification Lab
pitch: A WebMCP-enabled WebGPU lab where agents can safely run correctness-gated GPU experiments, share state with the human UI, and refuse unsupported performance conclusions.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-enabled WebGPU lab where agents can safely run correctness-gated GPU experiments, share state with the human UI, and refuse unsupported performance conclusions. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Main app + green safety notice Four WebMCP tools visible in Chrome DevTools Completed WG1/WG32 comparison result Inspiration I originally built this project to explore whether CapStash Proof-of-Work could be implemented and verified in the browser with WebGPU. Part of the idea was crypto onboarding: giving people a low-barrier way to inspect how this kind of computation works on their own hardware, run some basic tests, and see the results for themselves without needing to set up a traditional miner. I also liked the idea of eventually making it a little more playful — something where a person could contribute a small amount of browser compute and get something back like a meme, a fortune, or maybe some kind of AI or social interaction. The underlying workload comes from a cryptocurrency Proof-of-Work algorithm, but this project is intentionally a local research and verification tool. There is no live mining . It does not connect to a blockchain network, mining pool, wallet, payout system, RPC service, or block-submission service. Before the WebMCP Challenge, the project had already grown into a fairly complete human-operated WebGPU experiment lab with CPU reference verification, CapStash Core-derived test vectors, profiling, workgroup experiments, and a Guided/Advanced browser UI. Sometime in early August, after manually clicking through my testing suite again, I said to myself, “Why can’t I just make this automated and operable by AI?” At the time, I was bouncing back and forth between ChatGPT, Codex, browser windows, screenshots, and different settings. Because the agent was still interacting with the interface indirectly, I often had to send screenshots or find things manually myself. I was also learning a lot of the underlying technology as I went. When I saw the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, the project seemed like a natural fit for a different question: What happens when an AI agent can operate a technical browser instrument through structured tools instead of scraping the DOM or pretending to click buttons? What it does The browser exposes four WebMCP tools: inspect_compute_environment verify_correctness start_workgroup_comparison get_experiment_status An agent can inspect the available WebGPU environment without starting computation, request bounded correctness verification, start a longer WG1-vs-WG32 experiment, and read structured experiment progress and results. The main workflow asks: Determine whether workgroup size 32 is meaningfully better than workgroup size 1 on this GPU. Verify both configurations first, run a matched comparison, and only recommend a winner if the evidence supports one. Before the longer workload begins, the page requires explicit user approval and clearly describes the local compute workload. After approval, the application automatically: validates WG1 support and compilation, runs its small correctness gate, verifies WG1 against all 294 CapStash Core vectors, performs the same checks for WG32, runs three matched profiling samples for each workgroup size, reports the result through both the human UI and structured WebMCP state. The same existing experiment controller is used by humans and agents. WebMCP does not duplicate the GPU engine or bypass its correctness rules. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent would have to interpret a complicated technical interface, manipulate controls, scrape visible text, and infer whether prerequisites had actually completed. That was one of the things I kept running into while using browser agents myself. They can do a lot by clicking through pages and interpreting what is on screen, but they do not always see an interface the same way a human does. Sometimes they are effectively working from fragments and inferring the rest. With WebMCP, the application can expose the intent and state of the experiment directly in a machine-readable form while still keeping the normal human interface. The agent can request a high-level goal while the application remains responsible for: prerequisite sequencing, correctness gates, experiment concurrency, structured progress, result accounting, safety boundaries, and recommendation policy. An important part of the project is that the agent cannot simply choose whichever performance number looks better. The pre-existing comparison logic includes variability limits and a minimum practical-difference threshold. If the evidence is too noisy or the performance difference is too small, the WebMCP result returns no recommendation. For example, validated runs have correctly returned classifications such as: host-side variability too high for a recommendation effectively tied within observed variability with: recommendationAllowed: false recommendation: null That behavior is intentional. WebMCP makes the instrument agent-operable without weakening its evidence standards. How I built it The application is dependency-free browser JavaScript with: HTML/CSS JavaScript WebGPU WGSL compute shaders a CPU Whirlpool-512 reference implementation deterministic CapStash Core-derived verification vectors WebMCP through document.modelContext static Cloudflare Pages hosting The public challenge repository contains a reconstructed, privacy-sanitized history that preserves the exact pre-challenge baseline and the exact challenge-period changes. The WebMCP work added during the challenge includes: structured WebMCP tool registration, environment inspection, correctness invocation, shared human/agent application state, an asynchronous experiment lifecycle, prerequisite-aware WG1/WG32 orchestration, structured recommendation blockers, consent for longer agent-triggered compute, and WebMCP-specific tests and documentation. The underlying WebGPU hashing, correctness engine, workgroup experiments, profiling, statistics, and human UI all existed before the challenge and are clearly documented as such. Testing and correctness The current project passes: 130 / 130 automated tests 294 / 294 CapStash Core vectors zero CPU/Core mismatches zero WGSL/Core mismatches in validated full runs The final release-hardened workflow was also tested in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. A full approved matched comparison completed: WG1 full verification: 294 / 294 WG32 full verification: 294 / 294 3 valid WG1 samples 3 valid WG32 samples 6 total valid samples 49,152 requested/completed/returned hashes 30 CPU spot checks 0 mismatches 0 pipeline errors 0 device losses 0 deterministic-ordering failures The deployed public site is HTTPS, WebGPU-capable, WebMCP origin-trial enabled, and exposes all four tools in ordinary Chrome. Challenges One thing that surprised me was how quickly the application could actually perform a lot of the work once the WebGPU path was working. I was still learning much of the technology, so seeing the verification and profiling complete as quickly as they did was pretty impressive to me. That also made correctness more important, not less. I added correctness gates fairly early in the project because I did not want speed or interesting benchmark numbers to mean anything unless the output was actually trustworthy. Those gates eventually grew into full CPU/Core/WGSL comparisons and the 294-vector verification used by the final workflow. One lesson I kept coming back to was that when you are building around unfamiliar technology — especially with AI helping — you need strict build rules, safety boundaries, and acceptance criteria. Otherwise it is very easy to get something that looks impressive without really knowing whether it is correct. A more specific WebMCP challenge was handling long-running browser GPU work. Cold WebGPU pipeline compilation could sometimes take more than 20 seconds, which was not a good fit for holding a single WebMCP tool invocation open. The solution was an asynchronous experiment lifecycle: the start tool returns immediately with an experiment ID, while get_experiment_status exposes structured progress and the final result. Another challenge was preserving user control. The longer comparison now enters an awaiting_consent state and starts no GPU work until the user explicitly approves the local workload. A third challenge was provenance. This project existed before the challenge, so I wanted the public submission to make that completely transparent. The repository preserves an exact pre-challenge tree followed by the WebMCP challenge changes and documents the original private source SHAs in PROVENANCE.md . Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am especially proud that the final WebMCP workflow does not bypass the testing system I had already built. The agent uses the same experiment controller and the same correctness gates as the human interface. WG1 and WG32 both have to pass full verification before the comparison is allowed to continue

An agent-native production ops dashboard built with WebMCP allowing AI agents to monitor telemetry, execute Kubernetes replica autos-caling, and perform synthetic web tests in real time.

 Inspiration 

 During high-severity incident responses, engineers often spend critical minutes toggling between multiple monitoring dashboards, terminal windows, and cloud control panels. We wanted to build a web application designed specifically for the agent-native era—a unified workspace where human operators and AI agents collaborate seamlessly during system outages to diagnose latency spikes, inspect telemetry, and execute infrastructure remediation natively. 

 What it does: 

 OpsDesk WebMCP is an agent-native DevOps management workspace that exposes client-side operations directly to AI agents using the WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ). Key functionalities include: 

 
 Cluster Health Inspection ( get_cluster_metrics ): Enables agents to fetch live CPU usage, memory footprint, p99 latency, and error rates for targeted microservices. 
 Dynamic Infrastructure Autoscaling ( scale_service_replicas ): Allows agents to scale pod replica counts up or down to mitigate degraded service performance, updating the visual dashboard UI in real-time. 
 Synthetic Availability Testing ( run_synthetic_web_test ): Triggers browser automation benchmarks to check UI accessibility and endpoint response times. 
 

 How we built it: 

 
 Frontend & UI: Built using React and Tailwind CSS to render real-time service health, status indicators, and active pod replica counters. 
 WebMCP Integration: Integrated @modelcontextprotocol/sdk on the client side, exposing native tool signatures directly via document.modelContext.registerTool . 
 Agent Interoperability: Designed structured JSON input schemas and return payloads compatible with ChatGPT's in-app browser and WebMCP-enabled environments. 
 

 Challenges we ran into: 

 
 Client-Side Tool Synchronization: Ensuring state changes executed by an agent tool call (e.g., scaling replicas) triggered immediate visual UI updates in the React component hierarchy without requiring page refreshes. 
 Schema Precision: Crafting clear, deterministic tool descriptions and JSON schemas so LLMs select the correct diagnostic or action tool under varied prompting scenarios. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of: 

 
 Successfully implemented a functional browser-native WebMCP interface that allows an AI agent to execute end-to-end incident triage and infrastructure mitigation. 
 Created a clean visual bridge where human engineers can monitor automated agent actions live on screen. 
 

 What we learned: 

 
 How WebMCP transforms static web applications into interactive, agentic workspaces by standardizing client-side tool discovery. 
 Best practices for structuring agent inputs and fallback handling for robust client-side execution. 
 

 What's next for OpsDesk WebMCP 

 
 Adding multi-cluster support for cross-region failovers. 
 Expanding tool execution security with human-in-the-loop confirmation prompts prior to executing high-impact scaling or rollback operations.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Proofboard
pitch: Evidence-first decision rooms where browser agents structure source-backed research while humans retain approval and final-decision authority.
about_excerpt:
Evidence-first decision rooms where browser agents structure source-backed research while humans retain approval and final-decision authority.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Technology decisions are usually split between chat transcripts, spreadsheets, browser tabs, and memory. Research becomes hard to audit, conflicting claims are easy to miss, and an agent can appear more certain than the evidence allows. Proofboard turns the decision page itself into a durable, inspectable collaboration surface. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Proofboard is a strong fit for WebMCP because the agent must work with the exact state the person is viewing—not a detached copy hidden inside a chat. Native tools let an agent read human-authored constraints, add structured candidates and source-backed claims, and immediately update the same interface. Human edits are visible to the next tool call. 

 What people and agents do together 

 A browser agent can read the room, add candidates, attach validated evidence URLs, and ask Proofboard to surface conflicts and missing fields. It can prepare a shortlist proposal for human review. People can directly edit constraints, inspect every source, exclude or restore candidates, review proposals, and make the final decision. 

 This division of authority is intentional: Proofboard exposes no finalize_decision agent tool. The Make final decision action exists only in the human interface, and the audit trail distinguishes human and AI changes. 

 Better user experience 

 Instead of copying research out of chat, users get one persistent decision room with structured evidence, visible uncertainty, validation errors, provenance, and a human gate. Tool calls update the UI immediately; UI changes are available to subsequent tool reads. The human interface remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 How it was built 

 Proofboard is a React/Vinext application deployed on ChatGPT Sites. The UI and all 16 native WebMCP tools share one immutable reducer and browser-persisted state model. After client mount, the app obtains document.modelContext and registers tools with registerTool(...), typed JSON input schemas, read/write annotations, bounded inputs, URL validation, duplicate rejection, and abort-based unregister lifecycle handling. 

 Read tools cover decision state, constraints, candidates, evidence, conflicts, missing evidence, history, and approval status. Write tools create rooms, constraints, candidates, exclusions, evidence, and shortlist proposals. Applying a shortlist is gated on prior human approval. 

 Verified behavior 

 In Chrome's native WebMCP environment, the public site exposed 16 tools and passed a 5/5 native smoke check. A real natural-language tool run added three candidates to the live UI. A later live state contained four source-backed records, one conflict, and nine missing evidence fields, with AI-attributed history and persisted state visible. 

 The recorded demo does not claim that the pending human-approval step or shortlist application was completed. It shows only the behavior actually captured and verified. 

 Challenges and learning 

 The main challenge was preserving one source of truth across direct human edits, asynchronous agent writes, persistence, and strict validation. WebMCP made the product boundary clearer: agents contribute structured work, while consequential approval and final selection remain visibly human-controlled.

title: Prompt Canvas
pitch: A shared visual workspace where you shape the brief and Codex turns it into polished images—then returns them to your canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual workspace where you shape the brief and Codex turns it into polished images—then returns them to your canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI image workflows collapse an entire creative project into one long prompt buried in chat. That makes the work difficult to inspect, refine, reuse, or hand off. References, constraints, visual direction, and prior results all become conversational context instead of durable project state. I built Prompt Canvas to explore a different model: a shared visual workspace where the human directs the creative work and Codex executes it. The brief, references, creative direction, results, and variations remain visible on a spatial canvas. The human can edit those elements directly, while Codex can read and update the same live project through WebMCP. What it does Prompt Canvas begins with a curated library of image-making recipes. These range from simple tasks—creating an image from words, changing a background, or removing an object—to more structured systems for posters, brand exploration, sequential storytelling, technical visuals, and reference-driven transformations. Starting a recipe creates a focused project on a tldraw canvas. Depending on the task, the project may include: a Brief describing the intended outcome; References with explicit roles and preservation requirements; a Direction surface for composition, style, format, and mood; a dominant Result area; Variations for continued exploration. Users can shape the project manually or ask Codex to help. Through Prompt Canvas’s WebMCP Website Tools, Codex can search the official recipe library, retrieve an exact approved recipe version, create or update a project, inspect its current revision, prepare generation context, and return generated assets to the correct canvas output. Image generation remains native to Codex. Prompt Canvas supplies the structured creative context and receives the result; it does not introduce a separate page-owned generation service. The result is a single inspectable workspace where the human and agent operate on the same project rather than maintaining separate versions in chat and in the application. How I built it Prompt Canvas is a React and TypeScript application built on the tldraw SDK. Recipes are schema-backed YAML documents that define prompts, controls, references, output slots, layout, preservation rules, and supported operations. The application compiles those recipes into custom tldraw panel shapes while retaining the full underlying recipe snapshot for the agent. The official recipe library is curated and versioned. On the published ChatGPT Site, approved recipes are served from Cloudflare D1. User-created recipes remain local to the user’s browser and are never silently added to the official catalog. Prompt Canvas exposes 11 semantic Website Tools through WebMCP. These tools cover recipe discovery, exact recipe retrieval, project creation and updates, project inspection, generation-context preparation, and generated-asset return. The project also includes: immutable official recipe versions and content hashes; revision numbers and stale-write rejection; local project persistence; validated reference and generated-asset handling; explicit output-slot targeting; parent-child output lineage; undo and reload durability; deterministic catalog and browser tests. Challenges The largest design challenge was making the canvas feel like a creative workbench rather than a visual programming graph. Early versions displayed nearly every prompt variable as a separate connected card. Although technically accurate, the interface visually resembled an automation workflow and gave configuration more importance than the image itself. I simplified the interaction model around a smaller set of creative surfaces: Brief, References, Direction, Result, and Variations. Permanent dependency arrows were removed from the primary workflows, controls were grouped into meaningful decisions, and the Result became the visual center of the project. A second challenge was explaining the collaboration boundary clearly. Clicking a button on the Site cannot itself perform native Codex image generation. The application therefore needed to communicate that the user shapes the project in Prompt Canvas, then asks Codex to act on its current state through WebMCP. The final interface makes that division of labor visible from the first screen, previews the information Codex will use, and explains where the resulting image will return. The third challenge was preserving trust across two interfaces. Codex must always act on the newest project revision, respect the selected recipe version, return assets to the intended output, and avoid overwriting newer human edits. Revision checks, exact recipe identity, validation, and output lineage were essential to making the workflow reliable. What I learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes an application’s real semantic actions rather than asking an agent to imitate mouse and keyboard behavior. The agent does not need another copy of the user interface. It needs structured access to concepts such as “search recipes,” “inspect the active project,” “use the latest creative direction,” and “return this image to the primary result.” I also learned that agent collaboration must be explained before the first handoff. Users should understand what they control, what Codex will use, what the agent is about to do, and what remains editable afterward. What’s next The next frontier is deeper support for multi-reference creative work: assigning separate images authority over identity, composition, palette, product geometry, or visual style. I also plan to expand the curated recipe library, introduce reusable style and constraint kits, and develop richer result branching and comparison while keeping the workspace simple, inspectable, and local-first. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Lense
pitch: Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface. Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface with WebMCP, explicit approvals, screen observation, and a bounded local desktop bridge.
about_excerpt: Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface. Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface with WebMCP, explicit approvals, screen observation, and a bounded local desktop bridge. Like Comment Story Updates setup bridge Drawing a picture of a house Drawing and Evaluating picture of house lense chopping wood Inspiration Lens explores what happens when WebMCP needs to reach beyond the webpage. It combines structured WebMCP tools, screen observation, explicit human approval, verification, an inspectable event log, and an optional paired local desktop bridge to create a controlled path from an agent in the browser to workflows running elsewhere on the computer. WebMCP gives websites a powerful new capability: instead of making an AI agent infer what a site can do by looking at the interface, the site can expose structured tools directly. That made me wonder: What about software that isn't a website? A huge amount of important software still runs as: Desktop applications Legacy enterprise applications Internal Windows tools Creative software Games Testing environments Operating-system interfaces A normal webpage cannot and should not be allowed to arbitrarily control those applications. Lens explores whether WebMCP can still act as the structured control plane while preserving that security boundary. It gave your web browser eyes. What I Built Lens is a local-first WebMCP application combining: Screen observation Structured action proposals Target resolution Policy checks Human approval Desktop action execution Post-action verification An inspectable event timeline Reusable workflows Deterministic Paint, Notepad, and Claims demonstrations An optional local native companion for bounded desktop input The basic workflow is: Observe → Propose → Approve → Act → Verify Rather than sending a long blind macro, Lens can represent workflows as individual inspectable steps. WebMCP Tools Lens exposes structured WebMCP capabilities around the control loop. The tools allow agents to interact with the same runtime used by the UI for operations involving: Session state Screen observations Planned actions Action sequences Approval state Execution Verification Clipboard workflows Reusable recorded workflows Demo scenarios Event history The application currently contains 19 strict WebMCP tools when native WebMCP support is available. The WebMCP documentation page derives directly from the tool definitions and includes example prompts and chained workflows. Why WebMCP Traditional desktop automation tends to fall into one of two categories. One is a fixed macro. The other is an autonomous computer-use system that attempts to understand the entire interface visually. Lens explores something in between. WebMCP provides a structured agent-facing control surface. The application can then layer: policies approvals local capabilities observation providers verification around those tools. That means reasoning and permission do not have to be the same thing. An agent may be capable of proposing an action without automatically being allowed to execute it. The Local Bridge Browsers intentionally cannot issue arbitrary operating-system mouse and keyboard commands. Lens does not try to bypass that. For real desktop input, the user explicitly runs and pairs a small local companion. The companion provides a narrow local bridge for approved desktop operations. The bridge is intentionally constrained. It does not expose a general-purpose shell, unrestricted filesystem API, remote command server, or privilege escalation mechanism. The user can pause or disconnect it, clear pairing, create a new pairing code, and use an emergency stop hotkey. Screen sharing also requires explicit browser permission. Human + Agent Collaboration The human remains part of consequential workflows. Lens is designed around visibility. The user can see: what the agent observed what it proposed what action is waiting whether approval is required what was executed what changed afterward This makes the automation inspectable instead of hiding it behind an autonomous loop. The deterministic demonstrations make that architecture visible through scenarios such as drawing in Paint, typing in Notepad, and stopping before a fictional consequential claims submission. How I Built It The browser application is built with Vue, Pinia, TypeScript, IndexedDB, browser screen capture, and WebMCP. A shared runtime coordinates: planning target resolution policy approval execution observation verification The normal UI and WebMCP tools both use that same runtime. The optional native companion is written in Rust and implements local desktop input backends. The browser application remains the control surface while the bridge is intentionally limited to the local actions it has been designed to accept. Challenges I Faced The largest challenge was the browser security boundary. There are good reasons a webpage cannot simply start controlling the user's desktop. The solution had to make desktop capability explicit rather than trying to hide or bypass that limitation. That led to pairing, origin checks, strict message formats, local-only communication, approvals, and emergency controls. Another challenge was separating what is deterministic today from what could eventually be powered by more advanced semantic vision. The submitted architecture does not need to pretend that arbitrary desktop applications can already be perfectly understood. Richer observation systems can be added later while keeping the same policy and execution architecture. What I Learned The biggest lesson from Lens was: Capability and permission should be modeled separately. An agent being able to determine the next action should not automatically grant it permission to perform that action. WebMCP provides a useful structured capability layer. The application can then determine when those capabilities are safe to execute automatically and when the human should remain involved. What's Next The most interesting extension would be adding stronger semantic screen-understanding providers. Those providers could improve how targets and state are identified while keeping the existing WebMCP interface, approval model, pairing system, execution engine, and verification loop. The same architecture could potentially apply to: Legacy enterprise software Desktop QA Accessibility tools Creative applications Internal company software Remote support Specialized computer-use agents The broader experiment is whether WebMCP can become a structured control plane for experiences that extend beyond the page itself. title: DataBridge Agent
pitch: AI-powered business data agent using WebMCP to inspect datasets, find issues, compare records, detect anomalies, create action plans, and safely export cleaned data with human approval.
about_excerpt:
AI-powered business data agent using WebMCP to inspect datasets, find issues, compare records, detect anomalies, create action plans, and safely export cleaned data with human approval.
