 Inspiration i built data bridge from watching bloomberg tv on a segment where they spoke about fragmented data being held in all these companies. That was my inspiration for this project 

 Businesses often rely on data spread across CSV files, supplier records, inventory systems, purchase histories, and other disconnected sources. The idea behind DataBridge Agent was to create a practical AI workflow that can inspect that fragmented data, identify problems, and turn the findings into clear business actions without allowing the agent to make consequential changes without human approval. 

 What it does 

 DataBridge Agent is a WebMCP-enabled business data assistant. 

 It exposes eight structured tools: 

 
 inspect_dataset 
 find_duplicates 
 detect_missing_fields 
 compare_datasets 
 detect_anomalies 
 analyze_price_changes 
 create_action_plan 
 export_clean_data 
 

 The agent can inspect loaded business data, detect duplicate records and missing fields, compare related datasets, identify unusual numeric values, analyze price movements, and generate a prioritized action plan. 

 Export is intentionally protected by a human-approval gate. The source data remains unchanged, and a cleaned copy is only created after explicit approval. 

 How I built it 

 I built DataBridge Agent as a React and TypeScript application hosted on Replit. 

 The WebMCP tool layer is registered through the browser model context so compatible agents can discover and call structured tools instead of relying on page scraping or fragile UI automation. 

 The application also includes an embedded AI Agent Demo that runs the same DataBridge business logic locally when native WebMCP is unavailable. The interface clearly distinguishes native WebMCP activity from local demo-agent activity. 

 The core data-analysis functions are shared between the WebMCP tool wrappers and the embedded demo workflow so the results come from the loaded data rather than hardcoded demo values. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One major challenge was testing an experimental browser capability across different environments. In a normal browser, the WebMCP API was not exposed, so I added clear capability detection rather than falsely presenting local execution as native WebMCP. 

 After enabling WebMCP testing in a compatible Chrome environment, the live application successfully detected native WebMCP support. 

 Another challenge was designing safe agent behavior. Data analysis can run automatically, but export is treated as a consequential action and requires explicit human approval. 

 I also focused on making the execution transparent by showing the tool sequence, results, data source, and approval status directly in the interface. 

 What I learned 

 This project showed me how WebMCP can make web applications much more useful to AI agents by exposing structured capabilities instead of forcing agents to interpret interfaces visually. 

 I also learned that agent capability should be paired with transparency and human control. A useful business agent should not only produce an answer; it should make its actions auditable and clearly separate analysis from actions that can affect data. 

 What's next 

 The next step is to expand DataBridge Agent beyond CSV-based workflows into more live business systems, including databases, procurement platforms, inventory systems, and other operational data sources. 

 I would also like to add more configurable tool schemas, stronger cross-dataset matching, and reusable approval policies for different business actions.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most.  Inspiration 

 Travel planning is fragmented: people jump among sites to research, compare, schedule, and book. We imagined an agent that can help with the full planning loop while keeping people in control of every important decision. 

 What it does 

 Arion Trip Planner turns a natural-language request into a flexible itinerary. It searches stays and activities, compares options against budget and preferences, builds day-by-day plans, and replans when constraints change. The traveler approves any booking or payment step. 

 How we built it 

 We built Arion as a WebMCP-enabled web app. It exposes structured tools for searching travel options, creating itineraries, saving shortlists, checking budgets, and replanning. Provider adapters normalize external travel data into one planning experience, while WebMCP lets an agent use these tools directly in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was making recommendations useful without letting the agent take irreversible actions. We designed explicit approval points for booking and payment, and kept search, comparison, and planning separate from confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a planning experience where an agent can do more than suggest links: it can assemble, update, and explain a realistic trip plan. We are especially proud that the user remains the final decision-maker throughout. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native products need clear tool boundaries, structured data, and transparent state. WebMCP makes these interactions more reliable than asking an agent to navigate a traditional website visually. 

 What's next for Arion Trip Planner 

 Next, we plan to add more live provider integrations, collaborative trip planning for groups, richer availability data, and secure, user-approved checkout flows.

 I built Arion Trip Planner, an AI trip-planning app for Vietnam self-drive trips, with WebMCP as the core interface between the app and any AI agent - not an add-on.

The site's own built-in chat assistant is just one WebMCP client among many - an external agent like ChatGPT or Claude can drive the exact same trip through the exact same tools, no scraping, no bespoke integration.

title: RoomCraft
pitch: Website that helps humans and agents work together to design living spaces
about_excerpt: Website that helps humans and agents work together to design living spaces Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most room-planning tools make you do all the work manually. Image generators have the opposite problem: they can show you a nice-looking room, but the result is not an actual plan. You cannot reliably move the bed, check whether the door is blocked, or ask the system to fit a piece of furniture into a specific space. We built RoomCraft around a simple idea: the agent should edit the room itself, not generate an image of it. The person still decides what the room should feel like. The agent handles measurements, placement, and repetitive changes. What it does RoomCraft lets a user and an agent work together to design a 2D room layout through WebMCP tools. You can ask the agent to resize the room, add a door or window, find furniture, create a custom item from provided details, and place everything in the room. The canvas updates as the agent works, so you can see exactly what changed. RoomCraft also checks whether the layout works. It flags furniture that overlaps, extends outside the room, blocks a door, or leaves too little walking space. You can then move things yourself, ask the agent to fix them, save a layout variant, or undo the last change. The important distinction is that the agent edits an actual floor plan. It is not generating a room image that looks right but cannot be meaningfully edited. How we built it We built RoomCraft as a visual editor and connected the agent directly to it through WebMCP. The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Konva. Instead of giving the agent a screenshot and asking it to guess, we expose the room’s dimensions, doors, windows, furniture, positions, and constraints through WebMCP tools. The agent can call tools to inspect the room, change it, search for furniture, add custom items, place objects, and validate the result. Those changes go through the same update and history system as direct user edits. When the agent places a bed, it appears immediately on the canvas. The user can move it, inspect the result, fix it, or undo it. The layout checks are deterministic, so problems like overlaps, blocked doors, and insufficient clearance are checked by RoomCraft rather than left entirely to the agent. Challenges we ran into Getting agents to discover and call the WebMCP tools was one of our main challenges. Registering the tools on the page was not enough. Agents did not always know that the website supported WebMCP or where to find the tool definitions. We addressed this by documenting the tools and room conventions in /llms.txt, and by explicitly mentioning WebMCP support in the agent prompt. We also had to make the tool results clear enough for an agent to understand what changed and what to do next. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an interactive webpage that an agent can work with without taking control of the browser. It does not need to pan, scroll, or move the pointer around just to make a change. It can use the WebMCP tools while the user keeps working in the editor. It also feels like something we would actually use ourselves. That is the part we are most proud of. What we learned An agent does not need to use a webpage the same way a person does. For RoomCraft, having direct tools for changing the room works better than making the agent click through every control. We also learned that registering tools is only half the job. Agents need to be told that the tools exist and given enough context to use them, which is why the prompt and llms.txt ended up mattering. What's next for RoomCraft RoomCraft currently supports rectangular rooms, USD prices, and projects stored locally in the browser. Next steps are: Support room shapes beyond rectangles, Add more currency options, Add project saving, Add export, Add project sharing Built With cloudflare konva nextjs tailwindcss webmcp Try it out roomcraft.rohankakar.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Built the project from ideation to production and burned tokens. title: Consensus
pitch: Your agent can find what it cannot read. Drop confidential PDFs in — your agent searches without seeing the text, requesting human approval before reading a single page.
about_excerpt: Your agent can find what it cannot read. Drop confidential PDFs in — your agent searches without seeing the text, requesting human approval before reading a single page. Like Comment Story Updates Consensus The agent can find what it cannot read. A decision workspace for choices that run on confidential documents. You drop the PDFs in — they are parsed in your browser and never uploaded. Your ChatGPT agent can search them and tell you where the answers are, but it cannot read a single page without your explicit release. The problem I researched about & wanted to work on: So basically if u look at security evaluation, in most of the cases it looks like: multiple PDFs & SOC 2 Type II reports, vendor Data Processing Agreements (DPAs), pricing annexes, and a filled-in security questionnaire, and it leaves them in a frustrating spot: that is they want an AI to help for searching through documents with a lot of pages of legal text (or something else), but uploading those documents isn't actually allowed. When you ask why they aren't using an AI assistant like ChatGPT to help parse all those hundreds of pages, the answer in most cases is: the documents are under strict NDA. The core contradiction is provided below with two facts: It is exactly the work an AI should do . Reading lots of pages of legal annexes and compliance schedules to find whether a vendor has an unqualified SOC 2 report covering availability exceptions is mechanical retrieval. People are usually slow at it, and they miss buried facts in that. It is exactly the work you are contractually forbidden to give an AI . SOC 2 Type II reports and DPAs are distributed under strict non-disclosure terms that prohibit uploading or redistributing them to third-party cloud tools or SaaS platforms. So basically the core problem is: The documents that would make an AI genuinely useful for a high-stakes decision are precisely the documents you are contractually forbidden to upload. 1> Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP After clear evaluation of the constraints, the requirement I ended up with were: An agent that can tell you where the answer is in a document it is not permitted to read. *** Considered Architecture: Basically there were four ways with which we could approach this problem, but each of them fails for their specific reasons, which are specified below in detail. (For detailed analysis: docs/WHY-WEBMCP.md ) Approach Why it fails Server-side MCP Searching server-side requires uploading the PDF to a cloud server first, which immediately violates the NDA. A backend cannot search a document without reading the text. REST API There is no shared live interface. Approving a single page in real time requires both the user and the agent to be on the exact same open tab at the same moment. Browser automation Vision and screen-driving agents read text through screenshots. Sending screenshots of confidential contracts into the model leaks the exact data we need to protect. OS / extension agent Lacks a structured in-browser contract. There is no clean way to tell an OS-level agent: "you are allowed to know where this file matches, but you cannot open the text." Alternatives I considered and rejected: Searchable encryption : Still requires sending data over the network, which leaks search access patterns. Under a strict NDA, transmitting the file anywhere is forbidden. Localhost MCP server binary : Requires users to install a native binary on their machine. Documents would persist on disk instead of living safely inside an ephemeral browser tab that clears when closed. ** Why WebMCP was the only real solution:** WebMCP's execute() function runs directly inside the browser tab that is already holding the in-memory document . Because tool execution happens locally in JavaScript under a strict JSON Schema, we can cleanly separate searching for matches from reading actual text into two distinct tools. ** Where WebMCP would be the wrong choice:** To be transparent about its limits: WebMCP is not meant for backend cron jobs, background workers, or anything that needs persistent cross-session databases. It fits best where data is private and local, the browser tab is the security boundary, and a human is actively present to approve sensitive actions. What only WebMCP makes possible: WebMCP tool execution ( execute() ) runs directly inside the browser process that already holds the document text in memory . And because the execution happens locally in the tab, we can separate finding evidence from reading evidence into two independent tools with their own JSON schemas. Also here we have about WebMCP's limits: WebMCP is not the right choice for every use case: Anything genuinely server-side or long-running is much better served by a traditional server MCP. WebMCP tools are ephemeral and live only for the duration of the browser tab. Consensus embraces this exact constraint: the lifetime of the browser session is the security boundary. WebMCP is the ideal architecture when data is private, execution must stay local, and a human is actively in the loop. 2> How it creates a better user experience Dividing the work where it makes sense So instead of giving the agent full control or doing everything manually, the workload is divided cleanly: | What the agent handles | What the human controls | |---|---| | Searching across hundreds of pages in milliseconds | Setting criteria weights and importance | | Proposing score suggestions with exact citations | Approving or rejecting every proposal | | Flagging contradictions when a score looks unsupported | Releasing each page snippet individually | | | Changing any score on the matrix | This division is enforced in code, not system prompts . Write tools like set_score , set_weight , add_option , and finalize_decision are completely absent from the tool catalog. An automated test fails the build if any of those write tools ever appear. Keeping approvals rare so they actually get read So instead of spamming a lot of confirmation dialogs for every small action because that trains users to click "Confirm" without reading, consensus only prompts the user when requesting to open a specific page snippet. UX Design Choice Why it matters "Deny" is focused first Prevents users from accidentally approving a page by pressing space out of habit. Agent's reason shown verbatim Shows the agent's exact intent so you know why it needs the page. Permissions reset on reload Closing or reloading the tab immediately reseals all documents. Declined requests are logged The audit trail records every decision, including what was denied. Decisions you can actually audit later Citations attached to cells : Any score proposed by the agent links directly to the specific page and snippet it came from. Clear "no source" tags : If a score was entered manually without document backing, it is marked with a clear amber "no source" badge so nobody mistakes an unbacked guess for verified evidence. Full Markdown Export : Clicking "Export Brief" generates a complete report containing all scores, weights, citations, open challenges, and the disclosure audit log. 3> What people and agents can do together that was impossible before Before You had to choose between protecting your documents or using an AI. Now You and your agent reason together over documents the AI is never handed in bulk. The agent understands the overall shape of the evidence — where matches cluster, which sections look relevant, and which matrix cells lack evidence — and asks for access one page at a time. The novel capability: unreadRefs Most AI tools only let a model talk about what it has already read. When Consensus's flag_inconsistency tool runs, the agent can also point to pages it has located but is not yet permitted to read , displaying: "I have not read these pages yet. May I check them?" Clicking release on that card lets the human approve those specific references directly. An agent that is transparent about what it doesn't know yet — while still pointing you in the right direction — is far more useful and trustworthy than an AI that guesses or stays silent. This is only possible because searching and reading are two separate capabilities running locally in the browser. title: UCE Evidence Lens
pitch: People and AI agents, alone or together, inspect the same public evidence - verifying integrity, chronology, assertions, and file matches with no work uploaded and creators keep control.
about_excerpt: People and AI agents, alone or together, inspect the same public evidence - verifying integrity, chronology, assertions, and file matches with no work uploaded and creators keep control. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Seven typed, read-only WebMCP tools discovered directly from the live production site. An agent invokes verify_uce_record and receives a structured, source-bound result—without DOM scraping. Browser checks verify schema, record identity, ES256 signature, and public transaction chronology. Chronology separates claimed dates, recorded system events, and independently retrieved public evidence. Authorship, identity, AI-use, and rights remain recorded assertions—not verified facts. A public UCE record binds the asset to its manifest hash, timestamps, source, and recorded authorship context. The verifier is itself evidenced: the production v1.0.0 site release has its own independently checkable UCE record. Overview A shared browser verifier where people and AI agents inspect the same cryptographic evidence, chronology, rights assertions, and local-file match. Problem Creators, agencies, reviewers, counsel, and journalists increasingly receive public evidence records that combine cryptographic facts with human claims. Understanding one record can require moving among a verification page, machine-readable JSON, a signature, an Arweave transaction, and the original local file. A person can miss a distinction; a general-purpose agent scraping the visible page can do worse by promoting a publisher statement or authorship claim into a verified fact. The difficult part is not merely retrieving data. It is preserving evidentiary boundaries: what this browser independently checked, what the publisher reported, what the claimant asserted, what is temporarily retryable, and what the public format does not yet support. Solution UCE Evidence Lens is a static, browser-first public record inspector. A person can load a CbyUCE verification URL, a direct Arweave manifest, pasted public JSON, or the bundled demonstration. The browser validates the record, checks its public ES256 signature, binds chronology to public Arweave block metadata, separates recorded assertions from verified results, and can compare a user-selected file by locally calculated SHA-256. The same page exposes seven read-only WebMCP tools. An agent can load, summarize, verify, inspect chronology, list assertions, inspect rights declarations, and report an already-selected local file comparison through structured operations rather than guessing from the interface. The human sees the same underlying state and wording. Why This Matters Evidence review is a strong fit for WebMCP because the workflow is structured, multi-step, and precision sensitive. Without page-defined tools, an agent has to infer controls and semantics from layout, possibly leaving out technical details or overstating a legal conclusion. With WebMCP, the site defines exactly which evidence operations are available and returns typed, source-bound results. For a reviewer, the experience changes from manually correlating several technical sources to asking one focused question while retaining a visible and easily understood inspectable record. For an agency or production team, the demonstration also shows a credible market path: a work can originate in the published Copyright by UCE Figma plugin ( the Figma plugin is now available for use), become a public UCE record, and then be inspected by both a person and an agent before delivery. This does not turn evidence into a legal verdict. It makes the evidence easier to inspect without erasing its limits. How We Used AI The product is agent-enabled without placing a model inside the trust boundary. Deterministic browser functions perform parsing, cryptography, chronology retrieval, and digest comparison. WebMCP lets an AI agent select and compose those operations, explain the structured results, and guide a person through the same evidence the interface displays. The key collaboration is intentional: the agent can inspect an already-selected digest but cannot open a file picker or access file bytes. The person controls the sensitive local input; the agent works with the resulting evidence state. How We Used Codex Codex helped scope the public/private boundary, scaffolded the TypeScript application, implemented and reviewed the seven WebMCP tools, debugged browser discovery and CORS, hardened trust and concurrency boundaries, built regression tests, ran security and dependency audits, tested responsive and live-browser behavior, prepared Cloudflare deployment, and helped me tighten the judge-facing language because I can get a bit wordy and go off on tangents...(see what I mean...). The development process repeatedly challenged optimistic claims. For example, canonical manifest recomputation remains explicitly unsupported because the public format does not define the exact hash construction. Publisher flags are recorded rather than substituted for browser checks. The result is a narrower but more defensible product. As the Copyright by UCE product grows, so will UCE Evidence Lens as an Open-Source resource helping creatives to secure their creativity. The Copyright by UCE Canva App plugin is in design review now having passed functional and technical review and the Pro Tools and Ableton plugin and extension respectively are being finalized over the next few weeks. The UCE Evidence Lens is poised to be a very useful tool for creatives and the agencies and organizations that serve them. Key Features Seven top-level, imperative WebMCP tools with strict JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint: true . Human/agent parity through shared controller operations and shared result wording. Public ES256 compact-JWS verification against a reviewed, application-owned P-256 key registry. Direct Arweave transaction, block, height, timestamp, and confirmation inspection. Consumer-oriented result states that distinguish verified, mismatch, retryable, reported, and unsupported outcomes. Recorded authorship, identity, originality, AI-use, and rights values clearly separated from verified facts. Local SHA-256 comparison without uploading the file or exposing its bytes to the agent. Bundled demo, direct Arweave, CbyUCE JSON, and pasted-JSON resilience paths. Static Cloudflare deployment with no account, backend, analytics, database, runtime secret, or production dependency. Architecture UCE Evidence Lens is a static Vite and TypeScript single-page application. Pure modules parse and verify records; a memory-only controller binds each result to its source and manifest hash; a semantic DOM renderer and the WebMCP adapter call the same controller operations. Browser Web Crypto provides SHA-256 and ECDSA P-256. WebMCP tools register before asynchronous demo loading and confirm same-origin discovery through document.modelContext.getTools() where available. Production headers opt the page into an origin-keyed agent cluster and allow same-origin tools. Remote access is restricted to validated HTTPS CbyUCE and Arweave routes, with byte, depth, and timeout limits. There are no production npm dependencies and no server function, Worker, proxy, database, or persistent application storage. Testing Instructions Open https://uceevidencelens.com/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the page reports: “7 read-only AI-agent tools registered and discoverable.” The bundled public UCE record loads automatically. Ask the agent to call verify_uce_record and summarize verified checks separately from recorded assertions. The result should begin with “No integrity problems found.” Ask the agent to call inspect_uce_chronology . Confirm it distinguishes the claimed creation date, system events, and the independently retrieved Arweave block. For the real Figma-origin example, load https://cbyuce.com/verify/cc7680c80721f69295dab10bb547065fd74c14de420d915df0da051ee5e0727a with load_uce_public_record , then repeat the verification and chronology calls. Optional local comparison: choose the matching public PNG in the normal interface. The browser displays its SHA-256 result; compare_local_file_to_uce_record can report that result but cannot access the file bytes or trigger selection. No login or credentials are required. If live retrieval is temporarily unavailable, reload the bundled demo or use the direct Arweave manifest URL shown in the public record. Known Limitations Independent canonical-manifest recomputation is unsupported until CbyUCE publishes a reproducible hash profile with test vectors. Direct chronology uses a public Arweave gateway rather than a trustless light client; pending or unreachable results are retryable, not mismatches. title: VibeCheck
pitch: You already do this by hand, you add Reddit to the search and read threads until a picture forms. VibeCheck does the reading. You decide who to believe.
about_excerpt: You already do this by hand, you add Reddit to the search and read threads until a picture forms. VibeCheck does the reading. You decide who to believe. Like Comment Story Updates VibeCheck: what people actually said Inspiration This came out of a habit I didn't think about much until I tried to explain it to someone. When I'm actually deciding on something — a laptop, a bank, a framework — I don't trust the first page of results. I search for it, then I add "reddit" to the end and go read threads until I've got a real picture in my head. Marketing pages tell you what a product is supposed to be. Threads tell you what it's actually like to own the thing. I wasn't trying to build another search tool or another recommendation engine. There's no shortage of those and most of them aren't much help when you're actually trying to decide something. What I wanted to build was the reading part — go gather what real people are saying, put it somewhere useful, and then get out of the way. Because there's one part of this I don't think a model should be doing for you, and that's deciding who you trust. WebMCP came into the picture later than the idea itself, but once it clicked, it kind of reframed the whole thing. Say you're researching a laptop and you've got an agent helping. Halfway through, you notice one of the sources reads like an affiliate blog wearing a Reddit post's clothes, so you reject it. Or you find one comment that nails the exact problem you're worried about, so you pin it. None of that exists anywhere except in your head and on your screen, right then. It's not sitting in a database somewhere, and it's definitely not something you'd think to type into a prompt. WebMCP is what lets the agent reach into that. Not a summary of it, not a description of it after the fact — the actual state, live, while you're both looking at the same board. That's also, concretely, what it buys you that you didn't have before. Reject a source mid-conversation and the agent doesn't need you to explain what changed — its next call against the board already sees the claim re-weighted, because it's reading the same object you just edited. And it runs the other way too: the agent can pin a claim or apply a constraint on its own, and instead of that decision getting buried three messages back in a chat log, it shows up as a card on your board, right where you'd notice it, and you can undo it with a click if it got it wrong. Neither of you is re-explaining state to the other. You're both just looking at the same thing. That turned into more than an integration detail for me. It's a big part of why the whole app is shaped the way it is. What I learned Honestly the biggest lesson wasn't technical. It's that "gather opinions" is a lot harder than "run a search." A search API hands you results. Turning those into something usable is where it gets messy. Ask it "is the Mac Mini a good device for developers?" and you'll get close to nothing back. Strip it down to "mac mini developers" and suddenly there are real threads with real replies. Search engines want keywords, not questions, and getting from one to the other without losing what the person actually meant took more tuning than I expected going in. Then there's the discussion-vs-not-discussion problem. A big chunk of what came back technically matched the query but wasn't a discussion at all — Facebook groups, LinkedIn posts, promotional junk dressed up to look like a real thread. I ended up writing a whole layer just to translate a person's actual sentence into something the search API would respect, and then another pass to figure out which of the results were even worth reading. Trust modeling was the other one. My first pass at "how strong is this claim" was just a source count — more sources, stronger claim. Which sounds fine until you notice that three people copying the same affiliate article isn't three opinions, it's one opinion wearing a disguise three times. So I moved to weighting the evidence instead of counting it: $$ \text{raw}(claim) = \sum_{s \in \text{evidence}} w(s) $$ where $$ w(s) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{you rejected it} \ 1.5 & \text{you trusted it} \ 0.4 & \text{it's a low-signal source} \ 1 & \text{ordinary discussion source} \end{cases} $$ and then normalized against whatever the strongest claim on the board is: $$ \text{weight}(claim) = \min\left(1,\ \frac{\text{raw}(claim)}{\max_{c \in \text{claims}} \text{raw}(c)}\right) $$ Once that was in place the UI more or less designed itself. The support bar isn't a decoration sitting on top of the claim — it's that formula, visible. Reject a source and the segment it owned just goes away, and you can watch a claim that looked like consensus a second ago drop down to "thin." That's probably my favorite thing in the whole app. It makes "trust" a thing you can actually see move, instead of a number some model handed you with no way to check its work. How I built it I kept the architecture small on purpose. One state shape, one reducer — and both the UI and the six WebMCP tools go through that same reducer to touch the board. Nothing gets a side door. That constraint came from something specific I wanted to avoid: a tool that quietly changes something you can't see. The second that happens, this stops being collaboration and starts being something closer to surveillance, and I didn't want to build that even by accident. The actual pipeline under the UI is smaller than you'd guess. SerpApi's google_forums engine goes and finds the threads first. Then an LLM — routed through OpenRouter, free model first with a paid one as backup — does three things with what comes back: decides whether a thread is actually relevant, figures out whether the person sounds like they've used the thing versus just repeating something they heard, and clusters the recurring points into claims with the evidence attached to each one. Everything downstream of that — the reducer, the support math, the whole board — is only as good as that step, so it ended up eating far more of my time than I planned for. Challenges SerpApi's free tier is 250 searches a month, so credit discipline wasn't optional. I built it as two stages — google_forums runs alone first, and only if that comes back too thin does a second, broader search fire. There's also a disk cache for local dev, so I'm not burning real credits every time I tweak a font size. Deciding what "too thin" even means turned into its own small project, since real google_forums results are noisier than I expected — Facebook and LinkedIn show up constantly, looking like discussion when they're really not, which pushes the fallback to trigger more than I originally planned for. The more frustrating problem was getting the model to stop finishing other people's sentences. Search snippets get cut off mid-thought, sometimes literally ending in "…", and a language model's instinct is to complete that thought for you. Normally that's a fine instinct. Here it's dangerous — if a source says "the battery life is good, but…" and the model decides the rest was probably "not great under heavy load," that's a completely plausible sentence sitting right next to a citation, and it's also something nobody ever actually said. I had to write out very literal rules against it: don't finish a cut-off snippet, don't invent a detail that isn't in the text, don't borrow a phrase from one source's snippet into another source's line. None of that is clever prompting. It's just closing off, one by one, all the small ways a model fills gaps with confidence instead of silence. The last challenge is the one with no clear finish line, which is making the board itself worth spending time on. It's not hard to build something that's technically correct and still nobody wants to open twice — an accurate list of claims with checkboxes next to them is not, on its own, a reason to come back. The support bar had to feel like it was actually moving when you rejected something, not just updating a number. Rejecting a source needed to feel like a decision, not a form field. Even the empty state needed a reason for someone to click something instead of staring at a blank input box. None of that had a spec. It was mostly just looking at it, deciding it wasn't quite right, and doing it again — and if I'm honest, that's the part I kept circling back to more than anything else in the project. title: AgentPerf
pitch: The ecosystem quotes "10x faster" for WebMCP with no methodology behind it. AgentPerf measures it: 2.4x on a small page, 13.8x on a real one. And it ships the React layer that produces the gap.
about_excerpt: The ecosystem quotes "10x faster" for WebMCP with no methodology behind it. AgentPerf measures it: 2.4x on a small page, 13.8x on a real one. And it ships the React layer that produces the gap. Like Comment Story Updates What it does AgentPerf answers the question every frontend team is about to be asked: if we build and maintain a second surface for AI agents, what do we actually get? Three pieces answer it end to end. agentperf, the benchmark CLI. Runs the same task, on the same page, with the same model, twice. Once by DOM driving, an accessibility-tree driver that reads, clicks, fills and selects, the way browser agents work today. Once through the page's WebMCP tools. Identical agent loop, identical prompt, identical verification. It reports wall-clock, tokens, round-trips and success rate, per run and aggregated. @agentperf/react, the fast lane. Three primitives that turn an existing React app into a WebMCP surface without touching the human UI. Two instrumented demo pages and a landing page, all live, all publishing their own tools. The landing page will hand your agent its own benchmark data with the caveats attached. The measurement gpt-5.6-luna, n=5 per lane, both lanes 100% successful on both pages: page accessibility tree lane wall-clock tokens round-trips salon booking 1,010 chars DOM driving 7.5s 10,079 5 salon booking WebMCP tools 5.0s 4,268 4 72-product catalog 32,916 chars DOM driving 24.3s 102,537 7 72-product catalog WebMCP tools 6.0s 7,434 5 2.4x fewer tokens on the tiny page. 13.8x on the realistic one. Make the page 32x heavier and DOM driving pays 10x more, while the tools lane barely moves, because it never reads the page. It asks. That is the finding, and it is not the one anyone is quoting: the gap is a property of the page, not of WebMCP. A single number for "what WebMCP saves" is meaningless without the page it was measured on. That is why this ships as a harness you point at your own site, not as a headline. It replicates across model families: claude-sonnet-5 via OpenRouter, with no vendor-specific workarounds, pays 2.5x on the small page with identical round-trip counts. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP demos show that an agent can drive a site. The open question is whether a team should pay to build that, and nobody could answer it with data. The "10x faster, ~90% fewer tokens" figures in circulation trace to one methodology-free blog post and to token-only counts measured against screenshot baselines by the ecosystem itself. Google's own WebMCP Evals guide covers correctness (does the agent pick the right tool) and explicitly provides no metrics, no harness, and no comparison against DOM automation. So the fit is direct: WebMCP is the thing being adopted, and the missing artifact is the evidence for adopting it. AgentPerf is built on WebMCP twice over. The demo pages publish tools through document.modelContext, and the harness implements the other half of the protocol, acting as a WebMCP host so it can measure any page that speaks it. How it creates a better experience For the person: the agent's work happens in their tab, in their UI. When it searches, the grid filters. When it orders, the confirmation appears where they can see it. A dock states plainly how many tools the page has exposed. Agent-readiness usually means a headless side door the user cannot observe; here it is a visible second doorway onto the same app. For the developer: the fast lane is additive. Delete agent-surface.tsx from either demo and you have an ordinary React app. In a browser without WebMCP, everything no-ops. For the agent: it stops guessing. It gets typed actions and a state snapshot pruned to a token budget, with explicit "+N more" markers wherever a list was elided, so a partial read is legible as a partial read instead of becoming a confident hallucination. What people and agents can now do together that was hard before Buy correctly from a real catalog in four tool calls. On a 72-product store, "find the cheapest in-stock wireless keyboard rated 4.5 or higher and order it" is a filter, a comparison and a checkout. Through tools that is search_products, add_to_cart, place_order, for 7,434 tokens. By DOM it costs 102,537 tokens of reading and re-reading the same grid. Let an agent write to an app without letting it corrupt the app. Every action is zod-gated. A malformed email never reaches the handler; the agent gets back the exact violated field paths and a deterministic fix-and-retry instruction, and corrects itself in one turn instead of re-sending the same bad call. Ask a marketing page to justify its own claims. The landing page publishes get_benchmark_results. An agent reading it gets the numbers and the caveats (n, model, page sizes, known biases) instead of adjectives. Benchmark a WebMCP page you did not write. The harness supplies the host, so it works on any page that speaks the protocol, in stock Chromium, with no flag and no origin trial. How I implemented WebMCP Publishing side, @agentperf/react: useAgentState(key, value): every slice flows into a single get_page_state tool, serialized within a token budget (default 1,000) with deterministic pruning and explicit elision markers. useAgentAction(name, config): registers a tool whose input schema is generated from a zod schema via z.toJSONSchema, so the contract and the schema the agent sees cannot drift. readOnly and destructive map to WebMCP annotations. A reserved, currently inert price field anticipates x402 settlement without a future breaking change. AgentBoundary: scopes state keys and tool names the way the component tree scopes the UI. Registration hygiene: handlers, descriptions and values are read through refs at call time, so re-renders never tear down and re-register a tool. Each tool holds an AbortController and unregisters on unmount, which fires toolchange so an idle agent learns the surface moved. Host side, the harness: WebMCP lives behind an origin trial and a Chrome flag, which makes reproducible measurement painful and CI impossible. So the harness ships a host shim and injects it with Playwright's addInitScript before page load. The page registers into that shim, and window.__agentperf.listTools() and .call() bridge those tools into the agent loop as function tools. Verification is the benchmark. A run counts as a success only if the model calls task_complete and the rendered page matches the task's successPattern. For the catalog that pattern pins the product and the price, so ordering the wrong keyboard fails the run instead of passing on a bare order number. A task whose pattern already matches at page load is rejected outright as unverifiable. Challenges I ran into My own benchmark was unfair, and I published it before I found out. The launched numbers were 2.4x tokens and 2.6x wall-clock. Then I had the methodology adversarially reviewed, and the review was right: the DOM lane's click returned only "Clicked button X", forcing a separate read_page to see the result, while every real accessibility-tree driver returns the post-action snapshot with the action result. I had doubled that lane's round-trips by design, then billed it for re-sending the transcript each time. Fixed and re-ran: the token ratio survived unchanged at 2.36x; the wall-clock claim did not. 2.6x was wrong, it is 1.5x. The correction is on the landing page and at the top of the README. Then it nearly happened again, in my favour. The first heavy-page run was spectacular: the DOM lane succeeded 1 time in 5, ordering a keyboard rated 4.2 when the task demanded 4.5 or higher, and announcing success every time. "DOM driving doesn't just cost more, it buys the wrong thing" is a far better headline than any cost ratio. It was also my bug: the catalog's rating filter is a select element and my DOM lane had no way to operate a dropdown. Adding select_option took it from 20% to 100%. Two rules came out of that: a lane is only a baseline if it can do what the real thing can do, and a result that flatters your conclusion gets audited harder, not published faster. Rate limits were silently biasing the result. A 429 failed a run outright, which penalizes whichever lane spends more tokens, the lane under measurement. Retries now back off exponentially. Crashed runs also used to record zero tokens and get averaged in, dragging a failing lane's cost toward zero; central tendencies are now over successful runs only, with failures in the success rate. gpt-5.6 returns a 400 on function tools unless reasoning_effort is "none". My first instinct, swallowing provider errors so a run doesn't abort, was exactly wrong for a benchmark: it turns a broken configuration into a plausible-looking failed run. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Every number that moved, moved against me, and I shipped it anyway: on the landing page, in the README, and inside a WebMCP tool the page itself serves. benchmarks/METHODOLOGY.md: the full adversarial review of my own harness, both

title: Gates of Galloo
pitch: A voice-directed voxel world where people and AI reshape the same live scene through WebMCP, from bridges and domino chains to characters, weather, and contextual commerce.
about_excerpt: A voice-directed voxel world where people and AI reshape the same live scene through WebMCP, from bridges and domino chains to characters, weather, and contextual commerce. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration In the HBO show Silicon Valley, Dinesh turns on a microphone inside a game and mentions pizza. The game immediately fills itself with Domino's advertising. It is funny because the world appears to be listening and rewriting itself around the conversation. Gates of Galloo asks a more useful version of that question: what if speaking to a game did not merely open a chatbot or trigger an advertisement? What if the AI could understand the actual world, change it with you, and let you interrupt whenever its taste became questionable? What it does Gates of Galloo is a voice-directed voxel world shared by a person and an AI character named Nika. The player can walk around the island and speak at the level of intention: "Build a bridge in front of me." "Create a domino path from the chapel to the harbor, but leave it standing." "Extend the island with a mix of grass, stone, and water." "I am hungry." "That is too much. Undo it." Nika reads the current state of the island and turns the request into visible actions. Terrain grows, objects arrive, characters move, weather changes, dominoes fall, and contextual storefronts can become part of the scene. These changes happen over time, so the player can watch, interrupt, redirect, or reverse the result. The commerce interactions are no-charge previews. They demonstrate how a product, delivery, or storefront could enter a game as a playable event rather than as a detached banner. Why WebMCP matters The useful context is already inside the page: terrain, buildings, player position and facing, selected regions, actors, shops, domino runs, camera state, and recent changes. Ordinary computer control would force an agent to infer all of that from pixels and simulate mouse clicks. WebMCP lets the website expose the world directly through meaningful actions. Gates of Galloo registers six page tools: inspect_world list_assets place_asset erase_at paint_path undo_last_action The agent works with island objects and validated grid coordinates instead of screen positions. The available vocabulary is intentionally defined by the game, while the model remains free to decide what to create with it. This makes WebMCP part of the creative medium. The person and agent can see and change the same evolving artifact without repeatedly describing what is already on screen. How it creates a better experience The conversation stays inside the activity. The player does not have to export a screenshot, explain the map to a separate assistant, wait for generated code, and reload the result. Instead, an idea becomes visible inside the current world. If the interpretation is wrong, the player can correct it while it is happening. References such as "here," "in front of me," or "beside the bridge" work because the agent receives the live player and scene state. The result feels closer to improvising with another participant than issuing commands to a detached chatbot. How we built it The project began with the open-source Mykonos Island Voxels game by Ibrahim Boona. During the submission period, we transformed it into Gates of Galloo. The browser adapts the live game controller into WebMCP tool definitions and registers them through document.modelContext.registerTool() . For voice interaction, OpenAI Realtime handles the live conversation and transcription. It has one high-level function called direct_world . That function sends the player's original request, together with a semantic snapshot of the island, to a server-side director built with the OpenAI Responses API. The director produces a structured sequence of terrain, object, actor, camera, commerce, and domino operations. The browser validates that plan and performs it incrementally. The production interaction is model-directed rather than selected through keyword rules or canned responses. We also added an embodied isometric player, pathfinding, bridge traversal, camera follow, open-ended terrain growth, mixed-terrain paths, live transcripts, interruption, conflict-aware undo, actors, weather, chain reactions, and contextual storefront scenes. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was giving the model enough live context to make those actions feel intentional. We had to solve placement validation, connected terrain painting, object footprints, isometric occlusion, bridge traversal, camera framing, world expansion, interruption, and undo without allowing one half-finished plan to corrupt the next. We also learned that the design of the tool vocabulary changes the personality of the agent. A model with raw DOM access behaves like an operator. A model given verbs such as inspect, place, paint, stage, and undo can behave more like a collaborator. Gates of Galloo is one playful example, but the same pattern can extend to design software, educational simulations, music tools, filmmaking environments, and any website where the human and agent should remain inside the work together.  Inspiration 

 Cerveza Tools started several years ago as a small open-source project: a collection of React components and TypeScript functions for common homebrewing calculations. Over time, it became one of those side projects that mostly sat untouched. 

 While exploring ideas for the WebMCP Challenge, I realized it was a good project to bring back to life. The calculators already represented useful, deterministic domain capabilities that could be exposed to agents without asking a language model to perform the calculations itself. 

 That idea became Cerveza Tools Lab. 

 What it does 

 Cerveza Tools Lab is a shared brewing workspace where a brewer and an AI agent can work on the same batch. 

 Through WebMCP, the agent can read the current brew, use tools for hydrometer correction, alcohol, dilution, IBU and carbonation, and update the brew when requested. Changes made manually in the UI are also immediately available to the agent. 

 For example, if the measured gravity is higher than the target, the agent can read the values directly from the brew, calculate the required dilution and, after user approval, apply the adjustment. 

 How I built it 

 Cerveza Tools is my existing React and TypeScript library. During the challenge, I added optional WebMCP bindings to expose its calculation functions as agent-accessible tools. 

 Cerveza Tools Lab is the new application built for the challenge. It adds shared Current Brew state and contextual WebMCP tools, allowing the UI and the agent to work with the same data and underlying brewing logic. 

 Challenges and learnings 

 The main challenge was deciding where agent capabilities should live and keeping human and agent state synchronized. 

 Separating deterministic calculations from application context resulted in a simple architecture: Cerveza Tools knows how to calculate, while the Lab knows what the user is currently brewing. 

 My primary takeaway was that WebMCP becomes particularly beneficial when an application reveals both its existing functionalities and its current context. Instead of merely adding a chatbot on top, it facilitates the seamless collaboration between humans and agents within the same application.

title: ArchMorph
pitch: Browser-based architecture studio where a human and an AI agent design a building together on the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: Browser-based architecture studio where a human and an AI agent design a building together on the same live canvas. Like Comment Story Updates ArchMorph lets people and WebMCP agents shape, inspect, and validate the same live architectural model. A broad architectural perspective showing the finished envelope, outdoor spaces, and material palette. Connected living, dining, kitchen, guest suite, service core, and a clear daylit stair. Primary suite, sky lounge, garden suite, two baths, balcony, terrace, and aligned stair gallery. Balcony, entrance canopy, timber frame, slatted gate, and layered modern massing. Horizon House pairs exposed concrete with warm timber accents, deep shading, and framed glazing. Inspiration I have a dream of building a house for my family and being involved in designing it myself. For almost a year, I tried turning that dream into a floor plan using pen and paper and later Figma. I could imagine the house in my mind, but I was rarely satisfied with the result. Without architectural training, it was difficult to understand room relationships, circulation, dimensions, setbacks, and whether the design would actually feel comfortable. The biggest limitation was that a flat drawing could not show me what the finished house would feel like. I wanted to see it from the outside, walk through it from the inside, find problems, and keep improving it without needing years of training just to explore an idea. When I discovered the WebMCP Challenge, I realized I could build the tool I had been wishing for: an architecture studio where a person and an AI agent work on the same live building. That idea became ArchMorph . ArchMorph is intended for people who want to explore their future home visually before taking the design to a professional architect. It does not replace architects or engineers; it makes the early stage of imagining, testing, and communicating a home much more accessible. What it does ArchMorph is a Human + Agent Architecture Studio for designing residential buildings in the browser. A user can configure a plot, define its orientation and setbacks, and create a house using rooms, walls, doors, windows, stairs, floors, balconies, terraces, boundary walls, gates, and façade features. The design can be experienced through three connected views: Floor Plan for precise 2D planning and editing 3D Orbit for inspecting the building from different exterior angles Walk Mode for exploring the house from the inside ArchMorph also calculates architectural measurements in real time, including room areas, gross covered area, open-site area, plot coverage, and floor-area ratio. For example: $$ \text{Floor Area Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Gross Covered Area}}{\text{Plot Area}} $$ The application can inspect circulation and identify early layout problems such as disconnected rooms, missing exterior access, invalid openings, overlapping geometry, and incorrect stair connections. These checks are meant to support early design decisions, not provide final building-code or structural certification. What makes ArchMorph WebMCP-native is that an AI agent can directly understand and operate the same project through 57 typed architectural tools . The agent can inspect the plot and existing design, create or modify elements, calculate measurements, validate the layout, control the 3D view, enter Walk Mode, capture snapshots, and export the project. The human and the agent are not working on separate versions. They share one live model, and every change made by either side appears immediately on the same canvas. How we built it I built ArchMorph using Codex as my main development partner . I used it to help shape the product, research architectural workflows, plan the system, implement the interface, debug geometry, design the WebMCP tools, test interactions, and refine the final experience. The foundation of ArchMorph is one canonical project model. The plot, floors, rooms, walls, openings, stairs, exterior elements, measurements, and validation results all come from the same structured state. The 2D plan and 3D building are different representations of that state. When a room is moved or resized, its walls, hosted doors and windows, measurements, validation results, floor-plan geometry, and 3D model update together. Each architectural element has a stable ID. This allows the agent to inspect a particular room, wall, door, window, or staircase and make precise changes to the correct object. The WebMCP layer is organized around clear architectural operations: Inspect the project, plot, floors, rooms, walls, openings, circulation, and exterior Design rooms, walls, doors, windows, stairs, floors, and façade elements Measure and validate areas, distances, coverage, access, and layout quality Present and export the design through 2D, 3D, Walk Mode, snapshots, SVG, and structured JSON Human edits and agent actions pass through the same operation system. This keeps the model synchronized and makes changes visible and understandable. Projects are also autosaved locally in the browser so users can continue working without creating an account. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was maintaining one reliable source of truth across the visual editor, WebMCP tools, calculations, layout checks, 2D plan, and 3D model. Architectural elements are strongly connected. Moving one room can affect several walls, openings, measurements, circulation paths, and both visual views. Doors and windows must remain attached to valid host walls, while staircases must connect the correct floors and respond to changes in storey height. Another challenge was making the WebMCP tools precise enough for an agent to use safely. The tools needed typed inputs, real measurement units, stable element IDs, useful inspection results, and clear errors. Invalid geometry had to be rejected without leaving the rest of the project in a broken state. I also wanted agent actions to remain visible. ArchMorph is designed around collaboration, so the agent should not silently modify a hidden data model. When it changes something, the result must appear on the human’s canvas, update the measurements, and remain available in the project history. Finally, balancing capability with simplicity was difficult. Architecture software can quickly become overwhelming, so I had to decide which controls should remain visible, which operations belonged in the inspector, and which details the agent could manage more efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that ArchMorph became more than a visual prototype. It is a working architecture environment where a user can create a measured floor plan, generate the corresponding 3D building, walk through it, inspect layout problems, and continue editing the same design. I am especially proud of the WebMCP integration. The agent can inspect the existing project before acting, reason about individual architectural elements, perform precise operations, and show the outcome directly in the live interface. Building 57 connected WebMCP tools during the hackathon was a major accomplishment. Together, they allow an agent to participate across the complete early design workflow rather than performing a single isolated demo action. Most personally, I am proud that I can now use ArchMorph to explore ideas for my own family home—the same need that originally inspired the project. What we learned The most important thing I learned is that WebMCP can turn a website from a human-only interface into a shared working environment for humans and agents. I also learned that useful agent integration is not simply about exposing many tools. An agent needs to inspect before acting, identify objects reliably, understand exact units, receive structured results, and make changes that the human can immediately see and verify. Building ArchMorph also gave me a much deeper appreciation for the complexity of architecture software. A simple-looking floor plan contains many connected systems: geometry, circulation, openings, measurements, floors, stairs, exterior features, and human experience. Codex helped me move much faster across product thinking, design, implementation, debugging, and testing. However, I also learned that the human still provides the purpose, judgment, creativity, and final decisions. That became the central idea behind ArchMorph: the best result comes from a human and an agent contributing different strengths to the same project. What's next for ArchMorph The next step is to make the collaboration more conversational. A user should be able to describe their family size, plot, lifestyle, privacy needs, climate, and budget, then ask an agent to create a thoughtful starting design through ArchMorph’s existing tools. I also plan to add deeper analysis for daylight, ventilation, accessibility, privacy, climate, and energy use. Location-aware planning guidance could help users make better early decisions while clearly distinguishing guidance

title: Sivan AI

about_excerpt: Autonomous multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents, enabling milestone payments on Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and bank payouts. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents inside web browsers (ChatGPT, Google Gemini in Chrome, Claude) are rapidly advancing from passive text generators to active digital workers capable of negotiating deals, booking services, and coordinating freelance work. However, when browser agents attempt commercial transactions, they hit a major bottleneck: UI Fragility: Scraping DOM elements or simulating blind clicks often fails when layouts shift. Direct Transfer Risk: Upfront payments carry severe counterparty risk with zero delivery guarantees. Disconnected Financial Rails: Agents lack unified multi-chain settlement capabilities and cannot bridge crypto assets into local fiat banking. Sivan AI was built to solve this by providing the first autonomous, multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents using the open W3C WebMCP standard. What it does Sivan AI enables AI agents in browsers to negotiate, draft, fund, and complete commercial Service Agreements with milestone protection. By registering typed financial tools on document.modelContext, web pages allow browser agents to interact with Sivan AI natively: Create Milestone Agreements: The agent drafts clear deliverables and milestone terms. Query Spendable Balances: The agent checks available USDC balances across Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and BSC. Human-in-the-Loop Safety: Every funding action and milestone payout requires on-screen human approval via interactive review cards before any blockchain transaction moves. Instant Local Fiat Settlement: Settled USDC can be off-ramped directly into local bank accounts (e.g. Nigerian Naira via instant NGN bank rails). How we built it WebMCP Client Layer: Implemented in TypeScript using official webmcp-types declarations, registering document.modelContext tools on https://staging.sivantech.online . Multi-Chain Core: Node.js and Fastify microservices orchestrating Privy embedded wallets, Stellar Horizon RPC, Solana web3.js, and EVM adapters. Edge Gateway: Cloudflare Workers (sivan-gateway) managing edge routing, CORS, and Model Context Protocol streaming. Cloud Backend: High-availability microservices deployed on Render with PostgreSQL persistence on Neon. Challenges we overcame Multi-Chain Fan-Out Latency: Grouped multi-chain RPC reads into deduplicated queries, preventing public RPC rate limits and timeouts from blocking balance rendering. Agent Security Boundaries: Designed a strict human-in-the-loop authorization modal so autonomous agents can never drain or move funds without explicit user confirmation. Cross-Chain Key Unification: Unified distinct cryptographic wallet families (ed25519 Solana, secp256k1 EVM, Stellar StrKey) under a single cohesive WebMCP tool schema. Accomplishments that we are proud of Delivering a fully functional, live multi-chain settlement platform on staging ( https://staging.sivantech.online ) and Telegram AI (@SivanStaging_Bot). Achieving sub-second Solana and Base transaction broadcasts with verifiable block explorer receipts. Creating an open-source, standards-compliant WebMCP tool provider available on GitHub ( https://github.com/Sivan-Technologies/Sivan ). What we learned WebMCP fundamentally transforms web applications from human-only interfaces into dual-purpose environments where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly without breaking authentication or state boundaries. What is next for Sivan AI Extending WebMCP tools to background service workers for asynchronous milestone monitoring. Enabling automated recurring service agreements and escrow-free micro-payouts. Onboarding global freelance marketplaces to Sivan AI agentic settlement rails. title: funlabkids
pitch: Your kid learns one way at school. You teach another. So I built an app on NC Department of Education materials to fix that, with fun features that make kids actually want to do homework.
about_excerpt: Your kid learns one way at school. You teach another. So I built an app on NC Department of Education materials to fix that, with fun features that make kids actually want to do homework. Like Comment Story Updates Home Labs Progress Lab Catalogue Math Lab Math Assessments WebMCP Tools Inspiration My kid comes home with homework that doesn't match how I'd explain the same thing. I'd try to help and we'd both get frustrated. The method in the textbook, the method I know, and whatever the AI suggested were all different. That disconnect is what started this. I wanted an AI that doesn't just talk at a kid through a chat window. One that actually works on the same board the child sees. WebMCP made that possible. With it, the agent can move pieces, run checks, and suggest next steps right alongside the child, on the same board, using the same NC Grade 2 materials their teacher assigned. What it does I built Fun Lab Kids to give my kid a shared board where an AI tutor works alongside them, not in a separate chat window, not as a voice in the corner, but right there moving pieces and checking answers. The child stays in control the whole time. The agent helps, but the kid drives. I mapped all 77 NC Grade 2 standards across Math, ELA, and Science, the same ones their teacher is working from, so my kid isn't learning from some random content library. They open labs, earn Fun Points, build streaks, and unlock badges. Progress saves on the device. No account needed, no data leaving the house. The three main labs, Place Value Lab, Opinion Builder, and Matter Lab, show what working together with the agent actually looks like. The agent can open a lab, place pieces, run checks, ask for hints, and suggest changes. Big moves still need my kid to confirm them on screen. That boundary was non-negotiable for me. How we built it I built it with Vite, React, and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The stack was familiar from my day job. The harder parts were the curriculum and the agent layer, not the frontend. I pulled all 77 NC Grade 2 standards directly from NCDPI and mapped them so a parent can see exactly what each lab covers. Everything runs on the same shared board state. The kid's UI and the WebMCP tools use the same logic underneath, so the agent never sees a different version of the board than my kid does. WebMCP tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool . I split them into two groups: curriculum tools (list standards, open activities, read progress) and board tools (get state, apply actions, undo, check, hint, reset). The app works fine without an agent. WebMCP is purely additive, so the experience never depends on whether a model is connected. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't the code. It was the screen design. Ed-tech UIs are built for clicks, not agents. I had to think carefully about which board actions an agent could trigger on its own and which ones still needed my kid's hand on the button. Getting that line wrong in either direction breaks the experience. Shared board state sounds simple until the agent does something unexpected and your kid is staring at a screen that doesn't make sense. I made reveal, reset, and revision all require confirmation from my kid, not because I didn't trust the model, but because my kid needs to stay on track at every step. Covering all of Grade 2 in a weekend-scale build meant making a hard call: go deep on three showcase labs and build reusable templates for the rest, rather than shipping 77 shallow activities that don't actually teach anything. Accomplishments we're proud of I'm most proud that it's a real product, not a thin demo. My kid can sit down, open any lab, and work through it on their own. The agent is there if needed, but the app works either way. The agent works on the same board my kid sees, not in a separate chat window next to it. It moves pieces, runs checks, and responds to what's on screen. That's the thing I set out to build, and it works. The curriculum and board tools use the same checks as the on-screen controls. I didn't want a separate agent-only code path that could drift out of sync, so there isn't one. No account, no data leaving the device, no personal info stored anywhere. I wasn't willing to trade my kid's privacy for a leaderboard feature. The characters are genuinely fun. Codex sprites with custom voices from Fish Audio. My kid noticed immediately, which told me that part was worth the effort. What we learned WebMCP works best when the UI is already a shared board. I didn't have to build a new way for the agent to interact. The board was already there, and the agent just needed tools to use it the same way my kid does. Using the same checks for both the agent and the kid is what keeps the agent honest. The moment you give the agent its own code path, it starts seeing a different board than the child. I learned that early and built around it from the start. Kid safety isn't something you add at the end. I had to think about it at the design level: which moves are safe to automate, which ones need my kid in the loop, and how to make that feel natural rather than annoying. What's next for Fun Lab Kids I want more question sets for every standard, not just the three main labs. The templates are already there. Filling them out is the next big push. The agent coaching needs to get smarter. Better hints, guiding questions that actually adapt to where my kid is stuck, and revision suggestions that feel like a tutor rather than a spell-checker. Grade 2 was the starting point. The goal is the full K-5 range, same shared board model, same focus on real curriculum, just a lot more labs. I want to add progress views for teachers and parents so the adults can see what's clicking and what isn't, without changing the privacy defaults I built in from day one.
