title: Tandem
pitch: Tandem is a spaced-repetition study board where students and AI agents share live context, improve weak topics, and build lasting study plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Tandem is a spaced-repetition study board where students and AI agents share live context, improve weak topics, and build lasting study plans through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Study apps remember what a student has practiced, while AI assistants are good at explaining difficult ideas. The problem is that these two sides usually do not share context. A chat assistant cannot reliably see the card on screen, understand which topics the student repeatedly misses, or make its explanation available during the next study session. I built Tandem to explore what happens when a study app and an agent work on the same persistent state instead of communicating through copied text or brittle interface automation. What it does Tandem is a working spaced-repetition study board for students and their AI agents. The student can create decks, study flashcards, reveal answers, grade recall, inspect weak topics, and follow a revision plan. Through WebMCP, an agent can directly access the structured learning state and help with the same workflow. For example, the agent can: Rank topics using real lapse counts and difficulty data Start a study session focused on the weakest material See the exact card currently on screen Check whether an earlier explanation actually improved the student’s results Replace an ineffective explanation and save the new one directly on the card Build a revision plan from the exam date and weak-topic history Request permission to remove a card without being able to approve the deletion itself Agent actions and human actions appear together in a visible activity feed, so the collaboration remains understandable rather than happening invisibly. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than an agent clicking through a website. A student should not have to repeatedly explain which deck, topic, or card they are viewing. Tandem exposes that information as typed WebMCP tools. When the student says “the card currently on screen,” the agent can call get_study_state and receive the exact card, session position, reveal state, and study progress. WebMCP also lets the agent work with durable application state. An explanation written with annotate_card becomes part of the card and remains available in future sessions instead of disappearing in a chat transcript. The tool surface changes with the application state. Tandem exposes 16 live tools on the dashboard. When a study session begins, session-specific tools such as reveal_answer , grade_current_card , queue_cards , and end_session become available, bringing the live surface to 19 tools. They are withdrawn again when the session ends. Human and agent collaboration Tandem deliberately keeps important decisions with the student. For destructive actions, delete_card does not delete anything. It creates a permission request in the interface and returns a pending result. The student sees exactly which card would be removed and how many recorded reviews would be lost. Only the student can press the confirmation button. The agent can later read the decision through get_approval , but it cannot approve its own request. This creates a clear division of responsibility: the agent can inspect, explain, organize, and propose, while the student remains responsible for studying, grading, and irreversible decisions. How I built it Tandem is built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel. Study data is stored locally in the browser, so the project requires no account or backend. The WebMCP adapter registers tools through document.modelContext , supports contextual registration and withdrawal, and reads current application state when each tool executes. Every tool has a typed input schema, a detailed agent-facing description, structured output, and safety annotations. The app includes 20 tools covering deck inspection, card search and editing, study sessions, note-impact analysis, revision planning, interface highlighting, and human approval. Challenges One challenge was ensuring that tools never operated on stale React state. The executors therefore read the current store at call time instead of capturing an old snapshot when they are registered. Another challenge was designing a dynamic tool surface without duplicate registrations. The registry compares the tools that should currently exist with the tools already registered and changes only the difference. The most important design challenge was human approval. A simple confirm: true argument would only be the agent claiming that permission had been given. Tandem instead separates requesting, deciding, and reading the result into different actions, with the actual decision taking place in the user interface. Accomplishments I am especially proud that Tandem is a complete study product rather than a static WebMCP demonstration. The same structured tools used by the agent affect the real interface and persistent study data. The project includes automated coverage for the spaced-repetition scheduler, tool schemas, contextual tool registration, note-impact calculation, revision planning, approval boundaries, accessibility states, and an end-to-end agent simulation. What I learned Building Tandem changed how I think about agent-enabled websites. A useful tool description is not just API documentation; it explains when an agent should use the tool and where the human boundary begins. I also learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes domain logic and live context that would be difficult to reconstruct from screenshots or interface automation. What’s next Next, I would add optional cross-device synchronization, richer study analytics, document-to-deck importing, and longer-term measurements of whether agent-written explanations improve retention across multiple review cycles. title: Handoff
pitch: A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page.
about_excerpt:
A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Handoff 

 A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page. 

 Inspiration 

 Every "agent + your app" story today follows the same pattern: the agent takes a screenshot, guesses which pixel is a button, clicks it, waits, screenshots again. It's slow, it's fragile, and it treats the agent like a human with a mouse instead of software that could just... call a function. 

 Task management felt like the clearest place to make that contrast obvious. A Kanban board is something people already share with teammates why not share it with an agent too, and let both act on the same live state at the same time? 

 What it does 

 Handoff is a collaborative Kanban board. A human drags cards between To Do, In Progress, and Done exactly like any other Kanban tool. An AI agent manages the same board through seven WebMCP tools registered directly on the page: 

 
 create_task , list_tasks , move_task , update_task , delete_task the core actions any task manager needs 
 prioritize_tasks applies a batch of priority changes the agent has already reasoned about (via list_tasks ), atomically, in one call 
 summarize_board a natural-language rollup of what's open, in progress, and done 
 

 Both the human and the agent are working against the exact same Supabase-backed state, synced live over Supabase Realtime. When the agent creates or moves a card, it shows an "agent" badge and a brief highlight pulse, so at a glance you can see who did what. A live activity log underneath the board narrates the handoff as it happens: "You moved 'Fix login bug' to In Progress," "Agent created 'Update docs.'" 

 There's no chat window bolted onto the side. The agent works through the same UI you're looking at. 

 Why WebMCP fits this use case 

 Without WebMCP, an agent that wants to help manage your board has exactly two bad options: a bespoke backend API it has to be specifically integrated with, or screen-scraping a drag-and-drop UI that was never designed to be driven programmatically, inferring which <div> is a card, simulating a drag gesture, and hoping the DOM didn't change underneath it. 

 WebMCP replaces both of those with the page just telling the agent what it can do. document.modelContext.registerTool() exposes move_task with a typed schema ( id , status ) instead of forcing an agent to identify and drag a specific card. The agent doesn't need a separate integration, and it doesn't need to understand your UI, it needs to understand your tools, which you've defined precisely. 

 That's the UX improvement in one sentence: an agent can now say "reprioritize my sprint so the login bug is high priority" and it works , live, immediately reflected in the same board a human is looking at, without OpenAI, Anthropic, or anyone else needing to have built a Handoff-specific integration ahead of time. The website itself is the integration. 

 What's newly possible 

 Before WebMCP, "human and agent share a task board" basically meant the agent had its own separate interface (a chat window, a CLI) that happened to write to the same database, two disconnected experiences bolted together. WebMCP lets both parties act through the same page, the same session, the same state, at the same time. You can watch a card move because you dragged it, or because you asked an agent to move it, and the board doesn't care which, it just reacts. That's a genuinely different interaction model, not just a faster version of the old one. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js / React , deployed on Vercel 
 Supabase (Postgres + Realtime) for shared task storage; every client (human tab or agent-driven tab) subscribes to the same Realtime channel, so changes from either side propagate instantly 
 WebMCP , implemented via direct document.modelContext.registerTool() calls (see hooks/useWebMCPTools.js ) each tool's execute function calls the exact same functions the drag-and-drop UI calls ( hooks/useTasks.js ), so there is one source of truth for board logic, not a parallel "agent path" that could drift out of sync with the human path 
 @hello-pangea/dnd for the human-facing drag-and-drop 
 The activity log is derived from the same Realtime subscription that drives the board, no separate logging table, just an in-memory feed of what the subscription already sees 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is genuinely early. I hit a real interoperability bug where a React wrapper library's handler callback wasn't being translated into the native execute property the browser's registerTool() implementation expects, which surfaced as execute is not a function only at call time, not at registration time, which made it harder to catch. We moved to calling the native imperative API directly rather than depending on a wrapper layer, which fixed it and also made the WebMCP usage more explicit in the codebase. 

 Accomplishments 

 A full round trip, human drags a card, agent calls a tool, board updates live for both working end to end, verified both through direct browser console calls to document.modelContext.executeTool() and through a real natural-language agent (Google's Model Context Tool Inspector) discovering and calling our tools correctly. 

 What's next 

 Multi-board support, authenticated multi-user boards, and finer-grained permissions per tool (e.g., a read-only list_tasks -only agent versus a full-access one) 

 Built with 

 Next.js, React, Supabase, Supabase Realtime, WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), @hello-pangea/dnd, Vercel

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Nepal Disaster Watch
pitch: Synthesizing 6 public crisis feeds with the help of 11 WebMCP tools so AI and responders uncover hidden disaster reporting gaps.
about_excerpt: Synthesizing 6 public crisis feeds with the help of 11 WebMCP tools so AI and responders uncover hidden disaster reporting gaps. Like Comment Story Updates Nepal Disaster Watch Inspiration On August 26, a devastating flood tore through Nepal's Bhote Koshi river system, sweeping water, mud, and debris through Rasuwa and downstream communities. I wasn't thinking about hackathons that night I was refreshing tab after tab at 2am, trying to find out if people I knew were okay. That's when the second gut-punch hit: I couldn't even get a straight answer. Incident reports lived on one government portal, river levels on another, road closures on a third, flood forecasts and satellite damage assessments somewhere else entirely each written for a different audience, none of them talking to each other. Every empty page made me more anxious, because I couldn't tell if "no data" meant "nothing happened" or "the power's out and nobody can report anything." That fear of mistaking silence for safety is the whole reason Nepal Disaster Watch exists. What it Does Nepal Disaster Watch is a live emergency-intelligence platform covering all 77 districts of Nepal. It pulls together six public data sources government incident reports, river gauges, road closures, disaster alerts, flood forecasts, and field or satellite damage assessments into one consistent, constantly refreshing picture. It isn't just a dashboard. It's built with 11 native WebMCP tools that let a person and an AI agent investigate the same evidence, side by side, on the same screen. Some tools read information checking source health, summarizing the national situation, cross-referencing a district across every feed. Others act on the interface itself, like focus_district("Rasuwa") , which pans and zooms the live map the person is already looking at. There's no separate "agent view." We share one screen and one investigation. How we Built It The core of the system normalizes those six data sources into a single schema, refreshed every three minutes: $$t_{\text{refresh}} = 180\text{s}$$ Every record is transformed into a standardized model with strict provenance metadata: $$R_i = {\,id,\ district_id,\ timestamp,\ source_type,\ payload,\ confidence_score\,}$$ On top of that pipeline sit the 11 WebMCP tools, split between read tools (source health, situation summaries, cross-source comparisons, record inspection, feed filtering) and action tools that mutate the dashboard state directly moving the map, opening records, changing what's on screen for both the human and the agent at once. Challenges we Ran Into The hardest part wasn't technical it was resisting the urge to smooth things over. Cross-referencing sources often surfaced sharp, uncomfortable disagreements: a district with zero official incident reports sitting right next to satellite imagery showing widespread structural damage. It would have been easier to just pick a number and show it. Instead, the app says plainly: these sources disagree, and here's probably why because honesty about what we don't know is worth more than false confidence during a crisis. Underneath that were two harder engineering problems: Source availability. Public emergency portals go down during real disasters exactly when they're needed most, from traffic spikes or infrastructure failure. I had to build fallback logic and explicit "source health" indicators so the system stays useful even when parts of it go dark. Context synchronization. Keeping the agent's actions and the human's view in perfect sync zero-latency state updates between a WebMCP tool call and what actually renders on screen took real care to get right. Accomplishments that We're Proud Of I'm proud that this doesn't feel like a technical demo bolted onto a real tragedy it feels like the tool I actually needed at 2am on August 26. I'm proud that the system never quietly papers over a gap in the data; it surfaces disagreement and uncertainty instead of pretending to have a single clean answer. And I'm proud of building a genuinely shared human-agent interface — not an agent-only backend and a human-only frontend, but one investigation the two of us run together. What we Learned Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. In disaster intelligence, an empty feed usually means broken infrastructure, not a safe district. I had to design the whole system around that distinction instead of treating "no data" as good news. Uncertainty deserves to be shown, not hidden. Source freshness, health, and reporting delays turned out to matter more than forcing everything into one clean "source of truth." WebMCP changes what "using an AI agent" even means. Instead of an agent screen-scraping a website and guessing which button to click, it can call purpose-built tools and act inside the same interface a person is looking at genuinely side by side, not behind the scenes. What's Next for Nepal Disaster Watch Nepal Disaster Watch doesn't issue official warnings or make emergency decisions, and that boundary matters it's a step, not the finish line. Next is expanding source coverage beyond the initial six feeds, tightening the confidence-scoring model so confidence_score reflects real reporting-chain conditions rather than a rough proxy, and getting the platform in front of the people who were living through nights like the one that inspired it so the next time information is scattered, it doesn't have to stay that way. title: Hubit
pitch: A storefront where you can hand an agent the shopping without handing over your wallet.
about_excerpt: A storefront where you can hand an agent the shopping without handing over your wallet. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration People will happily let an agent research a purchase. Almost nobody lets one finish it. The reason is not that agents shop badly. It is that "it can look but it cannot buy" has never been a mechanism, only a promise. Every guardrail on offer today is a server saying no, and a refusal is just a message. A model can retry a message, argue with it, or try again with different arguments. What it does Hubit is a storefront where you can hand an agent the shopping without handing it your wallet. You write your rules in plain language: under $1,200, I already have a laptop, prioritise quality. The agent searches the store, compares specs, finds cheaper alternatives, fills the cart, and types your delivery details. You watch every move it makes on screen while you edit the same cart yourself. Then it goes to check out, and checkout is not in its toolbox. Not refused. Not there. The agent has nothing to retry and nothing to argue with. Its only remaining move is to ask you: "$1,255 against your $1,200 budget. Raise it by $55?" You click approve, and checkout appears in the agent's toolbox, live, in the same tab, with no reload. Three things have to be true before that happens, and all three are visible on the page: the cart is inside your rules, your delivery details are complete, and you approved this basket. Change any of them and the approval goes with it. You approved a particular cart going to a particular address, so an agent cannot quietly redirect a parcel you already said yes to. How we built it A static storefront on Next.js, React and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. Seventeen tools the agent can use. No backend, no database, no server anywhere in the project, which is the whole argument: there is no API for the agent to go around, because the authority lives in the page you are looking at. The agent writes to the same place your keyboard does. There is no separate agent path, which is what makes it honest rather than theatre. Every field the agent typed into your delivery form is marked on screen and tagged as agent-written, and you can overwrite any of it. That single screen carries the entire idea: the agent can type your address and still cannot spend your money. The store never just goes quiet on the agent either. It always says why checkout is being withheld, so the agent knows to come back and ask instead of retrying into a wall. Challenges we ran into Handing back a tool while you are using it. Checkout places the order, and placing the order is exactly what takes checkout away. The tool was pulling the rug out from under itself mid-call, so the agent saw an error on an order that had actually gone through fine. Accomplishments that we're proud of An uncoached model shopped the store on its own, in production. Given nothing but a plain shopping prompt, it compared desks, chairs, monitors and keyboards, built a $1,255 basket against a $1,200 budget, hit the missing checkout, went looking for cheaper alternatives, found the nearest one only saved $50, and proposed raising the budget on its own initiative. We never told it to do any of that. The full transcript is in the repo. 105 automated checks against the live site, all passing. They drive the real tools the way an agent would, and they open the gate by clicking the actual approve button on the page, not by flipping a flag in test code. Nothing in this project is faked. No mock agent, no simulated run, no fallback path. Everything in the demo is the real thing working. What we learned That the interesting part of WebMCP is not that a web page can offer tools to an agent. It is that which tools exist can change while the agent is working , and that it can change because a human just made a decision. We also learned to be precise about what we are claiming. This is a consent boundary, not a security boundary, and it sits one step earlier than a server check. A server saying no is something a model retries. A tool that is not there is something it never thinks to reach for. A real shop wants both, and WebMCP is what makes the earlier one possible at all. What's next for Hubit Real payments behind the gate , so both layers do their proper job: the missing tool stops the agent from ever forming the intent, the server stops anything that goes around the page. Approvals with shape, instead of one yes or no. Approve up to an amount, approve one merchant, approve for the next ten minutes. The mechanism already handles this, since each one is just a different question asked at the same moment. Approval that survives a refresh , tied to the exact basket so it cannot be reused on a different cart or a different address. The pattern beyond shopping. Nothing about this is specific to retail. Sending an email, filing a pull request, booking a flight, moving money: any page where an agent should do the whole job except the last irreversible step can hold back exactly one tool, and hand it over when a human says so. Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP People will happily let an agent research a purchase. Almost nobody lets one finish it. The reason is not that agents shop badly. It is that "it can look but it cannot buy" has never been a mechanism, only a promise. Every guardrail on offer today is a server saying no, somewhere behind an API. A refusal is a message, a message is an input, and a model can be argued into retrying an input. WebMCP has one property that no server-side guardrail can imitate: the tool surface is a live, mutable property of the tab. registerTool takes an AbortSignal , so a capability can be absent, then appear mid-conversation because a human decided something, then disappear again when they change their mind. Hubit registers checkout only while a gate is open. When that gate is closed the agent cannot call checkout , cannot retry it, and cannot argue with it, because there is nothing there. getTools() does not list it, and a stale handle captured before the abort is rejected at browser level. To be exact about what we are claiming: this is not a security boundary, and we have never presented it as one. It is a consent boundary, and it operates one layer earlier than a server check. A server refusal is a runtime "no" that a model retries, reasons around and argues with. A capability that is absent from the surface means the planner never forms the intent, so there is no retry loop to lose. In production both exist the server check is the security boundary, and this is what stops an agent from ever reaching it without you. WebMCP is what makes that earlier layer possible at all, because tools are registered per session in the page and can be revoked mid-conversation. How it creates a better user experience The tedious half of a purchase gets delegated. The half that needs judgment does not. The agent searches, compares specs side by side, finds cheaper alternatives, fills the cart, and types your delivery details name, email, address, postcode, country, delivery speed, courier notes. It writes to the same store your keyboard writes to. There is no separate agent path, and that is exactly what makes the provenance honest: every field the agent typed is outlined in the accent colour and tagged agent , and you can overwrite any of them. That one screen carries the whole thesis the agent can type your address and still cannot spend your money. You also watch it work instead of reading a transcript of it. Two tools move your screen filter_catalog changes the shelf you are looking at, focus_product opens a quick view and every call streams into a rail on the right with its real arguments. The rail renders from the tool host's own registry rather than from a hardcoded list, so if a tool ever failed to register it shows that instead of claiming it is live. And the store always tells you why checkout is withheld: over budget, no delivery address, or this basket is not approved. The agent's only remaining move is to ask you. propose_constraint_change queues a proposal and changes nothing by itself. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Grant a capability mid-conversation and take it back. Approve the basket and checkout appears live, in the same tab, with no reload. Then change the cart, move the budget, edit the delivery address, switch to express delivery, or click "Withdraw approval", and it leaves the surface again. Consent is per basket, not per session : you approved a particular cart going to a particular place, so any change to either withdraws it. Emptying a required delivery field withholds checkout , and restoring that field does not silently re-open it, because the approval left with the change. title: ThermalMesh Lab
pitch: Let AI agents understand, benchmark, and optimize heterogeneous inference infrastructure through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Let AI agents understand, benchmark, and optimize heterogeneous inference infrastructure through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP-powered inference routing lab comparing Round Robin with capacity- and load-aware routing on heterogeneous workers Inspiration AI inference infrastructure is increasingly heterogeneous: workers can have very different capacities, yet simple strategies such as Round Robin still treat them as interchangeable. A slow worker can build a large queue while faster capacity remains available elsewhere. At the same time, browser agents often interact with applications indirectly by inspecting interfaces, finding controls, and deciding what to click. For infrastructure software, however, operations like comparing routing policies or inspecting a bottleneck have much richer semantics than the buttons that trigger them. ThermalMesh Lab grew from one question: What if an AI agent could understand and operate inference infrastructure through domain-level tools instead of automating a dashboard by sight? What it does ThermalMesh Lab is a browser-based simulator for heterogeneous AI inference clusters. Users can configure workers with different abstract capacities, generate deterministic workloads, and compare two routing strategies: Round Robin — equal distribution without considering capacity or load. Inference-Aware (ThermalMesh) — a simplified strategy using capacity, load, and estimated completion time. The simulator exposes TTFT, queue latency, throughput, completed and unfinished requests, worker utilization, and queue depth. The same application can also be operated by an AI agent through WebMCP Site Tools. An agent can configure the cluster and workload, run benchmarks, compare policies, inspect bottlenecks, and apply a routing strategy. Humans and agents share the same application state, so every agent action is immediately reflected in the dashboard. ThermalMesh Lab is a browser-based simulation, not a hardware benchmark. How we built it ThermalMesh Lab is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and runs entirely in the browser. The simulation engine generates a deterministic seeded request trace and gives both routing policies the same workload, making comparisons reproducible. WebMCP is integrated through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The application exposes seven domain-level Site Tools: get_cluster_state configure_cluster configure_workload run_benchmark compare_routing_policies inspect_bottlenecks apply_routing_policy The WebMCP layer does not maintain separate agent state. Site Tools and the visible React interface call the same validated application/store operations. We also implemented a state-dependent tool lifecycle. After a valid comparison, ThermalMesh Lab dynamically exposes an eighth tool: apply_winning_configuration If the cluster or workload changes, the comparison becomes stale and that tool is removed. In the deployed application this creates a live: 7 tools → comparison → 8 tools → scenario change → 7 tools lifecycle driven entirely by application state. The application requires no backend, database, authentication, or paid API and is deployed as a static site on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making WebMCP a real application interface rather than a collection of tools that simply mimic button clicks. Operations such as compare_routing_policies and inspect_bottlenecks needed to represent actual infrastructure semantics while keeping the human UI and agent perfectly synchronized. Dynamic registration also introduced lifecycle problems. We had to prevent duplicate or stale registrations, ensure tools always operated on current state, and remove the winning-policy tool immediately when its comparison became invalid. The simulator itself required careful handling as well. Both policies needed identical request traces, overloaded scenarios had to remain numerically safe, and unfinished requests could not appear as misleading zero-latency samples. One of our first live agent tests produced an unexpected result: the agent realized its initial workload had completely saturated the cluster, reduced the workload, reran the comparison, and then selected a better routing policy. That showed us both the potential of semantic tools and the importance of precise tool descriptions when working with autonomous agents. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that WebMCP is not an isolated demo layer. The human interface and the AI agent genuinely operate the same application. In live testing, ChatGPT successfully discovered the Site Tools, configured the cluster and workload, compared routing strategies, analyzed the bottleneck, and applied the selected routing policy. The state-dependent lifecycle also works end to end: 7 base tools → comparison → 8 tools → invalidation → 7 tools We are also proud that the simulator does not artificially make Inference-Aware routing win. With homogeneous, lightly loaded workers, both strategies can produce effectively identical results. Under heterogeneous load, differences emerge naturally. In one live test: Round Robin completed 620 requests Inference-Aware routing completed 741 requests TTFT p95 fell from roughly 23.1 seconds to 1.7 seconds Unfinished requests fell from 123 to 2 More importantly, the agent was able to explain why: Round Robin continued sending equal traffic to a much slower worker, creating a large queue, while Inference-Aware routing shifted work toward available capacity. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP becomes much more powerful when tools represent application semantics rather than UI actions . A tool such as compare_routing_policies gives an agent far more reliable context than asking it to discover controls, run separate simulations, locate the results, and infer how the metrics relate. We also learned that agent capabilities do not need to remain static. Exposing apply_winning_configuration only when a valid comparison exists gives the agent an interface that reflects what the application can meaningfully do at that moment. The simulator taught us another important lesson: overloaded-system benchmarks can be misleading when unfinished work is ignored. A policy may appear to have better median latency simply because its slowest requests never complete inside the observation window. We therefore treat completion and unfinished work as first-class comparison signals rather than hiding them. What's next for ThermalMesh Lab The challenge version intentionally focuses on a small, reliable WebMCP experience. Next, we would like to add additional well-defined routing baselines such as Weighted Round Robin and Least Queue , along with richer workload patterns, request classes, worker failures, and longer-running experiments. ThermalMesh Lab could also evolve into a broader agent-native environment where agents design experiments, compare multiple strategies, explain tradeoffs, and iteratively search for better infrastructure configurations. The broader idea we want to explore is simple: Instead of teaching AI agents how to click through infrastructure software, make infrastructure software directly understandable to agents. title: Tether
pitch: Teach one site, and a site that has never met you is already configured. A shared memory layer for the agent-native web, built on WebMCP. Delete a memory, and the next build forgets it.
about_excerpt: Teach one site, and a site that has never met you is already configured. A shared memory layer for the agent-native web, built on WebMCP. Delete a memory, and the next build forgets it. Like Comment Story Updates Logo Inspiration You tell one site you want dark interfaces, compact layouts, and TypeScript. Then you open the next tool and type all of it again. And again. Agents were supposed to remove that friction, but each one starts cold at the tab boundary, so the person ends up carrying context from site to site by hand. Being the integration layer is the last unautomated job on the web, and nobody was treating it as a problem. WebMCP changes what a website can hand an agent: real capabilities the page declares, instead of a DOM that was never built to be driven. That made one question worth answering. If every site can expose genuine tools, what is the single shared capability that would make all of them better at once? Memory. Not an assistant's private chat history sealed in a vendor cloud, but structured context that any participating site can read and write, with the person holding the delete key. What it does Tether is a shared memory layer for the agent-native web, plus two working sites that prove context survives the jump between them. DesignLab is the producer, a small design studio. Ask the agent to remember your preferences and its save_preference tool applies them to the canvas and writes them to Tether in the same call. DevForge is the consumer, a project scaffolder whose form has a project-name field and nothing else. Its create_project tool asks Tether what you prefer, then configures six things it never asked about: language, theme, layout density, framework, package manager, and styling, down to the lock file and the install command. The Tether control plane shows every memory with its source site, the tool that wrote it, tags, a confidence score, and a timestamp. Inspect, search, edit, add, or permanently delete any of it. Try it in 30 seconds Open DesignLab and ask the agent: "Remember that I prefer dark interfaces, compact layouts, and TypeScript." The studio turns dark and compact, and three structured memories land in Tether. Open the dashboard . They are already there, each carrying its full lineage. Open DevForge and ask for a starter project. It comes back TypeScript, dark, compact, with every value tracing back to the memory that produced it. Now delete the TypeScript memory and scaffold again. The language falls back to JavaScript. The others hold. Step 4 is the whole project. A cross-site demo can be faked with a hardcoded path, and a judge should assume it was until shown otherwise. So deletion is part of the demo: pull one row out of the layer, and a different site's output changes in front of you. None of this is limited to a fixed set of toggles. Both DesignLab and the control plane accept context in your own words through the same validated path. Say "I prefer pnpm over npm" or "I prefer Tailwind CSS for styling" , and the next scaffold picks it up, install command included. How we built it Next.js 15 App Router and TypeScript. Tailwind for a dark, high-density developer-tool surface. Zod on every boundary. Supabase Postgres for persistence, behind a pluggable store: with no environment variables at all, a fresh clone runs immediately on an in-process driver. Memories are structured rather than free text: content, category, tags, source, confidence, scope, timestamps. That schema is what makes the whole thing work. A pile of chat transcripts cannot be filtered, ranked, explained, or selectively deleted. Security got real attention for a hackathon MVP. The service-role key lives only in server-only modules, so an accidental client import fails the build instead of leaking a credential. Row-level security is enabled on both tables with no permissive policies. Memory content is rendered as text by React and never injected as HTML. Sessions are opaque random ids in an httpOnly first-party cookie, with no accounts and no PII. Challenges we ran into Making the memory falsifiable. The cross-site moment only convinces if it can visibly fail. Building deletion into the demo, and making the fallback path genuinely fall back rather than run a second hardcoded branch, is what turned a nice animation into evidence. Refusing to simulate. It would have been easy to fake tool calls when no agent is present and let the video imply otherwise. Detecting the absence and labelling every manual invocation cost a day and made the architecture clearer, because you can now see that the agent path and the button path run the same handler. Keeping retrieval interpretable end to end. Carrying matchedOn reasons from the matcher through the API into the UI constrained the entire pipeline. It ruled out the easy embedding approach, and it is the reason the product can show its work. Serverless state. The in-process store is perfect locally and wrong in production, because serverless functions do not share memory between invocations. The /api/health endpoint reports which driver is live specifically so a misconfigured deploy looks like a misconfiguration instead of a broken app. Accomplishments that we're proud of The delete-and-rescaffold moment. It is the rare demo that proves itself by breaking on purpose. You can verify our claims in ninety seconds. The test suite runs against the live deployment: curl https://tether-swart.vercel.app/api/health # {"status":"online","driver":"supabase"} git clone https://github.com/Dotman-Bei/Tether && cd Tether && npm install BASE_URL=https://tether-swart.vercel.app npm test It scopes itself to its own session cookie and cleans up after itself, so it is safe to point at production. It covers every route handler and, through them, the configured store driver: creation and defaults, numeric coercion, tag round-tripping, the duplicate guard, list ordering and filters, ranked retrieval with match reasons, update persistence, input validation, 404s, activity logging, session isolation, delete, and reset. No test framework and no dependencies. **A fresh clone runs with zero environment variables.** `npm install && npm run dev` and the whole demo works. **We did not overclaim the protocol.** WebMCP does not carry memory between unrelated sites on its own. It is the tool interface on each page, and Tether is the shared backplane those tools read from and write to. Saying otherwise would have been an easier pitch and a false one. ## What we learned **Structure is what makes memory shareable.** Category, tags, source, and confidence are what let a second site retrieve something specific, apply it, show its work, and let a person govern the result. Unstructured recall cannot do any of those four things. **Trust surfaces are product features, not compliance overhead.** The lineage drawer and the labelled telemetry stream are what make people believe the rest of it, and they were among the cheapest things in the build. **Explainability is a design constraint, not a feature you add later.** Choosing lexical matching over embeddings looked like a downgrade until we tried to render *why* a memory was applied. The interpretable pipeline turned out to be the product. ## What's next for Tether **Per-site scoped consent and real accounts.** The cross-origin story above, which is the difference between a demo and infrastructure. - **A small client library** so a site joins in a few lines instead of reimplementing the contract. - **Memory decay and conflict resolution.** Preferences change, and the layer should notice when a new statement contradicts an old one instead of accumulating both. - **Richer context types past preferences:** working conventions, project constraints, domain vocabulary. The two demo sites are an illustration. The direction is a shared memory layer that any experience can build on, where the person keeps the keys. Built With javascript lucide-react model-context-protocol next.js node.js postgresql react rest-api serverless supabase tailwindcss typescript vercel webmcp zod Try it out tether-swart.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Heisbei: Solo build. The thesis, the product design, the ten WebMCP tools, the memory layer and the API underneath are mine, with Claude Code as implementation partner. The decision I would defend hardest is the delete step. A clean cross-site handoff would have demoed fine, but a demo that cannot visibly fail proves nothing, so I made deletion part of the flow and let the scaffold fall back on camera. The second is making the app admit when no agent is present instead of faking the call. That cost a day, and it is the reason you can trust anything else on the screen. title: ImageLens
pitch: ImageLens — Agent-Native Image Forensics\nAn image forensics engine that gives AI agents structured evidence to investigate and explain through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
ImageLens — Agent-Native Image Forensics
An image forensics engine that gives AI agents structured evidence to investigate and explain through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Images are increasingly difficult to evaluate. 

 AI assistants can explain images, but they often don't have direct access to the forensic evidence behind an analysis. 

 I wanted to explore a different approach: what if an image forensics application could expose its own analysis directly to an AI agent? 

 This led to ImageLens — a forensic analysis tool designed to work with AI agents through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 ImageLens analyzes images using its own statistical and forensic detection engine. 

 It examines multiple signals and produces structured results such as: 

 
 Detection scores 
 Forensic signals 
 Image metadata 
 Noise characteristics 
 Frequency-domain analysis 
 A combined forensic report 
 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can access these results directly from the application. 

 The agent can then investigate the evidence and explain the findings in natural language. 

 The important distinction is that the AI does not perform the underlying forensic analysis. ImageLens does. 

 How we built it 

 ImageLens is a web application with a client-side forensic analysis engine and a WebMCP integration. 

 The application's analysis engine produces structured results that are exposed through WebMCP tools. 

 The agent can query capabilities such as: 

 
 analyze_image 
 get_detection_score 
 get_forensic_signals 
 get_metadata 
 get_frequency_analysis 
 get_report 
 

 These tools provide the agent with the same information available inside the application, without requiring the user to manually copy and paste results into an AI assistant. 

 The application and its WebMCP tools share the same underlying analysis logic, keeping the agent's information synchronized with the actual application state. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was deciding where the responsibility between the application and the AI should stop. 

 We deliberately did not make the AI the detector. 

 The forensic engine is responsible for analyzing the image and producing evidence. The AI is responsible for querying that evidence, connecting the different signals, and explaining them. 

 Another challenge was turning complex forensic information into structured WebMCP tools that an agent can understand and use effectively. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that ImageLens is more than an image analyzer with an AI chatbot attached to it. 

 The WebMCP integration allows an agent to directly access the application's real forensic data. 

 An agent can independently retrieve different types of evidence, combine them, and produce an investigation-style explanation. 

 This creates a clear division of responsibilities: 

 ImageLens analyzes.
The agent investigates.
The human makes the final judgment. 

 We also designed the application to avoid making absolute claims about image authenticity. Forensic signals can indicate suspicious characteristics, but they cannot provide mathematical proof that an image was generated by AI. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP can be particularly powerful for specialized applications. 

 Instead of trying to make the AI reproduce the application's domain-specific logic, the application can expose its expertise through structured tools. 

 This allows an AI agent to become an interface to specialized software without replacing the software itself. 

 We also learned that good WebMCP tools should expose meaningful domain-level capabilities rather than simply reproduce UI interactions. 

 What's next for ImageLens 

 The next step would be to expand the forensic toolkit with additional analysis methods and comparison capabilities. 

 Possible future features include comparing multiple images, detecting inconsistencies between image regions, generating more detailed forensic reports, and allowing agents to conduct multi-step investigations across several images. 

 The long-term goal is to make ImageLens a specialized forensic engine that AI agents can use as part of larger investigation workflows. 

 ImageLens doesn't just detect. It gives agents evidence they can investigate and explain.
