title: PixelForge Studio
pitch: A WebMCP-native pixel art studio where people and AI agents create, animate, and export sprites together.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native pixel art studio where people and AI agents create, animate, and export sprites together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Judge Quick Links Live Cloudflare mirror (start here): https://pixelforge-studio.himomohi.workers.dev Public GitHub source: https://github.com/himomohi/pixelforge-studio ChatGPT Sites (in-app browser fallback): https://pixelforge-studio.appcaster.chatgpt.site Demo video: https://youtu.be/-mTECXrUEy8 Fast judging path: Open the Cloudflare mirror, use a WebMCP-capable browser, and watch one shared project receive a frame, an undo, a duplicated frame, 180 ms timing, an Agent Highlights layer, and 10 cyan pixels—then undo or redo the same visible result in the editor. Inspiration Creative software is still split into two worlds. People work through rich visual interfaces, while agents are often forced to guess which controls to click and where to place the pointer. That is especially fragile in pixel-art production, where a single coordinate, frame, layer, or alpha value matters. PixelForge Studio explores a better model: one shared creative surface for both the artist and the agent. The artist keeps the complete visual editor, while WebMCP gives the agent precise, structured access to the same project. What it does PixelForge Studio is a professional browser-based pixel-art editor with: crisp pixel drawing and shape tools; palettes, foreground and background colors, grid, symmetry, selection, and zoom; multiple animation frames with timing, playback, duplication, and reordering; multiple layers with visibility, locking, opacity, duplication, and reordering; browser-local autosave and project management; browser-local reference images with split and floating views; adaptive image-to-pixel conversion with transparency and aspect-ratio guardrails; a measurable strict-99 reference fidelity audit; PNG, animated GIF, sprite-sheet, editable project, and game-engine bundle exports. It also registers 65 browser-native WebMCP tools. Compatible agents can inspect the current state, create and duplicate projects, place exact pixels, edit frames and layers, convert references, verify results, and export assets without inferring the UI. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Pixel art combines high-level creative intent with low-level precision. A person may ask for a highlighted animation frame, a palette adjustment, or a Unity-ready sprite bundle. Performing that work through screen coordinates is slow and error-prone because the agent must infer canvas geometry, selected frames, selected layers, active colors, and editor state. WebMCP makes those workflows explicit. Each action has a bounded JSON schema and a stable semantic meaning. The agent can read the project state, apply an atomic edit, and immediately return control to the artist in the visual editor. How it creates a better user experience The agent does not replace the editor. It accelerates precise or repetitive work while preserving human review and creative control. In the demo, the agent performs this exact real-editor run: add_frame ; undo , proving the first change is a normal reversible editor action; duplicate_frame ; set_frame_duration with 180 milliseconds; add_layer , then rename_layer to Agent Highlights ; draw_pixels with an exact batch of 10 cyan pixels. This is not a separate agent-only canvas. All 65 typed tools and the human interface use the same browser-local project state, so every change appears immediately on the canvas, timeline, and layer stack. The artist can inspect the result, refine it manually, play the animation, undo or redo changes, or export the finished asset. What was difficult or impossible before Before WebMCP, an agent had to navigate the editor visually and hope that pointer coordinates, focus, selections, panels, and timing controls had not changed. Exact pixel batches and multi-step animation edits were especially unreliable. With WebMCP, the agent and person share a stable project model. The agent can operate semantically while the person continues to work visually. This makes mixed-initiative creative workflows practical instead of brittle. How WebMCP was implemented The integration is implemented in lib/pixelforge/webmcp.ts using document.modelContext.registerTool . The 65 registered tools cover: project lifecycle and production presets; reference-image state and view controls; reference conversion and fidelity auditing; exact pixels, shapes, selections, palettes, colors, and brush size; frames, layers, playback, grid, onion skin, symmetry, and zoom; PNG, GIF, sprite-sheet, project, and game-bundle exports. Schemas enforce bounded dimensions, colors, array sizes, and enums. Operations accept cancellation signals. Read-only operations are annotated, destructive operations are identified, and raw reference image data remains browser-local. The live judging run is deliberately concrete: add_frame → undo → duplicate_frame → set_frame_duration (180 ms) → add_layer → rename_layer ( Agent Highlights ) → draw_pixels (10 cyan pixels). Because those calls update the editor's actual browser-local state rather than a demo surrogate, the visible result stays fully undoable and redoable. How we built it Next.js 16 and React 19 TypeScript Vinext and Vite Cloudflare Workers with Static Assets ChatGPT Sites backup Browser-native WebMCP Canvas rendering and browser-local storage Custom PNG, GIF, sprite-sheet, ZIP, and game-engine exporters Remotion for the public demo video We also focused the shipped surface: only 14 UI primitives used by the product remain, and the unused D1/notes scaffold was removed. That keeps the submission centered on the editor and its WebMCP workflow. Challenges Designing one project model that works for both visual editing and structured agent actions Keeping frame-layer cels complete and consistent across duplication and reordering Preserving alpha, aspect ratio, and subject bounds during reference conversion Making fidelity claims measurable instead of subjective Exporting useful assets for many game engines from one browser project Defining tool schemas that are powerful without accepting unbounded input Accomplishments 65 working WebMCP tools registered in the deployed app A complete editor rather than a single-purpose proof of concept Strict-99 reference conversion and audit guardrails Browser-local projects and reference images Animated GIF, sprite-sheet, editable project, and multi-engine bundle exports Public MIT-licensed source with automated tests A reproducible Remotion demo project using real captures from the live app What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to real product concepts instead of individual UI clicks. A strong agent-native app still needs an excellent human interface; the value comes from both surfaces sharing the same state and producing immediately reviewable results. What's next Natural-language creative recipes that combine several tools into reviewable plans More sprite animation presets and engine-specific export helpers Optional collaboration and project sharing Richer fidelity reports and side-by-side reference comparisons Community palettes, templates, and reusable agent workflows Built With ai-agents chatgpt cloudflare-workers next.js openai pixel-art react remotion typescript vinext webmcp Try it out pixelforge-studio.himomohi.workers.dev github.com pixelforge-studio.appcaster.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Appcaster kim Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Appcaster kim started this project — Aug 31, 2026 04:09 AM EDT

title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Jibe
pitch: Jibe uses WebMCP to build software with WebMCP. Toggle between dev and prod like switching themes: agents use your app in prod and build it in dev. Local-first design keeps your data on your machine.
about_excerpt: Jibe uses WebMCP to build software with WebMCP. Toggle between dev and prod like switching themes: agents use your app in prod and build it in dev. Local-first design keeps your data on your machine. Like Comment Story Updates Home origin tracks local installs About DOOM Editor preview Jibe Shell MCP Inspector Inspiration The first thing I thought when I saw the WebMCP spec was: that would be perfect for integrating dev tools into a frontend framework I'm building. Then I started thinking about putting the agentic coding environment itself in the browser. That unlocks a few extremely compelling qualities: The browser is an excellent sandbox. URLs are the easiest sharing mechanism on earth. The browser runtime eliminates an entire class of environment mismatches and runtime failures—things like process.env , missing binaries, incompatible runtimes, and "works on my machine" problems. The bigger idea behind Jibe is that an application doesn't have to be just its built dist/ . A mutable source tree, a runtime, and the capabilities needed to operate on them can travel together as one disposable software environment. WebMCP was the missing piece: Jibe can use WebMCP to build software that itself exposes WebMCP tools. In production, an agent can use the tools built into the application. Flip into development, and that agent can instead get the capabilities it needs to change the application itself. What it does Jibe wraps a web application with a small but pluggable framework that adds the concept of an environment to the browser. It allows for all kinds of interesting designs, but here's what happens in jibe.run when you switch a jibe from PROD to DEV : The service worker switches from serving built dist/ files to rendering the application's src/ . The root layout changes, moving the application from the root surface into a live preview panel inside an IDE environment. Development capabilities become available: a file explorer, editor, hot reload, shell, git, and MCP tools that allow an agent to inspect and modify the application live. The important part is that these are modes of the same environment. Switching between PROD and DEV should feel more like switching a theme than provisioning a new machine. Jibe is "batteries included" and built for people developing local-first applications with agents. You can build an agentic application that exposes WebMCP tools, then flip into development mode and your agent goes from using the tools you just built to building the feature that adds them. Jibe runs local-first using browser storage and can connect with WebMCP-compatible agents or local coding agents using the excellent @mcp-b/webmcp-local-relay package. A jibe hits the jibe.run server on first load to clone and bootstrap a project. After that, it can remain fully functional offline for as long as you want. Navigating to my-custom-app.jibe.run creates a local-first web application and its development environment in seconds. Point your agents at the URL and have fun. How we built it Jibe is structured as a core open-source project and a deployed Solid 2.0 application that consumes it. The core framework uses a plugin and capability model to support many different use cases. Most users will want to consume core plugins for things like: Git Transpiling and building source Local MCP Frontend frameworks Filesystems and storage An application manifest declares which capabilities are available to an environment, following a principle of least privilege. For example, agents can be given a virtual filesystem containing only files that are safe for them to edit rather than direct access to everything. One of my favorite agentic features is the Jibe Shell . Agents get a bash tool that parses shell expressions for viewing and editing files as an ergonomic alternative to a collection of bespoke tools like read_file and edit_file . This also doubles as a terminal surface inside the IDE for users. The shell supports commands that require additional capabilities—effectively sudo commands—which are gated rather than ambient. The result is something I'm pretty excited about: Bash ergonomics without ambient authority. I built this project on my own using Muse Spark 1.X and GLM 5.3 Flash with my trusty OMP and OpenCode harnesses. Lots of back and forth in web chat with Claude and ChatGPT as well. Coding with agents is the best thing ever.* When I needed to pick a bundler, I did a little research and then handed the problem to a subagent to stress-test and benchmark half a dozen different options. The approach I took with this project was to treat the entire project like a harness and make clear distinctions between intent and scratch. An early win was sketching the shape of the system in a messy repository, then treating that prototype as a library for seeding a new repository. Challenges we ran into Iteration. Agent speed is exhausting because, to keep the speed up, you have to keep entropy down. A particularly bad failure mode is agents placing shims and legacy compatibility code all over the place. Agents will hardcode a "fallback" until the fallback becomes the primary mechanism. Agent-written TypeScript is often effectively just verbose JavaScript. These are all antipatterns done in the name of preserving a green test suite, so it's a real challenge to see through the act. Identifying and preventing these failure modes is the primary implementation job. You have to distinguish between code that represents the intended architecture and code that exists because an agent needed to make the next step work. The faster the agents go, the more aggressively you need to manage that distinction. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Jibe Shell and workflows pattern are awesome. I'll be pushing both of these ideas much further. Bash ergonomics minus ambient authority is incredible. Agents already understand the shell as a general-purpose interface for operating on software. Giving them that ergonomics while constraining the capabilities underneath it feels like a very useful primitive. I'm also happy that the core interaction works as a proof of concept: Jibe uses WebMCP to build software with WebMCP. An application can expose useful tools to an agent in production. Flip into development mode and the agent gets a different environment with the capabilities required to change the source and build new tools. Flip back to production and those tools become part of the application. What we learned I learned how far the browser has come as a capable operating system. The tradeoffs compared with local development using a non-browser JavaScript runtime are worth seriously considering. The biggest feature in favor of the browser is that it sandboxes the agent extremely well. The big unlock with coding agents locally was allowing them to interface with software in the same way users do. WebMCP promises a similar unlock, with a very important distinction. Operating system evolution has generally assumed the terminal is safe. Browsers, meanwhile, have spent decades evolving under the assumption that users cannot be trusted. That distinction matters when the user is an agent. A browser-native development environment gives us a mature security model for software agents while still exposing the capabilities they need to operate on real software. What's next for Jibe I think Jibe has incredible promise for a wide variety of uses. It is effectively an executable git worktree that provisions from a URL and has better isolation. Fan out jibes for evals or bakeoffs, then visually inspect the results. Make vibe coding social and collaborative. Give Molty $20 and a jibe and see what happens. The roadmap includes: Agents inside of Jibe Secrets Full-stack framework support Jibe registries More plugins and capabilities Contributions and feedback are very welcome. title: Consular
pitch: Your agent fills in the visa form from your documents. It cannot pay, book or file without you.
about_excerpt: Your agent fills in the visa form from your documents. It cannot pay, book or file without you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Have you ever filled in a visa application yourself? Dozens of fields, many of them with no clear explanation or hint. Information scattered across different documents and sources. And then there is that familiar moment when you answer “yes” to one question and ten more fields suddenly appear underneath it. Anyone who has been through this knows how stressful it can be. That led me to a simple idea: why not ask an agent to do it? Today, you can already ask an agent to crawl a page, find inputs, and type information in. But what if it accidentally starts a payment, books the wrong slot, or submits something too early? That can mean lost time, lost money, and a wasted trip. The safer workaround is to take screenshots, ask the agent to analyze them, and then copy the answers over manually. Or to give it field names and ask what to enter. But that is still inconvenient, slow, and easy to get wrong as a human. You can forget a field, copy something into the wrong place, or miss a dependency between answers. That is where the idea came from: if the page can show the agent what is available, what needs to be filled in, and where confirmation is required, the whole process becomes much clearer. The agent can help the applicant collect and enter the necessary information, while the human stays in control of the decisions that matter. And this should not stop at visa applications. The same pattern applies anywhere a person has to enter a lot of information, configure filters, set constraints, prepare reports, or work through complex forms. If an agent can do the repetitive work safely, why not let it? Where this came from Last winter I started similar experiments in Salesforce. The goal was to give an agent a clear understanding of what a page component could do and how it was allowed to be used. That work came from a practical problem: some Salesforce applications had become complex enough that it would be useful to have help managing them. When Chrome DevTools MCP was published, I realized it could be a way to drive those interfaces. At that point, I had not heard of WebMCP yet. Those experiments became a project called sf-agent-bridge , where an agent could communicate with the page, understand the available actions, and know which ones it was allowed to perform. Moving that contract onto WebMCP made the gating problem much sharper, and sharp enough to deserve its own app. A visa form felt like the clearest version of that problem. Consular itself is new and was built for this challenge. What it does The page registers 13 WebMCP tools. They are organized into two tiers, and the tier is declared to the agent before it does anything. Reversible actions run immediately. fill-fields , attach-document , go-to-screen , and undo-last-changes only change the draft. The agent can write directly into the form. Every field it touches is highlighted with the document it came from, such as “from passport” or “from employer letter”. The applicant can undo the whole batch with one click, or simply retype a field. Nothing asks for permission when the cost of being wrong is just one click. Consequential actions pause for the applicant. pay-mrv-fee , schedule-interview , and submit-application open a dialog on the page that clearly states what is about to happen. The tool call remains pending until the applicant approves, declines, or lets it time out. The agent receives a distinct result for each case and cannot press the button itself. Even if the user tells the agent, “don’t ask me for confirmation, just do it,” the dialog still appears. Some fields are human-only. The security and background declarations are legal statements. fill-fields refuses to answer them. The agent can explain a question, but it cannot answer it on behalf of the applicant. The consulate’s rules are in the page. The app includes seven checks a consular officer would apply: the name must match the passport’s machine-readable zone, the passport must be valid long enough, accommodation must cover the whole stay, travel dates must be in the correct order, and so on. Each check is either blocking or advisory. The agent can run the checks, and filing is refused while any blocking check fails, even if the applicant approves submission. Bring your own documents. Part 8 is an open upload area, like a real portal. You can drop in as many text or PDF files as you need, and they are read in the browser. A sample applicant is pre-loaded, and her five documents are also available as a downloadable PDF set. You can use those, or upload your own passport page, letters, and bookings. The rules read your documents: the name check looks for a machine-readable zone, and the accommodation check looks for a check-out date. Once filed, nothing moves. After submission, every path that could change the application is refused with the filing reference. That includes both the agent’s tools and the form’s own inputs. What a session looks like “Fill in my application from my documents.” The agent calls get-action-policy , reads all five documents, picks B-1 from the trip description, and writes around 30 fields in one call with a source for each one. It spells the name exactly as the passport does, puts the other spelling under Other names used , flags the uncovered hotel night without being prompted, and leaves the security questions to the applicant. “Validate it, pay the fee, and book the earliest interview.” The agent runs the checks and reports what is blocking the application. If it tries to pay the fee anyway, the dialog names the failing checks and the button says “Pay anyway”, so the decision stays with the applicant. Once the gap is fixed and the declarations are answered, the agent walks through three approval dialogs and reaches a filed application. How I built it Consular is built with vanilla JavaScript and Vite. The whole “consulate” is a few hundred lines of rules in one file. Every scenario above was verified with a live LLM, not a script. A small harness gives the page’s tools to a fresh Claude session over the Chrome DevTools Protocol and lets it decide what to call. That is how I learned that agents which are not told about the gate up front only discover it after waiting on it for two minutes. That is why the policy is a tool of its own, with a description that tells the agent to call it first. It is also why every gated tool’s description opens with an approval tag. Before submitting, I had a second independent agent audit the whole project against a written protocol. It found 24 issues. The serious ones, including a filed application that could still be undone and a day-first date format that crashed validation, were fixed the same evening. The self-check it runs, 50 checks in plain Node, is in the repository together with the protocol. What I ran into Chrome’s preview build passes tool arguments as a JSON string, returns inputSchema stringified, drops destructiveHint from annotations, and collapses thrown errors into a generic “invocation failed”. Consular handles all of that: every tool answers with structured {refused, reason} text, and the gate queues a second dialog instead of dropping it. ChatGPT’s built-in browser discovers imperative tools only on the top-level page: no declarative <form toolname> , no iframes. So everything is registered imperatively. My first version staged every change as a proposal the applicant had to accept. Testing it as a user showed that this was the wrong boundary. Reversible changes should just happen and remain visible. The current two-tier design came out of that. Where this meets the edge of the spec The approval dialog lives on the page because WebMCP does not yet have a channel for a page to ask the user a question through the agent. This is covered by spec discussion #165 on elicitation. Holding the tool call open while the page asks the applicant is the fallback that works with every agent today. A native elicitation channel would allow the same confirmation to appear inline in the chat, the way Claude or Codex ask their own questions. The dialog says this, and the policy tells the agent to send the user to the page. Two things I know are imperfect The order of the flow is inverted compared with the real DS-160. In the real process, applicants file first, then pay the fee and book the interview with the confirmation number. Consular makes filing the last gate so the demo ends on the most irreversible action. It is easy to flip, and I chose the demo order knowingly. The page cannot tell the applicant’s click from an automated one. If a host browser presses the Approve button itself, the gate is defeated. Spec issue #288 describes exactly that case. The policy tells the agent never to operate the dialog, but only the host can enforce it. What’s next Elicitation through the agent when the spec supports it. OCR f

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 When autonomous AI agents (like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude) navigate portfolios, they run into a bottleneck: DOM trees, token bloat, and hallucinated developer claims. I wanted to treat AI agents as first-class citizens by implementing the official W3C WebMCP standard, Utilizing a passive display website into an interactive, zero-hallucination agent runtime. 

 What it does 

 
 Dual W3C WebMCP API : Implements both the Imperative JavaScript API ( document.modelContext.registerTool with 11 native capabilities) and the Declarative HTML Forms API ( <form toolname="send_inquiry" toolautosubmit="true"> with Resend email delivery). 
 UI Event Bus : Synchronizes a visual interaction in real time. When an agent queries skills or projects, matching nodes in the Skill Graph visual feedback can be seen. 
 Autonomous Recruiter Audit Workflow : AI recruiter agents can cross-reference declared skills against reviewed project evidence snapshots and generate a verified, printable Candidate Dossier. 
 In-Page Simulator Drawer : Allows Users to test all 11 tools, presets, and direct JSON arguments without needing Chrome 149 experimental flags. 
 

 How I built it 

 
 Framework & UI : Next.js 16 (App Router & Turbopack), React 19, TypeScript 5.9. 
 AI Standard : W3C WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) & Declarative HTML Attributes. 
 Graphics & Motion : Three.js WebGL particle field, Anime.js telemetry, Framer Motion. 
 Video Production : Programmatic motion graphics rendered using HyperFrames. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Designing an architecture that works in Chrome 149 with experimental flags while building an in-page fallback simulator so users on any browser can test the exact same tool execution pipeline. 
 Coordinating asynchronous tool execution events with React state across interactive 3D particle fields and physics decks without causing re-render lag. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 100% W3C WebMCP standard compliance across 11 registered tools and declarative forms. 
 Creating a bi-directional visual event bus where background agent calls manipulate the frontend UI. 
 Producing a verified, evidence-backed candidate audit workflow that eliminates LLM hallucinations. 
 

 What I learned 

 
 How standardized agent-to-browser protocols like WebMCP will web scraping on a person's portfolio can now be done easily with agents. 
 

 What's next 

 
 Adding multi-agent collaborative workspace inspection and real-time WebMCP code review sessions.

title: LedgerRehearsal
pitch: Rehearse before agents act.
about_excerpt: Rehearse before agents act. Like Comment Story Updates Deterministic receivables baseline — Three fictional accounts and three safe agent tools before approval. Approval changes the tool surface — One uniquely scoped execution capability appears after human review. Stale permission disappears — Drift applies nothing and removes the approved execution capability. Exact rehearsal before action — Complete simulated ACME reminder, Jones assignment diff, and Smith policy block. Receipt separates proposed, authorized, executed, and blocked — The final record explains what happened and whether reality changed. Rehearsal against current reality — ACME is no change, Jones remains proposed, and Smith remains blocked. Short description LedgerRehearsal is a WebMCP accounts-receivable demo where a human and an agent review the same exact business transition before the webpage exposes a one-time capability to execute it. If reality changes after approval, the page removes that capability and requires a fresh rehearsal. Inspiration Approval interfaces often live beside an agent rather than inside the interface the agent can actually use. A screen may say “approved” while the agent’s available actions remain unchanged. LedgerRehearsal asks a narrower question: what if the WebMCP tool surface itself became shared interface state between a person and an agent? The project uses a familiar accounts-receivable scenario because the stakes are easy to understand. An overdue reminder may be reasonable when an invoice is unpaid and wrong seconds later if a payment arrives. The interesting moment is not generating the reminder; it is proving that a previously reviewed permission disappears when its factual basis changes. What it does The agent begins with three safe tools: inspect_accounts , propose_collection_actions , and rehearse_transition . The first rehearsal proposes an overdue reminder for ACME, proposes assigning Jones to Maya Chen, and blocks a final notice for Smith because the invoice is disputed. The human reviews the complete simulated message, exact before/after values, effects, and blocked reason in the webpage. Human approval then makes one uniquely named, zero-argument execution capability appear. Before the agent uses it, the human simulates ACME’s payment. That state change invalidates the reviewed transition, so stale execution applies no business mutation, creates no outbox effect or receipt, and removes the capability. The agent rehearses again against current reality. ACME becomes NO_CHANGE , Jones remains PROPOSED , and Smith remains BLOCKED . A second human approval creates a distinct capability. Using it applies only the stored Jones assignment, adds one simulated outbox effect, writes one receipt, and consumes the capability so replay cannot duplicate the change. All customers, balances, messages, and effects are fictional. There is no real email, payment provider, financial API, or external financial operation. How it was built LedgerRehearsal is a React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vinext for Cloudflare Sites. A D1-backed transition store keeps deterministic fictional account state, reviewed manifests, expected account versions, exact typed changes, simulated effects, blocked items, and lifecycle events. The browser uses top-level imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , with the current Chrome compatibility path at navigator.modelContext . Each approved execution registration receives an AbortSignal so it can be removed when authorization expires, drifts, or is consumed. The execution tool accepts zero mutation arguments. The agent cannot substitute an account, owner, message, or value after review. On execution, the server claims the transition with compare-and-swap semantics, rechecks stored preconditions, applies only stored after-values, appends simulated effects, and records the receipt. Competing callers observe the transition as no longer available, so exactly one wins inside this application boundary. How LedgerRehearsal uses WebMCP LedgerRehearsal explores the WebMCP tool surface itself as shared interface state. Human approval makes one reviewed execution capability appear; changing business reality removes it; successful use consumes it. The choreography is visible in actual tool enumeration: 3 safe tools → 4 with reviewed execution → 3 after drift → 4 with replacement execution → 3 after consumption Human approval is deliberately not an agent tool. The consequential capability appears only after a person reviews the concrete transition in the webpage. Human-agent collaboration The agent is good at inspecting state, proposing work, and explaining exact effects. The person owns the consequential approval. The webpage connects those roles by changing what the agent can do only after the person reviews a specific transition. That division also makes disagreement legible. Smith is not silently omitted; the rehearsal shows the blocked action and its policy reason. When ACME pays, the system does not reinterpret the old approval. It revokes it and asks the agent and person to review the smaller current transition together. Creativity and ambition The project does not claim a new security primitive. Human approval, dry runs, optimistic concurrency, capability-based security, version checks, and single-use authorization all have prior art. The contest contribution is the shared-page experience: approval, drift, replacement, and consumption are reflected directly in the live WebMCP surface rather than only in a status label. Impact Agents become more useful when people can see not just what they plan to do, but exactly when permission exists, what that permission covers, and why it disappears. The pattern is relevant anywhere a reviewed action can become stale: finance operations, customer support, fulfillment, compliance, and other consequential workflows. Challenges The hardest part was keeping browser capability state, server authorization state, and business state aligned. Removing a tool from the browser is not enough if a stale handle can still reach the server, so the server rechecks the reviewed account versions and lifecycle on every execution. Another challenge was making the scenario comprehensible without hiding the mechanics. The interface exposes exact diffs, complete simulated messages, blocked actions, lifecycle events, outbox effects, and receipts while keeping the main story readable. Accomplishments A real 3 → 4 → 3 → 4 → 3 capability lifecycle in supported WebMCP runtimes. Zero-argument execution tied to a reviewed manifest rather than agent-supplied mutation values. Drift detection that applies zero stale business mutations and creates zero stale effects or receipts. Single-use application-boundary execution with replay and competing-caller coverage. Deterministic fictional data, visible reset, and judge-accessible public deployment with no signup. A 32-test suite covering registration, drift, replay, concurrency, blocked-action exclusion, outbox integrity, receipt integrity, and reset behavior. What I learned The most important lesson was that approval is not just a record; it can be part of an interface lifecycle. WebMCP makes that lifecycle observable to both sides of the collaboration. The browser registration still needs authoritative server checks, because a removed UI capability does not prove that no stale caller exists. I also learned that blocked work deserves first-class representation. A rehearsal is more trustworthy when it explains what will not happen and why, instead of showing only the actions that survived filtering. What’s next The next step would be to generalize the choreography carefully without turning the demo into a generic workflow engine: stronger audit export, additional accessibility testing, and more supported-runtime acceptance evidence. Real email, real payments, authentication, customer data, and external finance APIs are intentionally outside this challenge build. Testing instructions Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome restarted. Use Reset demo and verify three initial tools. Ask the agent to inspect accounts, propose current collection actions, and rehearse them without execution. Review the exact changes and approve them in the webpage. Verify a unique fourth execution tool appears. Click Simulate payment received before execution. Invoke the old execution handle. Verify drift, zero business mutations, zero outbox additions, zero receipts, and return to three tools. Inspect, propose, and rehearse again. Verify ACME NO_CHANGE , Jones PROPOSED , and Smith BLOCKED . Approve the smaller transition. Verify a distinct fourth tool appears. Invoke it once. Verify only Jones changes, exactly one simulated outbox effect and receipt exist, and the tool list returns to three. Attempt replay and verify no duplicate mu
video_transcript_excerpt: Ledger rehearsal is a web MCP receivables workspace where a human and an agent rehearse consequential business changes together before the web page allows execution. The agent begins with three safe tools. It finds Acme overdue with no reminder, Jones needing a follow-up owner, and Smith in an active billing dispute. The page rehearses exact effects before anything changes. I can read the complete simulated Acme reminder, see Jones move from unassigned to Maya Chan, and see why policy blocks Smith. Approval stays a human web page action. Once I approve this exact review, a uniquely scoped execution capability appears. The tool surface changes from three to four. No reality changes before execution. A visible payment sync records Acme's invoices paid in full. The overdue reminder no longer makes business sense. I approved this when Acme was overdue, but Acme paid before the agent acted. So, the page removes that capability instead of letting the agent use stale approval. Nothing executes. The agent must rehearse against current reality. Acme's reminder is gone. Jones is still valid, while Smith remains blocked because the dispute has not changed. I approve the smaller replacement transition. A new distinct execution capability appears, again changing the page's web MCP surface from three tools to four. The agent supplies no targets or replacement values. The application rechecks current state and applies only the stored Jones assignment. Smith's blocked action never executes. Successful use consumes the one-time capability. It disappears. The tool count returns to three and a replay cannot duplicate the change or simulated effect. The receipt records what was proposed, what the human authorized, what actually executed, what remained blocked, and whether reality changed after rehearsal. Rehearse before agents act. Approval changes what the page lets the agent do. Changing reality revokes that permission.

When human input is required, Novelist displays a large, clear message explaining what the user needs to do next. title: Plasma-trace
pitch: One physics model, two operators. A human drags sliders; an AI agent calls WebMCP tools. Both hit the same functions and the same chart -a shared instrument for sub-centimetre orbital debris detection
about_excerpt:
One physics model, two operators. A human drags sliders; an AI agent calls WebMCP tools. Both hit the same functions and the same chart -a shared instrument for sub-centimetre orbital debris detection
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Sub-centimetre orbital debris is a genuinely unsolved problem. Objects
this small are difficult to track with radar or optical systems, yet at
orbital velocities they carry enough energy to damage spacecraft. 

 NASA-funded research has been exploring an indirect approach: a charged
fragment moving through ionospheric plasma can excite nonlinear waves —
solitons — that might be detectable even when the object itself is not.
The physics comes from Sen et al. (2015) on forced-KdV soliton excitation
by charged orbital debris, developed further in Christine Hartzell's NASA
NIAC work at the University of Maryland. 

 I did not invent that science, and this project does not claim to. What
interested me was a different question: exploring a model like this means
sweeping parameters — size, velocity, altitude, day/night ionosphere —
and that is exactly the kind of tedious, click-heavy loop where a human
and an agent should be able to work on the same instrument instead of in
separate tools. 

 What it does: 

 Plasma-trace is a browser-based forward model for debris detectability.
Set a fragment's size, relative speed, and altitude, pick a daytime or
night-time ionosphere, and it returns a detectability score plus a
breakdown across eight altitude bins. 

 The point is that there are two ways to drive it, and they are the same
instrument: 

 
 A person drags sliders and watches the chart redraw. 
 An AI agent calls WebMCP tools registered on the page — and the
sliders and chart move exactly as if a person had dragged them. 
 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit: 

 Scientific parameter exploration is a bad fit for the usual ways agents
interact with web pages. Screen-scraping a slider is fragile and
lossy: an agent reading "38/100" off the DOM has a rendered string, not
a result it can reason over. 

 WebMCP changes the contract. The page exposes typed tools with schemas,
so the agent calls a function and gets structured data back, while the
human sees the same state update visually. Neither operator is
second-class. That is what makes this feel like a shared instrument
rather than an agent puppeting a UI built for someone else. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult before: 

 The clearest example is sweep_altitude . A person exploring where a
5 mm fragment is most detectable has to drag the altitude slider through
eight positions and read the chart each time. An agent runs the whole
sweep in one call and returns the best altitude with the full profile —
while the human watches the same chart update. 

 Before WebMCP, that meant either building a separate API (and now the
human and agent are using different systems that can drift apart) or
having the agent scrape the UI (fragile, and it gets strings instead of
data). Here there is exactly one code path. 

 explain_regime is the inverse case: the agent asks the instrument to
explain why detectability peaks where it does, so the reasoning comes
from the page's own model rather than the language model's guess. 

 How I built it: 

 One self-contained index.html — no backend, no database, no build
step. Chart.js from a CDN is the only dependency. 

 
 runForwardModel() computes detectability from an altitude-dependent
plasma density term, a size factor, and a speed factor. 
 The sliders call that function directly. 
 Four tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() :
 set_debris_params , run_forward_model , sweep_altitude , and
 explain_regime . Each one calls the same functions the sliders call
and updates the same chart. There is no parallel agent code path —
that constraint is the whole design. 
 The page feature-detects document.modelContext and degrades
gracefully: in a non-WebMCP browser it shows a banner explaining how
to enable it, and every slider still works. 
 

 Challenges: 

 The WebMCP API is new enough that several third-party guides describe it
incorrectly — a number of them say navigator.modelContext when the
spec defines document.modelContext . Writing that line from memory or
from a blog post would have produced a page that looks completely normal
and silently registers nothing. I sourced the signature from the W3C
explainer and cross-checked it against the spec IDL. 

 A second one: executeTool takes its arguments as a JSON string, not an
object. Passing an object returns "Failed to parse input arguments" with
no further detail. Worth knowing if you are testing via
 navigator.modelContextTesting in the console. 

 What's real, and what isn't 

 I would rather be precise about this than oversell it. 

 Real: the forward model runs in-page, the WebMCP registration is
functional, the deploy is live, and agent tool calls demonstrably move
the same sliders and chart a person uses. 

 Simplified: the ionosphere data is hardcoded. The model uses
closed-form terms, not a plasma solver. Nothing here is validated
against observations. 

 Not claimed: this does not detect debris. It is not an early-warning
system — solitons propagate near the ion-acoustic speed while debris
moves far faster, so this is a mapping and survey concept, not a
collision alarm. The science is attributed to published research. 

 The contribution I am putting forward is the interaction pattern: a
scientific instrument that a human and an agent operate through one
shared set of functions. 

 What's next 

 Real ionosphere data (IRI or GNSS TEC) instead of hardcoded values, a
trained ML model for the inverse problem — recovering fragment
properties from an observed signature, which is not analytically
solvable and is exactly what the NIAC team is working on — and
multi-sensor localisation.

title: Ghost Operator
pitch: A shared WebMCP workspace where an agent builds a voice-agent launch plan and the business owner keeps final approval.
about_excerpt:
A shared WebMCP workspace where an agent builds a voice-agent launch plan and the business owner keeps final approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for Ghost Operator 

 Inspiration 

 Local-service businesses lose real revenue when calls go unanswered, but deploying an automated front desk is consequential. The owner understands the business constraints; an agent excels at structured setup work. Ghost Operator gives both of them one shared, auditable workspace. 

 What it does 

 The owner enters industry, weekly call volume, missed-call rate, average job value, and desired coverage. Through WebMCP, an agent can read those values, update approved inputs, calculate calls at risk, recommend coverage, draft a constrained call policy, and open the completed plan for review. Every action appears in a visible activity ledger. 

 The human-agent boundary is deliberate: there is no tool for final approval, deployment, purchasing, calling, or messaging. The owner must inspect the visible plan and click Approve & save personally. Even then, the demo only saves locally and confirms that no external system changed. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow combines structured inputs, deterministic calculations, editable shared state, and a consequential handoff. Browser automation alone would need to infer form semantics and scrape changing output. WebMCP gives the agent six precise operations connected to the same logic and session the owner sees, making the workflow faster, more reliable, and easy to audit. 

 People and agents can now collaborate on a launch plan in plain language while keeping authority visible and constrained—something that previously required brittle UI automation or a separate integration disconnected from the page under review. 

 How we built it 

 Ghost Operator is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It registers six imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON input schema, read/write annotations, application-level validation, structured results, and an abortable lifecycle. Tool handlers reuse the same deterministic state and calculation functions as the human UI. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel, tested with Vitest, and published under the MIT License. All challenge code was created after the challenge opened on August 25, 2026; the public commit history documents the work. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest design decision was not exposing every UI action as a tool. We intentionally omitted approval and deployment operations so the agent can accelerate the work without silently crossing the human authorization boundary. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is strongest when the page remains the shared source of truth. The best agent experience is not invisible automation—it is structured collaboration where the person can see state, understand changes, and retain final control.
