title: ProbePilot Studio
pitch: A WebMCP circuit workspace where agents design and reason while people control measurements, evidence, and repair approval.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP circuit workspace where agents design and reason while people control measurements, evidence, and repair approval. Like Comment Story Updates What it does ProbePilot Studio is a browser-native circuit workspace where a person and an agent share one live design, simulation, and diagnostic bench. The agent can inspect exact circuit state, add or update components, create semantic terminal-to-terminal connections, validate the design, and run deterministic or local SPICE simulations. The same project renders as an interactive circuit, a PCB preview, and a 3D assembly preview. Diagnosis changes the control model. The person creates a faulty virtual bench. The agent can request measurements between exact test points, but ProbePilot stops until the person operates the virtual meter. Each reading becomes evidence with a stable ID. After two readings, the agent can publish evidence-linked hypotheses and stage a repair. Only the person can approve and apply that repair. The agent can then verify the repaired bench against the intended design. ProbePilot keeps the hidden fault outside the DOM, Zustand state, local project files, JSON exports, Circuit JSON, and every WebMCP response. The agent must diagnose from observations instead of reading the answer. Why WebMCP fits A circuit editor exposes structured concepts that coordinate-based browser automation handles poorly: components, terminals, wires, revisions, test points, measurement modes, evidence, and repair targets. ProbePilot registers nine narrow WebMCP tools that operate on those concepts directly. The agent does not need to infer a resistor from pixels or guess which terminal a click represents. Tool schemas describe supported component kinds, strict inputs, revision requirements, and human-owned boundaries. The browser UI and agent use the same command layer, so each action updates the circuit, inspector, activity history, and project persistence together. Better human-agent experience The agent handles repetitive construction, validation, simulation, and diagnostic reasoning. The person supplies the evidence that a software agent should not invent and controls the consequential repair decision. ProbePilot enforces those distinctions in application code: WebMCP can request a measurement but cannot take one. The agent cannot create the bench or reveal its private fault. Hypotheses cite completed human measurements. A repair needs at least two measurements. The agent stages a repair; the person applies it. Verification compares the repaired bench with the frozen intended design. WebMCP implementation ProbePilot registers nine tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : studio_inspect , design_build_circuit , design_update_components , design_remove_elements , design_validate_and_simulate , bench_request_measurement , bench_update_hypotheses , bench_stage_repair , and bench_verify . Zod validates each tool input. Mutation tools enforce expected revisions, component support, agent locks, and bench lifecycle rules. The public inspection DTO includes only the information the agent should see. A private bench engine owns the implementation fault and computes measurements and verification results without serializing the fault into public state. Challenges The hardest problem was preserving a useful shared workspace without turning the agent into an unrestricted UI robot. ProbePilot needed one command model for the UI and WebMCP, strict stale-revision handling, and a private bench state that could produce measurements without leaking the answer. The 3D viewer also needed a compatibility boundary. ProbePilot converts its project model into Circuit JSON, lazy-loads @tscircuit/3d-viewer , keeps the camera stationary until the person moves it, and falls back to a six-angle SVG preview when WebGL fails. Accomplishments Nine working WebMCP tools with strict schemas and revision checks. A complete design, simulation, diagnosis, repair, and verification journey. Human-only measurement and repair approval enforced below the UI. A hidden deterministic fault excluded from every agent-visible surface. Twenty-one components with honest Design, SPICE, and Bench capability labels. Local ngspice WASM plus circuit, PCB, and interactive 3D views. Local project CRUD, JSON import and export, URL-restored workspace state, and a 100-entry activity history. 346 automated tests covering the domain, UI, persistence, WebMCP contract, and viewer adapters. What I learned WebMCP works best when a site exposes domain decisions instead of mirroring every button. The useful boundary was authority: which facts the agent may inspect, which evidence only a person can produce, and which actions require human approval. Circuit JSON and tsCircuit provided a practical rendering and interoperability layer, but simulation support still needed explicit verification. ProbePilot labels each catalog item by capability rather than implying that every rendered component has a trusted behavioral model. What's next The next step is to add reusable diagnostic cases, richer SPICE models, and a portable evidence bundle that can be reviewed outside the browser. A future hardware bridge could let a person collect readings from a physical instrument while keeping the same WebMCP request, evidence, approval, and verification contract. video_title: ProbePilot Studio: Human-in-the-Loop Circuit Diagnosis with WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: AI agents can already assemble a circuit. The harder question is whether they should be allowed to invent evidence or approve a repair. ProPilot Studio answers no. This is a browser native circuit workspace built for the WebMCP challenge. The page registers nine semantic tools. So, an agent works with circuit concepts instead of guessing through buttons and coordinates. I start from a switched 9-V status LED. The agent can inspect the design, update components, and run a deterministic simulation. ProPilot also renders schematic, PCB, and interactive 3D views from the same state. Now, I create a faulty virtual bench. The implementation fault stays in private application memory. It never appears in page state, project export, or the agent's inspection response. The agent requests a voltage measurement between exact test points. ProPilot stops in an awaiting human state. I operate the virtual meter, and that reading becomes evidence M1. The agent requests a second reading. I perform it, producing evidence M2. Only now can the agent publish a diagnosis linked to both measurements. The agent stages a repair, but code prevents it from applying the change. I review the target, action, evidence, and expected outcome. I approve it. Then the agent verifies the repaired bench against the intended design. This is WebMCP as a collaboration contract. The agent handles structure design and reasoning. The person owns physical style evidence and the final repair decision. Together, they complete a safe diagnostic workflow that neither side can shortcut. title: Ackboard
pitch: An on-call page that audits the agent's contract, keeps every tool on a human control, and lets the operator undo an agent write.
about_excerpt: An on-call page that audits the agent's contract, keeps every tool on a human control, and lets the operator undo an agent write. Like Comment Story Updates About the project Why WebMCP fits this use case Incident response is a loop of health, logs, metrics, and deploys, plus a write when you know the cause. Those functions already live in the page. WebMCP exposes them as tools so an agent in the tab can call them instead of clicking the same six filters. The reason it has to be WebMCP, not a server MCP: three checks only exist in the tab. The page diffs its own store before and after every execute . Every registered tool has a DOM control the test can querySelector . Undo and ask_operator wait on the person looking at the same incident. A remote server has no Zustand snapshot, no human control, and no operator in the chair. WebKit opposed WebMCP because declared intent is unverifiable, because nothing keeps agent and human surfaces in parity, and because readOnlyHint is advisory. Ackboard treats those three sentences as tests. How it creates a better experience The agent does not scrape the DOM. It gets compact JSON, schemas, enums, structuredContent , and error objects. The UI still updates. Panels pulse. The header shows Ackboard's registered count next to the browser's own getTools() count. The Parity panel lists each tool beside the button a keyboard user would press. Reads that used to dump pretty-printed log lines now return 5 slim rows inside Chrome's 1500-character budget. Over-budget payloads truncate with a pointer to analyze_error_patterns . Log tools set untrustedContentHint . When the data cannot settle a question, ask_operator holds execute open until the person on the page replies. Create and update apply immediately and reverse from Undo last agent action. Only a runbook step still waits on Approve. What people and agents can do together that was hard before In one turn: "Why is payment-gateway red?" becomes health, signature-failure logs, the v1.8.3 chrony deploy, then a drafted incident. The operator can undo that ticket without asking the agent to delete it. The part other incident consoles skip: the page itself catches a lying tool. Call contract_probe . It claims read-only and mutates a probe counter. The audit row goes red. No human had to click Deny first. Remediation tools mount only while a P1 or P2 incident is open, then unmount. The count in the header changes. That is a shared live object, not a chat box next to a dashboard. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool in src/webmcp/register-tools.ts . Nested annotations . execute(input, { signal }) . Per-tier AbortControllers: core tools for the session, active-incident tools, remediation tools. Types from @mcp-b/webmcp-types . Reads return MCP structuredContent . The auditor is src/webmcp/contract-auditor.ts . Human selectors stay in a parallel map so Chrome does not see unknown fields. Undo is a page-owned journal, not a tool. HITL for runbook steps and operator questions use in-page dialogs; requestUserInteraction is still open (issue #165). See docs/adr/0002-human-in-the-loop.md , docs/adr/0004-contract-auditor.md , and docs/adr/0005-webkit-invariants.md . Live URL https://ackboard.vercel.app No login. Simulated fleet. Header badge says so. Seeded long-fuse incident is INC-001 on payment-gateway (NTP/chrony, Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 pattern). Public repo https://github.com/GunaPalanivel/ackboard MIT license, visible in the About sidebar. Which agent or client did you test with? Chrome with the WebMCP flag, against https://ackboard.vercel.app . Wording must match .idea/AGENT-VERIFICATION.md after the next npm run verify pass. ChatGPT desktop in-app browser was not run. Do not claim Atlas or ChatGPT desktop. What did you learn? The shipping Chrome surface is smaller than blog posts about elicitation. execute 's second argument today is { signal } , not requestUserInteraction . Tool count is a weak signal next to Duckboard's two tools. Nested annotations and structuredContent are a ten-second tell for a Chrome engineer. A tool's declared readOnlyHint is advisory until the page checks it. Human/agent parity is a selector, not a slogan. Vercel SSO on *.vercel.app will silently fail a judge who is not on your team. Atlas as a standalone browser was retired; the judge client is ChatGPT's in-app browser, which we did not run from this machine. title: PartnerBird
pitch: PartnerBird turns partnership pages and workflow into an agent-native experience, letting people and AI agents discover, evaluate, propose, negotiate, and manage collaborations together via WebMCP.\n
about_excerpt:
PartnerBird turns partnership pages and workflow into an agent-native experience, letting people and AI agents discover, evaluate, propose, negotiate, and manage collaborations together via WebMCP.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 2 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 From Context To Collaboration 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 PartnerBird Website 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 PartnerBird Demo 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Partnership Ideas and Synergy 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Propose Before It Produces 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agents Suggest Solutions 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 From Context To Collaboration 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 PartnerBird Website 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 PartnerBird Demo 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Partnership Ideas and Synergy 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Propose Before It Produces 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agents Suggest Solutions 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 From Context To Collaboration 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most partnership platforms are still designed around a very manual workflow. You browse profiles, compare opportunities, write outreach messages, manage proposals, follow up, and keep track of conversations yourself. 

 At the same time, AI agents are becoming much more capable, but they are often limited to giving advice beside the product rather than actually participating in the workflow. 

 PartnerBird started from a simple question: what would a partnership platform look like if both the human and their AI agent were first-class users? 

 WebMCP made that idea much more practical. Instead of asking an agent to visually navigate PartnerBird by clicking buttons and interpreting pages, PartnerBird can expose meaningful actions directly to the agent. The agent can understand the user's partnership page, discover opportunities, evaluate potential collaborators, prepare proposals, and help manage partnership workflows while the human remains in control of important decisions. 

 The goal is not to replace the person building the relationship. It is to remove the repetitive work around discovering, evaluating, preparing, and managing those relationships. 

 What PartnerBird does 

 PartnerBird is an agent-native platform for managing business partnerships and collaborations. 

 Users can create partnership pages that explain who they are, what they are looking for, what they can offer, and the types of collaborations they are interested in. 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can interact with those partnership workflows directly. 

 For example, a user could ask: 

 
 Find partnership opportunities that would be a good fit for my SaaS and shortlist the strongest ones. 
 

 The agent could search PartnerBird, inspect relevant partnership profiles, understand what each person is looking for, compare compatibility, and return a shortlist. 

 The user could then say: 

 
 Prepare a collaboration proposal for the top two. Suggest a newsletter swap for one and a co-marketing campaign for the other. 
 

 Instead of only generating text in chat, the agent can create those proposals inside PartnerBird. 

 From there, the human and agent can continue working together to revise proposals, evaluate responses, organize partnership opportunities, and manage the collaboration workflow. 

 The broader idea is that PartnerBird becomes a shared workspace between the person and their agent. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to understand PartnerBird largely through the visual interface. 

 With WebMCP, PartnerBird can expose structured capabilities representing the actual concepts within the product, such as searching for partners, reading partnership profiles, evaluating opportunities, preparing proposals, updating proposals, and managing collaboration workflows. 

 This creates a much more reliable interaction model. 

 More importantly, WebMCP changes the role of the agent. 

 Instead of being a chatbot sitting beside PartnerBird, the agent becomes an active participant inside the partnership workflow. 

 The human provides goals, context, preferences, judgment, and final approval. The agent handles much of the discovery, analysis, preparation, and workflow management required to move opportunities forward. 

 How I built it 

 PartnerBird was already being developed as a platform centered around partnership pages, collaboration opportunities, user profiles, dashboards, and an AI-assisted partnership experience. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending that existing experience with a WebMCP layer that exposes selected PartnerBird capabilities as structured tools for agents. 

 Rather than creating a completely separate agent backend, the WebMCP tools are designed to connect to PartnerBird's existing application logic and workflows. 

 An important part of the implementation is separating actions based on their consequences. 

 Low-risk actions such as discovering opportunities, reading profiles, comparing potential partners, and preparing drafts can be highly agent-assisted. 

 Actions that affect another user or create a meaningful commitment should remain visible to the user and, where appropriate, require human approval. 

 This creates a workflow where autonomy increases productivity without removing human judgment from important relationship decisions. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges is deciding what should actually become a WebMCP tool. 

 Technically exposing actions is relatively straightforward. Designing the right agent experience is harder. 

 If every button in the interface simply becomes a tool, WebMCP does not add much value. The more interesting approach is to expose higher-level capabilities that correspond to what someone is actually trying to accomplish. 

 For example, the user does not necessarily care about navigating several screens to create a proposal. Their intention is simply: 

 
 Prepare a partnership proposal for this person. 
 

 Designing around these intentions makes the agent experience much more natural. 

 Another challenge is balancing agent autonomy with human control. Partnerships involve reputation, relationships, negotiation, and potentially commercial commitments. PartnerBird therefore needs to distinguish between actions an agent can safely perform automatically and actions where the user should remain directly involved. 

 What I learned 

 Building PartnerBird around WebMCP changed the way I think about web application design. 

 Traditional web applications are primarily designed for humans operating graphical interfaces. 

 The emerging agentic web introduces another layer. Applications can still provide excellent human interfaces while also exposing structured capabilities that allow agents to understand and operate the product directly. 

 That means developers increasingly have to think about two interaction surfaces: 

 the interface humans see and the capabilities agents can understand. 

 WebMCP provides a bridge between those two worlds. 

 The most interesting opportunities appear when the agent is not simply automating clicks, but collaborating with the human around a shared application state. 

 What's next 

 The longer-term vision for PartnerBird is to make partnerships increasingly agent-native. 

 An agent should eventually be able to understand what its user is trying to accomplish, continuously identify relevant partnership opportunities, evaluate compatibility, prepare collaboration ideas, organize proposals, surface conversations that need attention, and help move successful partnerships forward. 

 The human remains responsible for the relationships and important decisions. 

 The agent becomes the operational layer that helps make more of those relationships possible. 

 PartnerBird's WebMCP experiment is an early step toward that idea: a web where people do not simply use applications themselves, but increasingly use them together with agents.

title: Benchkeeper
pitch: Community events are an important for social causes and supporting the local community. Benchkeeper uses WebMCP to help organizers plan these events and protect key bookings, and reveal trade-offs.
about_excerpt: Community events are an important for social causes and supporting the local community. Benchkeeper uses WebMCP to help organizers plan these events and protect key bookings, and reveal trade-offs. Like Comment Story Updates Many communities have these local events to support different causes to raise funds or just do stuff in the community like repairing community parks to clean up from emergencies and more. These community events require different skills for example a repair event, a clean up event etc. These different community events require different skills from different people. However it's really hard to plan these events particularly if one person doesn't show up. Rebuilding the schedule means deciding which promises can still be kept. I built "Benchkeeper" to help these community organizers work through their decisions with a browser agent. WebMCP lets the agent work with explicit scheduling constraints and shares a proposal directly for the organizer. What Benchkeeper is a sort of planning desk for small community events. Organizers can add repair requests, manage volunteer availability, reserve break or walk-in time, and protect promised appointments. Through ten browser-native WebMCP tools, an agent can inspect the event, explore cancellations, propose a revised schedule, and explain why an item cannot fit. The organizer can compare the current and proposed plans, see who moves or loses a slot, and review the tradeoffs before applying anything. The tools cannot apply a plan or release a protected appointment. Those actions remain in the organizer’s interface. Benchkeeper also supports spreadsheet intake, undo and redo, JSON backups, and printable schedules. It sends no messages to visitors, and manual planning works without WebMCP. How I built this. We built the interface with React, TypeScript, and Vite, using Zod to validate tool inputs and imported data. A deterministic, bounded scheduling search considers repairer skills, availability, visitor time windows, parts readiness, and protected appointments. The WebMCP tools and human interface use the same application state. Revision checks reject stale edits, and approval is tied to the exact proposal being reviewed. Event data is stored in the browser tab’s sessionStorage, with downloadable backups. Cloudflare Workers serves the app; there is no event-data backend or embedded chatbot. We used Vitest, Playwright, and axe-core for automated checks, alongside real native WebMCP execution tests. Challenges Browser implementation differences made WebMCP integration more involved than registering a tool catalog. We had to test actual execution and handle differences in argument formats. Scheduling also exposed a subtle distinction: keeping someone’s appointment at exactly the same time is different from keeping that person booked at all. We refined the planning preferences and comparison reports to make that tradeoff explicit. Keeping human edits, agent proposals, and saved state consistent required careful handling of stale reviews and browser Back navigation. Accomplishments that we're proud of I built a complete cancellation-and-recovery workflow where an agent’s proposal appears in the same desk the organizer uses. Protected appointments stay fixed during replanning, excluded requests have concrete explanations, and organizers can preview the cost of making room for another item. I also tested the scheduler against thousands of small, exhaustively checked cases and kept discovered failures as regression tests. Native WebMCP execution was tested separately from the clearly labeled scripted rehearsal. What we learned Useful agent tools need clear consequences as well as clear inputs. Organizers need to know whose appointment changed, why a request was excluded, and whether a proposal still reflects the latest event. I also learned that a passing build does not establish a working product. Native browser execution, keyboard navigation, printed schedules, and saved-state recovery each exposed issues that needed their own checks. What's next My next priority is testing Benchkeeper is to run it on a small clean up operation for a school in my area. the current examples is synthetic so doing something good in the community and using this seems like a good next step. Then the feedback should guide if this was useful to them. For now, the tool works for pre-event planning tool, and its bounded search does not guarantee the best possible schedule. There is also a bigger opportunity with other industries to help with planning and coordination particularly with health-care, education, plumbing and more. title: TabulaFlow
pitch: Auditable local-first data workflows where people and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Auditable local-first data workflows where people and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Data preparation tools are visually dense, stateful, and risky for agents to operate through generic browser automation. An agent can target the wrong dataset, repeat a mutation, lose track of the current revision, or expose sensitive values while inferring state from tables and graph coordinates. TabulaFlow explores a better model: one visible data workflow shared by people and agents, with precise semantic operations and explicit human authority. What it does TabulaFlow is an auditable, local-first data workbench built around Source → Prepare → Compose . Source imports Excel, CSV, JSON, JSONL, and NDJSON while keeping local data in the browser. Prepare profiles data quality, manages ordered transformation recipes, creates deterministic Formula columns, applies protected filters, and supports human-reviewed qualitative coding. Compose validates and chains Append, Join, Difference, Aggregate, Filter, Distinct, Pivot, and Unpivot operations. WebMCP exposes stable, strict tools for agents to inspect, validate, mutate, export, and monitor the same application state shown to the user. People retain control of local file selection, agent-upload consent, destructive confirmation, semantic declassification, and qualitative interpretation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Generic browser automation must guess from visual coordinates and transient UI state. TabulaFlow instead exposes a semantic agent API through WebMCP. Agents can discover action-specific contracts, target stable dataset and node IDs, dry-run changes, reject stale revisions, replay idempotently, poll asynchronous operations, and cancel before commit. This creates a better user experience because agent work is visible in the normal product, recorded in a shared privacy-safe activity ledger, and governed by the same validation and transaction boundaries as direct user actions. People and agents can now collaborate on multi-step data preparation and graph-based composition without hiding mutations inside an opaque autonomous workflow. How we built it Frontend: React 19 and Vite Analytical engine: DuckDB-Wasm in a dedicated browser worker Agent interface: document.modelContext.registerTool() with stable dispatcher tools and strict action-specific JSON Schemas Persistence: IndexedDB flow metadata, recipes, graph positions, and activity events Safety: optimistic workspace revisions, idempotency keys, protected-value bindings, bounded redacted previews, writer serialization, asynchronous lifecycle, cooperative cancellation, and visible user confirmations Hosting: ChatGPT Sites-compatible production bundle The current contract exposes 17 stable WebMCP tools and 60 bounded Source, Prepare, Compose, and qualitative-coding action routes. What people and agents can do together Agents can inspect schemas and quality, validate candidate changes, maintain recipes, create Compose operations, promote results, export datasets, and report evidence-backed qualitative coding suggestions. Users can see and review the same state, undo transformations, reject unsafe actions, and retain exclusive authority over sensitive boundaries. How we used AI Codex and ChatGPT supported implementation, debugging, regression testing, live WebMCP QC, documentation, and demo preparation. The human owner set product direction, reviewed trade-offs, controlled releases, and accepted or rejected changes. Testing instructions Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Download the synthetic fixture from the public repository at examples/webmcp-demo.csv . Import it manually in Source. No login is required. Call the capabilities, workspace-state, and workflow-guide tools. Inspect the dataset and data profile through Prepare. Add a Formula column named weight_gap_kg with [chargeable_weight_kg] - [actual_weight_kg] . In Compose, validate and create an Aggregate grouped by service , with count and average actual-weight metrics. Inspect the operation schema, preview, and quality. Demonstrate stale-revision rejection, idempotent replay, cancellation, or the shared activity ledger. Do not confirm deletion or reset. Full walkthrough: https://github.com/jacobcalvyn/TabulaFlow/blob/main/docs/DEMO.md Challenges and accomplishments The hardest work was making a complex data mutation surface agent-safe without duplicating application logic. We hardened strict schema discovery, protected recipe round-trips, privacy-aware previews, atomic tool publication, asynchronous cancellation, response pagination, and local-file recovery boundaries. The result passed live WebMCP regression coverage across Prepare and all eight Compose operation types, alongside repository tests and production build checks. Built during the challenge TabulaFlow's WebMCP integration, safety contracts, Formula workflow, Compose parity, agent upload consent, qualitative-coding boundary, and demo materials were implemented and hardened during the challenge period. Dated evidence is available in docs/HACKATHON.md and the Git history. Known limitations Browser imports are capped at 50 MB, 100,000 rows, and 1,000 stored columns. Local file permissions may require explicit re-linking. Formula columns intentionally exclude window, rank, LOD, regex, and nondeterministic current-time functions. WebMCP requires a compatible browser implementation. title: Revelus.ai | WebMCP Patient Navigation
pitch: Revelus.ai uses WebMCP to turn dermatology questions into grounded answers, the right appointment path, and live availability, making care easier to navigate without exposing private information.
about_excerpt: Revelus.ai uses WebMCP to turn dermatology questions into grounded answers, the right appointment path, and live availability, making care easier to navigate without exposing private information. Like Comment Story Updates Ask Revelus turns everyday dermatology questions into grounded answers, validated next steps, and live scheduling options. Revelus.ai turns patient questions into grounded answers, validated visit paths, and live scheduling options. One shared WebMCP layer connects plain-language questions to reviewed content, typed routing, and secure scheduling. One question can require two visits. Revelus.ai applies practice rules to return the right next step for each concern. Live provider times come from current scheduling inventory, while patients remain in control of the final booking. Public guidance stays separate from clinical care, private records, identifying data, and automated booking. Three native WebMCP tools share one action layer for search, visit routing, and current availability. Revelus.ai connects reviewed practice information, routing rules, and live availability through a focused WebMCP layer. A live ChatGPT test uses Revelus.ai to distinguish visit paths, retrieve current availability, and preserve patient control. Pre-deployment testing checks answer quality, routing logic, provider relationships, patient language, and safety boundaries. Inspiration Revelus Dermatology has been serving patients in Austin since 2014. Over that time, we have built a large patient-facing website with information about medical conditions, cosmetic treatments, providers, pricing, insurance, and scheduling. The challenge is that having the information available does not always make it easy to use. Patients rarely arrive knowing the exact medical term, provider, or appointment type they need. They ask questions like: "My hair is thinning. Who should I see?" "Can I get a skin cancer screening and talk about another concern at the same visit?" "Do you treat rosacea?" "Who performs Mohs surgery?" "What appointments are available next week?" A traditional website can contain the answers to all of those questions while still requiring the patient to search multiple pages, interpret practice-specific scheduling rules, and choose from a long list of appointment types. We built Revelus.ai to explore a different model. WebMCP is a strong fit because the problem is not a lack of information, but giving agents structured access to trusted practice content, scheduling rules, and live availability without requiring them to interpret the website like a human. The goal was not to build another healthcare chatbot. It was to make an existing healthcare website more useful to both patients and AI agents while keeping the practice itself as the source of truth. What we built Revelus.ai uses WebMCP to help an agent move from a natural-language dermatology question to a useful next step. The experience can: Search published Revelus Dermatology content about conditions, treatments, providers, pricing, insurance, and practice information Return answers grounded in that published content Translate everyday patient language into the appropriate appointment path Recognize when two concerns require two different appointments Identify provider-specific scheduling options Retrieve real-time appointment availability from our live scheduling system Provide the appropriate booking path while leaving the final scheduling decision with the patient Recognize requests that would require diagnostic inference and redirect them toward clinician evaluation rather than assigning a condition Reject requests for private medical information that should not be handled through a public website The live availability is not a demonstration dataset. It reflects actual appointment inventory from our scheduling system and can change as appointments are booked or released. The sample questions on the live Revelus.ai experience are examples, not its full coverage. The live deployment uses a broader private Revelus corpus. For reproducibility without publishing proprietary practice data, the public challenge repository includes a deliberately limited ten-query synthetic fixture that exercises the same WebMCP architecture. The application registers three native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : revelus.search_information Searches published Revelus Dermatology information and returns the complete source-backed page card, including answer evidence, FAQs, relevant providers, and response guidance. revelus.resolve_visit_path Applies Revelus-specific, non-diagnostic scheduling logic to determine an appropriate appointment path using structured, non-identifying inputs. revelus.get_availability Reads current provider and appointment-time availability for a resolved path and returns the appropriate booking options. Search now returns the complete answer card in a single response, so a separate native answer tool is no longer necessary. The underlying shared action layer still supports answer behavior for the visible interface, but the final WebMCP implementation exposes three focused native tools. The system can therefore move through a sequence such as: Patient question → source-grounded information → appointment routing → live availability → patient-controlled booking We intentionally do not allow the tools to reserve or finalize an appointment. The patient leaves the WebMCP experience and completes that step through our existing secure scheduling workflow. We developed and tested the WebMCP experience in Google Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled and the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser , verifying that an AI agent could discover the tools, call them, combine their results, and work through questions that were not specifically scripted for the demo. What was built during the challenge Revelus Dermatology, our primary website, published practice content, appointment offerings, and scheduling systems all predate the WebMCP Challenge. Ask Revelus / Revelus.ai and the WebMCP implementation were built during the challenge period. The new work includes: The standalone Revelus.ai agent-facing experience Three page-local WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext The structured content-matching and grounded-answer layers The typed, non-diagnostic visit-path resolver Multi-visit and practice-specific appointment routing The read-only live availability adapter and patient-controlled scheduling handoff Privacy safeguards that reject patient-record and identifying-data requests before retrieval A shared action layer used by both the visible interface and WebMCP tool calls The reproducible public synthetic corpus, schemas, tests, and deployment configuration The public competition repository documents the challenge-period implementation and commit history while intentionally keeping Revelus Dermatology's proprietary production corpus private. Challenges we faced The most difficult part of the project was not exposing information. It was deciding how an agent should safely use that information in a real healthcare environment. Patient language is messy Patients do not necessarily use the terminology found on a medical website. They use misspellings, symptoms, partial descriptions, and conversational questions. The system needed to understand requests such as "rosecea," "my face gets really red and hot," or "my hair is thinning" without pretending that it had diagnosed the patient. Our approach was to surface relevant published information and recommend an appropriate evaluation rather than turning the matching system into a diagnostic tool. Scheduling logic is more complex than search A strong information match does not always equal the correct appointment. Some concerns require a dedicated visit. Some medical and cosmetic requests need different scheduling paths. Returning patients may have different options than new patients. Provider availability also depends on the appointment reason. This required us to separate finding relevant information from resolving the correct visit path . Real-time availability introduced operational complexity Once we connected the system to live appointment availability, the project became more than a content search experience. Availability changes continuously, and broad questions can require checking multiple providers or appointment routes. We had to work through both accuracy and performance issues so the system could return useful live results without treating cached or example data as current availability. Healthcare requires clear privacy and clinical boundaries A public agent experience should not become an alternate path into a patient's medical record or a substitute for clinical judgment. Revelus.ai does not retrieve biopsy results, pathology reports, private messages, medical records, or other patient-specific clinical information.
